docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 2 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Upaniṣad Dīpikā: The Upaniṣads. It introduces the Upaniṣads — the speculative texts that close the Vedic corpus — and the traditions of thought that grew from them.

The first part of the book (Chapters 1–4) introduces the corpus and the evidence for its relative chronology, and then reads the principal Upaniṣads one by one, from the Īśā to the Śvetāśvatara, with the Kauṣītaki and the Maitrī, with the ritual meditations that fill much of the oldest texts, and with the kings, brahmins and patrons among whom they were first taught. Chapters 5, 6 and 10 treat the great sayings (mahāvākyas), the central doctrines of Brahman, Ātman, creation, māyā, karma and liberation (with the Buddhist and Jain critiques of the Upaniṣadic self), and the analysis of waking, dream, deep sleep and the “fourth” state. Chapters 7–9 survey the later Yoga, Sannyāsa, sectarian and general Vedāntic Upaniṣads. Chapter 11 begins with the Brahmasūtra and the Vedānta before Śaṅkara, introduces the great commentators — Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Madhva and others — and follows the Upaniṣads into Tamil, where the Śrīvaiṣṇavas called Nammāḻvār’s hymns a “Tamil Upaniṣad” and the Śaiva Siddhānta read the Upaniṣads through the Āgamas, and into the regional languages. Chapter 12 treats the modern reception of the Upaniṣads in India and the world, beginning with their passage to Europe through Persian and Latin.

Three principles have guided this edition. First, dates: the mainstream academic dating is given first (for example, c. 7th–6th century BCE for the oldest prose Upaniṣads), and traditional dates are labelled as such; the reader is told plainly that most of the 108 Upaniṣads of the Muktikā list, including the Yoga Upaniṣads, are medieval or early modern. Second, the texts and their interpreters are kept apart: much that is popularly presented as “the teaching of the Upaniṣads” is in fact the systematisation of a later school, usually Advaita Vedānta, and the theistic schools read the same texts differently. Third, honesty about claims and contexts: Sanskrit quotations have been checked and corrected or removed, claims that the Upaniṣads anticipated modern science have been withdrawn, and the social limits of the tradition — including the restriction of Vedic learning by caste and gender — are stated rather than passed over.

The Upaniṣads need no exaggeration. Read carefully, they remain among the most searching enquiries ever made into the self, reality and freedom. This volume is offered as a lamp (dīpikā) for that reading. A note on texts and references follows; a glossary and a chronology close the volume.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput, Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: A Note on Texts and References
docs.text:
Numbering. The principal Upaniṣads are cited by their traditional divisions: the Bṛhadāraṇyaka by chapter, section and paragraph in the Kāṇva recension commented on by Śaṅkara; the Chāndogya by prapāṭhaka, khaṇḍa and paragraph; the Kaṭha by adhyāya, vallī and verse (so “Kaṭha 1.2.20” is the twentieth verse of the second vallī; editions that number the six vallīs consecutively call it 2.20); the Muṇḍaka by muṇḍaka, khaṇḍa and verse; the Aitareya by chapter, section and paragraph (“3.1.3”, which some editions number 3.3); the Taittirīya by vallī and anuvāka; the Māṇḍūkya by mantra; and the Īśā, Kena, Praśna and Śvetāśvatara by chapter and verse. Numbering differs slightly between editions, and readers comparing a translation should allow for this.

Transliteration and translation. Sanskrit is given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST). Translations of Sanskrit passages are renderings meant to convey the sense of the original; for exact wording and for the readings of critical editions, readers should consult the editions and translations listed in the Select Bibliography, above all Olivelle’s The Early Upaniṣads (Olivelle 1998). See also Limaye and Vadekar’s edition (Limaye and Vadekar 1958) and, for Śaṅkara’s commentaries, Gambhirananda’s translation (Gambhirananda 1957).

Dates. Dates are given as the mainstream academic range first, with traditional dates labelled as traditional. A chronology is given at the end of the volume, after the glossary.

Interpretations. Much that is popularly called “the teaching of the Upaniṣads” is the reading of a later school. Where a statement reflects the interpretation of Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita Vedānta rather than the wording of the texts themselves, this is said.

Cross-references. Related subjects are treated more fully in other volumes of this series: the Vedic corpus in Volume 1 (Veda Prakāśa), the philosophical schools, including Vedānta, in Volume 3 (Darśana Darpaṇa), and yoga, including Haṭha Yoga, Kuṇḍalinī and prāṇāyāma, in Volume 5 (Yoga Taraṅgiṇī).

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction — What are the Upaniṣads?
1.1 The Word Upaniṣad: Etymology and Meaning
docs.text:
How the word Upaniṣad was understood tells us a good deal about how the texts were used. Sanskrit etymologies, traditional and modern, answer different questions, and both kinds are worth knowing.

upa-ni-ṣad upa = near, ni = down (with devotion), ṣad = to sit Literal meaning: “To sit down near” (the teacher for receiving esoteric instruction)

The root ṣad (to sit) with the prefixes upa (near) and ni (down) yields the familiar modern gloss: sitting down near the teacher to receive secret instruction. This derivation, popularised by nineteenth-century Indologists such as Max Müller and Deussen, evokes the guru-śiṣya paramparā — the disciple approaching the teacher with humility to receive teaching through personal transmission.

Historical philology suggests a different picture. In the Brāhmaṇas and the oldest Upaniṣads the word upaniṣad often means a hidden “connection” or “equivalence” between ritual, cosmic and bodily realities, and hence the secret teaching that discloses such connections; this is the sense emphasised by Louis Renou and by Patrick Olivelle in the introduction to his translation (Olivelle 1998). The traditional commentators, for their part, did not favour “sitting near”. Śaṅkara, introducing his commentaries on the Kaṭha and Taittirīya, derives the word from the root sad (listed by the grammarians as ṣad) in its three senses of “loosening/destroying” (viśaraṇa), “going/reaching” (gati) and “wearing down” (avasādana). Two lines of explanation follow from these. On the first, the root means “to destroy” or “to loosen”, and the Upaniṣad is the knowledge that destroys ignorance (avidyā) and the bondage of saṃsāra. On the second, the root means “to reach”, and the Upaniṣad is the knowledge that leads the seeker to Brahman.

Key Insight

The philological and the traditional explanations answer different questions. The first asks what the word meant when the texts were composed (a secret connection or teaching); the second asks what the knowledge does for the one who receives it (it loosens ignorance and leads to Brahman). Both agree that the Upaniṣads were regarded as esoteric teachings, transmitted to qualified students rather than recited publicly.

docs.title: 1.2 The Upaniṣads within the Vedic Corpus
docs.text:
The place of the Upaniṣads in Vedic literature is usually explained through the traditional fourfold division of each Veda. Each of the four Vedas — Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda — is traditionally divided into four kinds of text, which later tradition also matched with stages of life (Figure 1.1).

Figure 1.1. The Fourfold Structure of Each Veda

In the later Vedāntic reading, the progression from Saṃhitā to Upaniṣad mirrors a movement from the external world of ritual and action (karma-kāṇḍa) to the interior world of knowledge and liberation (jñāna-kāṇḍa). The fourfold scheme is, however, an idealisation. The boundaries between the genres are fluid: the Bṛhadāraṇyaka is the final part of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and is itself called an Āraṇyaka; the Aitareya and Kauṣītaki Upaniṣads are sections of Āraṇyakas; and the Chāndogya forms the later part of a Brāhmaṇa of the Sāmaveda. Much of the content of the oldest Upaniṣads is itself ritual speculation, as Section 4.3 shows. The correlation with the four life-stages (āśramas) given in Table 1.1 is a traditional schematisation, not a description of how the texts were actually used.

Table 1.1. The Fourfold Division of the Vedas and Their Characteristics Section Content Purpose Life Stage Saṃhitā Mantras, Hymns Praise and invocation of deities Brahmacarya Brāhmaṇa Ritualistic prose Explanation of sacrificial rites Gṛhastha Āraṇyaka Mystical texts Symbolic, internalised rituals Vānaprastha Upaniṣad Philosophical Knowledge of Brahman and liberation Sannyāsa

docs.title: 1.3 The Upaniṣads as Vedānta
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads are also called Vedānta (Veda + anta), the “end of the Veda”. The word has three senses. It names their textual position, since they come at the end of the Vedic texts of their schools. In the Vedāntic schools it also names their standing as the culmination of the Veda, the part that the earlier ritual portions are held to serve. And it names the goal (anta) of the Veda, the knowledge of Brahman (brahma-vidyā). The second and third senses are claims of the later tradition; the first is a description that every reader can check. The Gītā states the theistic form of the third sense:

vedaiś ca sarvair aham eva vedyaḥ Translation: “By all the Vedas, it is I alone who am to be known.” — Bhagavad Gītā 15.15

From the early centuries CE the Upaniṣads were systematised in the Brahmasūtra and read together with it and the Gītā as the “triple foundation” (prasthānatraya) of the Vedānta schools; both developments are described in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 1.4 How Many Upaniṣads Exist?
docs.text:
The Muktikā Upaniṣad — a late text, probably of the medieval period, that gives a canonical list — enumerates 108 Upaniṣads, distributed by Veda as follows: 10 of the Ṛgveda, 19 of the Śukla Yajurveda, 32 of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, 16 of the Sāmaveda and 31 of the Atharvaveda. The number 108 is a conventional sacred number; it is not a historical count. The actual number of texts bearing the title “Upaniṣad” is considerably larger: catalogues list more than two hundred, many of them late compositions, and some (such as the Allopaniṣad) composed as late as the Mughal period.

Modern scholars group the 108 Muktikā Upaniṣads by theme into principal (mukhya), general Vedāntic (sāmānya-vedānta), renunciation (sannyāsa), yoga, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Śākta texts. The exact allocation of individual texts to these groups differs between editions, so Figure 1.2 gives the categories without fixed counts except for the ten principal Upaniṣads named in the Muktikā itself. The principal Upaniṣads are read in Chapters 2–4, the Yoga, Sannyāsa and sectarian groups in Chapters 7–9, and the general Vedāntic group in Section 9.7.

Figure 1.2. Thematic groups of the 108 Upaniṣads of the Muktikā canon (modern classification)

docs.title: 1.5 The Vedic Affiliation of Major Upaniṣads
docs.text:
Each Upaniṣad is traditionally affiliated with one of the four Vedas. This affiliation is significant because it determines the paramparā (lineage of transmission) through which the teaching was preserved and also influences the recitation style and ritual context of the text (Table 1.2).

Table 1.2. Vedic Affiliation of the Principal Upaniṣads Veda Branch (Śākhā) Upaniṣad(s) Ṛgveda Śākala (Aitareya Āraṇyaka) Aitareya Ṛgveda Bāṣkala / Śāṅkhāyana (Kauṣītaki Āraṇyaka) Kauṣītaki Śukla Yajurveda Vājasaneyi (Kāṇva and Mādhyandina) Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Īśā Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Taittirīya Taittirīya Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Uncertain (named after the teacher Śvetāśvatara; often grouped with the Taittirīya by tradition) Śvetāśvatara Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Kaṭha (Kaṭhaka) Kaṭha Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Maitrāyaṇīya Maitrī (Maitrāyaṇīya) Sāmaveda Jaiminīya (Talavakāra) Kena Sāmaveda Kauthuma–Rāṇāyanīya Chāndogya Atharvaveda Śaunaka (by tradition) Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya Atharvaveda Pippalāda Praśna

docs.title: 1.6 The Mukhya (Principal) Upaniṣads
docs.text:
Among the 108 Upaniṣads, a smaller group has long been treated as pre-eminent. These are the mukhya (principal) Upaniṣads — those upon which the great Ācāryas, beginning with Śaṅkara, wrote their commentaries (bhāṣyas). The standard list comprises ten Upaniṣads, those on which commentaries generally accepted as Śaṅkara’s survive. Many lists add the Śvetāśvatara (a commentary on it is ascribed to Śaṅkara, but its authenticity is doubted), giving eleven. Robert Ernest Hume’s influential Thirteen Principal Upaniṣads (Hume 1921) adds the Kauṣītaki and the Maitrī to these eleven, giving thirteen (Table 1.3).

Table 1.3. The Ten Principal (Mukhya) Upaniṣads No. Upaniṣad Veda Central Theme 1 Īśā Śukla Yajurveda The Lord pervading all; renunciation with enjoyment 2 Kena Sāmaveda The power behind the senses; Brahman as the Unknown 3 Kaṭha Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Death and immortality; the Ātman beyond death 4 Praśna Atharvaveda Six questions on cosmology, Prāṇa, and meditation 5 Muṇḍaka Atharvaveda Higher and lower knowledge; Brahman as target 6 Māṇḍūkya Atharvaveda Oṃ and the four states of consciousness 7 Taittirīya Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Five sheaths (kośas); Brahman as bliss 8 Aitareya Ṛgveda Creation; the Self as consciousness 9 Chāndogya Sāmaveda Tat tvam asi; Sad-vidyā; diverse meditations 10 Bṛhadāraṇyaka Śukla Yajurveda The most extensive; Aham Brahmāsmi; Yājñavalkya’s teachings

The ten are listed in a verse of the Muktikā Upaniṣad (1.30), widely used as a mnemonic:

īśa-kena-kaṭha-praśna-muṇḍa-māṇḍūkya-tittiriḥ aitareyaṃ ca chāndogyaṃ bṛhadāraṇyakaṃ tathā Translation: “Īśā, Kena, Kaṭha, Praśna, Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya, Taittirīya, Aitareya, Chāndogya and likewise the Bṛhadāraṇyaka.”

docs.title: 1.7 The Form and Style of the Upaniṣads
docs.text: The Upaniṣads use many literary forms, and they lack the systematic arrangement of the later sūtra literature. The most characteristic form is the dialogue, between teacher and pupil or between rival sages: the Kaṭha is framed as a conversation between the boy Naciketas and Yama, the god of death, and the Praśna as six questions put by six seekers to the sage Pippalāda. The Chāndogya teaches through illustrative stories and analogies, as in Uddālaka Āruṇi’s instruction of his son Śvetaketu. The Īśā opens with a series of compressed verses whose sense the commentators still dispute. The Māṇḍūkya, the shortest of the principal Upaniṣads at twelve short prose sections, sets out a schematic analysis of the states of consciousness. The Śvetāśvatara is devotional verse addressed to a personal God. Chapter 2 begins the reading of these texts one by one.

docs.title: 1.8 The Central Concerns of the Upaniṣads
docs.text: Later Vedānta found six questions running through the Upaniṣads. What is the ultimate nature of reality (the doctrine of Brahman)? What is the self (the doctrine of Ātman)? How are the two related (the subject of the mahāvākyas)? Why does the self appear to be bound (in Advaita, the doctrine of māyā and avidyā)? How can it be freed (mokṣa)? And what is the self’s condition beyond waking, dream and sleep (the “fourth”, turīya)? The texts do not ask these questions in this order, and they give more than one answer to each. The questions nevertheless give a useful map of the doctrinal chapters of this book: the great sayings in Chapter 5, the doctrines of Brahman, Ātman, māyā, karma and liberation in Chapter 6, and the states of consciousness in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 1.9 The Oral Tradition and Textual Transmission
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads, like all Vedic literature, were originally transmitted orally. The guru-śiṣya paramparā (teacher-student lineage) carried these teachings across many centuries before they were committed to writing. The Upaniṣadic teaching was considered secret and was imparted only to students judged fit to receive it (adhikārīs); the qualifications later demanded of such a student are discussed in Section 1.15.

The preservation of the Vedic corpus by oral means is one of the best-documented achievements of cultural memory. The Vedic schools developed several redundant methods of recitation designed to ensure textual fidelity; the most elaborate of these “modified” recitations (vikṛti-pāṭha) were applied chiefly to the Saṃhitās, while the Upaniṣads were usually learned in continuous recitation (Table 1.4).

Table 1.4. Methods of Vedic Textual Preservation Recitation Method Sanskrit Name Description Continuous recitation Saṃhitā-pāṭha Words recited in their natural, continuous form with sandhi rules applied Separated recitation Pada-pāṭha Each word separated and pronounced individually, revealing the base forms Paired recitation Krama-pāṭha Words recited in overlapping pairs: 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, etc. Woven recitation Jaṭā-pāṭha Words interwoven: 1-2, 2-1, 1-2; 2-3, 3-2, 2-3; etc. Dense recitation Ghana-pāṭha The most complex pattern, combining forward and reverse sequences of three words

The śākhā (branch or recension) system meant that each Vedic school maintained its own version of its texts. This produced multiple independent lines of transmission, but also genuine textual variation: the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, for example, survives in a Kāṇva and a Mādhyandina recension that differ in wording and in the order of some passages, and Śaṅkara commented on the Kāṇva text. Variant readings are therefore a normal subject of Upaniṣadic philology, even though the core texts are stable.

docs.title: 1.10 The Śānti Mantras: Invocatory Prayers of the Upaniṣads
docs.text:
Each Upaniṣad traditionally begins with a Śānti Mantra — a peace invocation — that is chanted by both teacher and student before the commencement of study. The mantras are shared by the Upaniṣads of each Veda (Table 1.5). In the traditional explanation they invoke peace from the three sources of disturbance: ādhibhautika (from external beings), ādhidaivika (from supernatural forces), and ādhyātmika (from within oneself) — hence the threefold repetition of Oṃ Śāntiḥ.

Table 1.5. Principal Śānti Mantras and Their Associated Upaniṣads Śānti Mantra (Opening Words) Veda Associated Upaniṣads āpyāyantu mamāṅgāni… Sāmaveda Kena, Chāndogya bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ śṛṇuyāma devāḥ… Atharvaveda Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya, Praśna vāṅ me manasi pratiṣṭhitā… Ṛgveda Aitareya saha nāvavatu… Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Kaṭha, Taittirīya, Śvetāśvatara pūrṇamadaḥ pūrṇam idaṃ… Śukla Yajurveda Īśā, Bṛhadāraṇyaka

The best known of these is the Pūrṇamadaḥ mantra of the Śukla Yajurveda:

oṃ pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idaṃ pūrṇāt pūrṇam udacyate pūrṇasya pūrṇam ādāya pūrṇam evāvaśiṣyate Translation: “That (Brahman) is full; this (world) is full. From fullness, fullness arises. When fullness is taken from fullness, fullness alone remains.” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka 5.1.1 (Śānti Mantra of the Īśā and Bṛhadāraṇyaka)

This mantra states, in four lines, the Upaniṣadic idea of the plenitude of Brahman: Brahman is not diminished by the world that comes forth from it. Modern readers often compare this to the arithmetic of infinity, in which subtracting from an infinite quantity leaves it infinite; the comparison is a helpful modern analogy, not a claim about what the composers knew of mathematics.

docs.title: 1.11 The Dating and Historical Context of the Upaniṣads
docs.text:
The chronological dating of the Upaniṣads is one of the most debated issues in Indological scholarship. The Upaniṣads do not bear dates, and the oral tradition through which they were transmitted for centuries makes external dating exceptionally difficult. Nevertheless, scholars have employed a variety of methods — linguistic analysis, cross-references with datable historical events, comparison with Buddhist and Jaina texts, and internal evidence — to arrive at approximate chronological ranges (Table 1.6).

Table 1.6. Approximate Chronological Classification of the Upaniṣads Period Approximate Date Upaniṣads Oldest prose (pre-Buddhist) c. 7th–6th c. BCE Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya Early prose c. 6th–5th c. BCE Taittirīya, Aitareya, Kauṣītaki Verse Upaniṣads last centuries BCE Kena, Kaṭha, Īśā, Śvetāśvatara, Muṇḍaka Later prose c. turn of the Common Era Praśna, Māṇḍūkya; Maitrī (possibly later) Minor and sectarian early centuries CE to c. 1700 CE Sannyāsa, Yoga, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Śākta Upaniṣads (most medieval or later; see Chapters 7–9)

The Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya, generally acknowledged as the oldest, display linguistic features characteristic of late Vedic prose and contain references to social and political institutions that align with the pre-Buddhist period. The Kaṭha and Muṇḍaka, by contrast, exhibit a more polished metrical style and a greater degree of philosophical systematisation, suggesting a somewhat later date. The Māṇḍūkya, with its terse, aphoristic prose and highly abstract analysis of consciousness, is generally assigned to the latest stratum of the principal Upaniṣads.

Scholarly Note

The dates given above are approximate and follow the relative chronology set out by Patrick Olivelle (Olivelle 1998); absolute dates for this period are uncertain by a century or more. The Indian tradition itself does not regard the Upaniṣads as historical products of particular eras but as apauṛuṣeya — not of human authorship — and therefore timeless (anādi). This theological claim need not conflict with historical scholarship; it points to the tradition’s conviction that the truths revealed in the Upaniṣads are eternal, even if the verbal formulations through which they were expressed occurred at particular historical moments.

docs.title: 1.12 The Relative Chronology of the Principal Upaniṣads
docs.text: Table 1.6 is best read as a sequence rather than as a set of dates. No principal Upaniṣad names a datable king, mentions a datable event or survives in an early dated manuscript. The absolute dates are obtained by fitting the whole sequence between the later Vedic ritual literature, which comes before it, and the early Buddhist and grammatical literature, which knows something of the same world. The order within the sequence is the more secure part of the scholarship. It rests on several independent kinds of evidence, and its strength lies in the fact that they agree.

docs.title: 1.12.1 From Deussen’s Four Groups to Olivelle’s Ordering
docs.text:
The modern ordering goes back to Paul Deussen (Deussen 1897, 1906), who sorted the older Upaniṣads into four groups. The first was the ancient prose Upaniṣads (Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya, Taittirīya, Aitareya, Kauṣītaki and Kena). The second was the verse Upaniṣads (Kaṭha, Īśā, Śvetāśvatara, Muṇḍaka and the Mahānārāyaṇa). The third was the later prose Upaniṣads (Praśna, Maitrī and Māṇḍūkya). The fourth was the large body of Atharvavedic Upaniṣads. Deussen’s main criterion was form: prose of the Brāhmaṇa type first, then verse close to the epic, then a new, more technical prose.

Patrick Olivelle keeps the outline of this scheme but refines it in four ways (Olivelle 1998):

  • He separates the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya, the two oldest, from a slightly later prose layer formed by the Taittirīya, Aitareya and Kauṣītaki.

  • He moves the Kena, whose first two sections are in verse and whose last two are in prose, to the head of the verse group as its oldest member, followed probably by the Kaṭha, Īśā, Śvetāśvatara and Muṇḍaka.

  • He leaves the Maitrī and the Mahānārāyaṇa out of his collection of the early Upaniṣads altogether.

  • He attaches cautious absolute dates: the seventh to sixth centuries BCE, with a margin of a century or so either way, for the two oldest texts, which he regards as pre-Buddhist; the sixth to fifth centuries for the next prose layer; the last few centuries BCE for the verse Upaniṣads; and about the turn of the Common Era for the Praśna and Māṇḍūkya.

Olivelle stresses that the absolute dates are tentative. Signe Cohen’s study of the older Upaniṣads re-examines the sequence text by text, using among other things the way each text presents the authority of its own teaching (Cohen 2008). The relative order, however, has proved stable, because each of the following lines of evidence points the same way.

docs.title: 1.12.2 Position in the Vedic Corpus
docs.text:
The oldest prose Upaniṣads are not free-standing books. Each is the final part of a larger text belonging to a particular Vedic school, and each continues that text’s style of argument by correspondences (Section 1.1):

  • The Bṛhadāraṇyaka closes the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda.

  • The Chāndogya forms the last eight of the ten chapters of the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa of the Sāmaveda.

  • The Aitareya is a section of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (2.4–6).

  • The Taittirīya forms books 7–9 of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka.

  • The Kauṣītaki forms chapters 3–6 of the Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka (Section 4.7.1).

  • The Kena is a short section of the Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa.

Texts embedded in this way were composed and handed down by the schools whose ritual corpus they complete. They stand at the end of a long development of Brāhmaṇa prose, which is why their language and their habits of thought are continuous with it.

The verse Upaniṣads, by contrast, are independent compositions. They are attached to a school either by name, as the Kaṭha is to the Kaṭha branch of the Black Yajurveda, or only by later convention, as the Muṇḍaka, Praśna and Māṇḍūkya are to the Atharvaveda, a Veda that had no older Upaniṣad of its own. The Īśā is a special case. It is the fortieth chapter of the Vājasaneyī Saṃhitā (Section 2.1), but its verse form and its synthesis of knowledge and action place it with the verse Upaniṣads. Its position at the end of a Saṃhitā shows how the Vājasaneyins arranged their canon; it does not make the Īśā as old as the hymns before it.

The Kaṭha shows the same relation from the inside. Its frame story of Naciketas and Death is already told in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (3.11.8), where the boy’s boons concern the building of the Naciketa fire-altar. The Upaniṣad keeps the fire as its second boon (Kaṭha 1.1.19) and turns the third into the question whether a man exists after death (1.1.20). This is a philosophical reworking of an older ritual narrative, and it is one of the clearest signs that the Kaṭha comes later than the Brāhmaṇa literature.

docs.title: 1.12.3 Language, Form and Shared Verses
docs.text:
The linguistic evidence is set out in the next section (Section 1.13). The prose of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya is late Vedic. The verse of the Kaṭha and Śvetāśvatara is close to the language of the epic, and two verses of the Kaṭha (1.2.18–19) recur with small changes in the Bhagavadgītā (2.19–20). The prose Upaniṣads already quote verses as known material. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka introduces 4.4.7 with “on this there is the following verse”, and the same verse stands in the Kaṭha (2.3.14).

The verse Upaniṣads draw on a common stock (Table 1.7). The direction of borrowing cannot always be decided. The overlap nevertheless shows that the verse Upaniṣads belong close together in time and milieu. The Śvetāśvatara, which shares verses with the Kaṭha, the Muṇḍaka, the Ṛgveda and the Vājasaneyī Saṃhitā, has the character of a compilation standing late in the group.

Table 1.7. Some Verses Shared by the Principal Upaniṣads and Related Texts Opening words Occurrences Remark yadā sarve pramucyante kāmā ye ’sya hṛdi śritāḥ Bṛhad. 4.4.7; Kaṭha 2.3.14 Quoted in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka as an existing verse (śloka) dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā ṚV 1.164.20; Muṇḍ. 3.1.1; Śvet. 4.6 A Ṛgvedic riddle-verse read as an image of the two selves nāyam ātmā pravacanena labhyaḥ Kaṭha 1.2.23; Muṇḍ. 3.2.3 The Self is gained by the one whom it chooses na tatra sūryo bhāti Kaṭha 2.2.15; Muṇḍ. 2.2.10; Śvet. 6.14 Identical in all three aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān Kaṭha 1.2.20; Śvet. 3.20 Second half differs vedāham etaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam Śvet. 3.8; Vājasaneyī Saṃhitā 31.18 From the later continuation of the Puruṣa hymn na jāyate mriyate vā Kaṭha 1.2.18; BG 2.20 Close parallel; Kaṭha 1.2.19 likewise parallels BG 2.19

docs.title: 1.12.4 Doctrine, Milieu and the Buddhist Horizon
docs.text:
The verse and later prose Upaniṣads use a technical vocabulary that the oldest texts lack:

  • The Kaṭha arranges the senses, their objects, the mind, the intellect, the “great self”, the unmanifest and the Person in an ascending hierarchy (1.3.10–11), close to the later Sāṅkhya list, and it defines yoga as the steady holding of the senses (2.3.11).

  • The Śvetāśvatara names “Sāṅkhya and Yoga” as the means of knowing the first cause (6.13), and it worships the one God as Rudra.

  • The Muṇḍaka calls the sacrifices “unsteady boats” (1.2.7) and ranks all Vedic learning as the lower knowledge (Section 3.1).

  • The Māṇḍūkya reduces the analysis of waking, dream and sleep to a fixed scheme of four quarters.

Systematisation of this kind presupposes the looser explorations of the older prose.

The absolute dates hang on the relation to Buddhism. If the Buddha lived about 480–400 BCE (the short chronology adopted in this series), then the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya, which show no awareness of Buddhists or Jainas, are most naturally placed earlier. The Pali canon, for its part, knows the Vedic schools by name. The Tevijja Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 13) lists Adhvaryu, Taittirīya, Chandoga and Bahvṛca brahmins, each claiming a path to union with Brahmā. The canon also discusses positions that resemble Upaniṣadic teachings (Section 6.10).

Geography points the same way. The older Upaniṣads move between the Kuru-Pañcāla country and the eastern kingdoms of Kāśī and Videha (Section 4.5), not yet the Magadhan world of the Buddhist texts. Michael Witzel’s study of the Vedic schools traces this eastward movement of Vedic culture and of its centres of patronage (Witzel 1997).

The consensus has been challenged. Johannes Bronkhorst has argued that karma and rebirth entered Brahmanical thought from the culture of “Greater Magadha” further east. On his view, the passages of the oldest Upaniṣads that teach these doctrines need not be older than the Buddha (Bronkhorst 2007, 2011).

Dating is complicated further by the fact that the oldest Upaniṣads are composite. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka’s three sections each end in a list of teachers (vaṃśa, 2.6, 4.6 and 6.5), which suggests that they were once transmitted separately. The Maitreyī dialogue appears in it twice (2.4 and 4.5), and the Chāndogya moves from opening chapters devoted largely to the chants of the Sāmaveda (1–2) to the sustained philosophical teaching of its last three (6–8). To date such a text is to date its final redaction; a particular passage may be older or younger than the whole. The defensible conclusion is therefore modest but firm. The order Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya; then Taittirīya, Aitareya and Kauṣītaki; then the verse Upaniṣads; then the Praśna and Māṇḍūkya is secure in outline. The century attached to each stage is an informed estimate.

docs.title: 1.13 The Language and Linguistic Character of the Upaniṣads
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads occupy a distinctive position in the history of the Sanskrit language. They span a period of linguistic evolution from late Vedic Sanskrit (in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya) through a transitional phase to a form approaching classical Sanskrit (in the Kaṭha and Śvetāśvatara). This linguistic diversity is itself evidence of the long period over which the Upaniṣadic corpus developed (Table 1.8).

Table 1.8. Linguistic Features of the Upaniṣads Across Periods Feature Early Upaniṣads (Bṛhad., Chānd.) Later Upaniṣads (Kaṭha, Śvet.) Grammar Vedic forms; subjunctive mood; older verbal endings Closer to Pāṇinian classical norms Vocabulary Archaic Vedic terms; ritualistic vocabulary More philosophical technical terms Style Long prose passages; embedded dialogues Polished metrical verse; compact expression Sentence structure Paratactic; loose coordination More hypotactic; subordinate clauses Metre Prose dominant; occasional anuṣṭubh verses Triṣṭubh, anuṣṭubh, jagatī metres

The older prose Upaniṣads, particularly the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, preserve archaic grammatical forms that have largely disappeared in later Sanskrit. These include the subjunctive mood (leṭ-lakāra), the injunctive, and certain pronominal forms no longer current in classical Sanskrit. The later verse Upaniṣads, by contrast, employ the metrical patterns and polished diction of early classical Sanskrit poetry. The Kaṭha’s verse on the Self “subtler than the subtle, greater than the great” (aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān, 1.2.20, quoted in full in Section 2.3) is a typical example: its triṣṭubh metre, with eleven syllables to the line, gives the teaching a measured, solemn cadence.

docs.title: 1.14 The Upaniṣads and the Śramaṇa Traditions
docs.text:
The relationship between the Upaniṣads and the Śramaṇa traditions — particularly Buddhism and Jainism — has been much discussed. The Śramaṇa movements arose in the same intellectual world that produced the middle and late Upaniṣads, and the traditions overlap at several points (Table 1.9).

The doctrines of karma (action and its consequences), saṃsāra (the cycle of rebirth) and liberation (mokṣa, nirvāṇa) appear in both the Upaniṣads and the Śramaṇa traditions. Which side gave them to the other is debated (Section 1.12); it is likely that they developed in a shared milieu (Samuel 2008; Bronkhorst 2007). The divergences are as important. The Upaniṣads affirm a permanent, unchanging self (ātman), which early Buddhism denies (anātman). Jainism affirms a self (jīva), but conceives it as one of countless individual souls, not as a self identical with all. These disagreements generated a debate that lasted more than a thousand years; the Buddhist critique and the Jain alternative are examined in Section 6.10. Both the Upaniṣadic teachers and the Śramaṇas also moved away from the sacrificial religion of the Brāhmaṇas towards an interiorised discipline: the Kaṭha’s choice between the “good” (śreyas) and the “pleasant” (preyas) is close to the Buddhist and Jaina emphasis on renunciation.

Table 1.9. Upaniṣadic and Śramaṇa Traditions: Points of Convergence and Divergence Concept Upaniṣads Early Buddhism Jainism Self Ātman (eternal, unchanging) Anātman (no permanent self) Jīva (eternal but with karma-body) Ultimate Reality Brahman (non-dual Absolute) Nirvāṇa; no permanent substrate (Mahāyāna later speaks of śūnyatā) Infinite jīvas; no creator God Karma Overcome by jñāna Overcome by the Eightfold Path Overcome by austerity and knowledge Liberation Mokṣa (identity with Brahman) Nirvāṇa (cessation of suffering) Kaivalya (isolation of the soul) Authority of Vedas Accepted (Śruti pramāṇa) Rejected Rejected

The relationship is therefore not one of simple opposition. The traditions asked overlapping questions — about the self, suffering and the possibility of release — within different metaphysical frameworks, and each sharpened its answers in argument with the others.

docs.title: 1.15 The Concept of Adhikāra: Qualification for Upaniṣadic Study
docs.text:
The Upaniṣadic tradition places great emphasis on the qualifications of the student. The tradition presents this as pedagogical realism: just as advanced mathematics requires a foundation in basic arithmetic, the knowledge of Brahman is said to require a foundation of ethical discipline and mental steadiness. But adhikāra also had a social side that should not be passed over. Vedic study was reserved for initiated men of the three upper varṇas; Śaṅkara, commenting on Brahmasūtra 1.3.34–38, denies Śūdras the right to study the Veda, and women were generally excluded from initiation. Section 8.11 returns to these restrictions.

The classical Advaita formulation of the student’s fourfold qualification belongs to the post-Upaniṣadic period. Śaṅkara, commenting on Brahmasūtra 1.1.1, names four prerequisites for the enquiry into Brahman: discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, dispassion towards enjoyment here and hereafter, the “sixfold wealth” beginning with calm and self-restraint, and the desire for liberation. The label sādhana-catuṣṭaya and its systematic elaboration come from later Advaita manuals such as Sadānanda’s Vedāntasāra (15th century) and the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi, which tradition ascribes to Śaṅkara but whose authorship most scholars doubt. The Upaniṣads themselves supply the raw material, notably Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.23, which says that one who knows the Self becomes “calm, restrained, withdrawn, patient and collected” (śānto dānta uparatas titikṣuḥ samāhito bhūtvā) (Figure 1.3). The Muṇḍaka (1.2.12) adds the outward form of the approach: the seeker is to go “fuel in hand” (samitpāṇi) to a teacher learned in the Veda and established in Brahman, the fuel signifying readiness to serve the teacher’s household (Section 4.5).

Figure 1.3. The fourfold qualification (sādhana-catuṣṭaya) of later Advaita, with Upaniṣadic passages cited as its sources

docs.title: 1.16 The Upaniṣadic Pedagogy: Methods of Teaching
docs.text: The Upaniṣads teach in several ways. Unlike the systematic treatises of later philosophical traditions, they are primarily dialogic — they unfold through conversations between teachers and students, through questions and answers, through stories and parables, and through the progressive deepening of an enquiry. Two techniques deserve mention besides those discussed below: progressive instruction, as when Varuṇa sends his son Bhṛgu back again and again to practise austerity until he finds Brahman successively as food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss (Taittirīya 3.1–6); and repetition, as in the ninefold refrain tat tvam asi of Chāndogya 6.8–16.

docs.title: 1.16.1 The Dialogue Form (Saṃvāda)
docs.text:
The most characteristic literary form of the Upaniṣads is the dialogue. The great Upaniṣadic conversations — Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī, Yama and Naciketas, Prajāpati and Indra, Uddālaka and Śvetaketu — are literary compositions, but they reflect a practice of teaching in which a doctrine was tested by question and response (Table 1.10).

Table 1.10. Major Upaniṣadic Dialogues and Their Pedagogical Significance Upaniṣad Teacher Student Pedagogical Method Chāndogya Uddālaka Śvetaketu Progressive examples from nature leading to “Tat tvam asi” Kaṭha Yama Naciketas Testing of resolve through temptation before revealing Ātma-vidyā Bṛhadāraṇyaka Yājñavalkya Maitreyī Direct declaration followed by the method of neti neti Muṇḍaka Aṅgiras Śaunaka Distinction between lower and higher knowledge Praśna Pippalāda Six students Systematic question-answer on six fundamental topics Kena Unknown guru Student Apophatic teaching: pointing to the unknowability of the Knower

The dialogue form is not accidental. In these texts a teaching is reached through guided enquiry rather than simply announced. In Advaita this is why the teacher is said not to produce new knowledge of the Self but to remove the ignorance that hides it: the Ātman, being self-luminous, needs only the removal of obstructions to be known.

docs.title: 1.16.2 The Method of Analogy (Dṛṣṭānta)
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads use analogies drawn from everyday experience to make abstract claims intelligible. The commentators treat these analogies as more than illustrations: they lead from what has been seen (dṛṣṭa) to what has not.

Principal Upaniṣadic Analogies

  1. Clay and pots (Chāndogya 6.1.4): Just as all clay products are essentially clay, all the manifold names and forms of the world are essentially Brahman. The modification (vikāra) is a matter of name (nāma) only; the substance (vastu) remains one.

  2. Rivers and ocean (Praśna 6.5; Muṇḍaka 3.2.8): Just as rivers flowing into the ocean lose their individual names and forms and become simply “ocean,” so the sixteen parts of the person dissolve into the Person (Praśna), and the knower, freed from name and form, goes to the divine Person beyond the beyond (Muṇḍaka).

  3. Salt in water (Chāndogya 6.13): Just as salt dissolved in water pervades the entire body of water invisibly yet can be tasted everywhere, so Brahman pervades the entire universe invisibly yet is the essence (rasa) of all experience.

  4. Spider and web (Muṇḍaka 1.1.7): Just as a spider projects its web from within itself and again withdraws it, so the Imperishable projects the universe from within itself without any external material cause.

  5. Fire and sparks (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.1.20; Muṇḍaka 2.1.1): Just as sparks fly forth from a blazing fire, so all beings emanate from the Imperishable and return to it.

docs.title: 1.16.3 The Method of Negation (Neti Neti)
docs.text: A third method is the negation “not this, not this” (neti neti) used by Yājñavalkya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.3.6; 3.9.26; 4.2.4; 4.4.22; 4.5.15). It denies every predicate of the Ātman; a parallel series of negations describes the imperishable (akṣara) in Yājñavalkya’s reply to Gārgī — “not coarse, not fine, not short, not long” (3.8.8). The fullest statement, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.9.26, is quoted in Section 4.2, and the Advaita interpretation of the method — that it negates only the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) superimposed on the self — is discussed in Section 6.2.

docs.title: 1.17 The Spirit of Enquiry in the Upaniṣads
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads are also texts of open enquiry. Their teachers question, debate and test one another’s answers, and some of their best-known passages are questions rather than answers. The Kena opens with one:

keneṣitaṃ patati preṣitaṃ manaḥ kena prāṇaḥ prathamaḥ praiti yuktaḥ keneṣitāṃ vācam imāṃ vadanti cakṣuḥ śrotraṃ ka u devo yunakti Translation: “Directed by whom does the mind alight upon its objects? Commanded by whom does the first breath move? Impelled by whom is this speech that people utter? What god directs the eyes and ears?” — Kena Upaniṣad 1.1

The Upaniṣad takes the most familiar activities — thinking, breathing, speaking, seeing, hearing — and asks what power stands behind them all. Its answer is given in Section 2.2.

docs.title: 1.18 The Upaniṣads and the Later Schools
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads became the authoritative source (pramāṇa) for every school of Vedānta, and their vocabulary was shared, accepted or contested by most other Indian schools, orthodox (āstika) and heterodox (nāstika) alike (Table 1.11). The commentators and their readings are the subject of Chapter 11.

Table 1.11. The Upaniṣads and Major Indian Philosophical Schools School Key Figure or Text Relation to the Upaniṣads Advaita Vedānta Śaṅkara Upaniṣads as primary pramāṇa; non-dual Brahman as sole reality Viśiṣṭādvaita Rāmānuja Upaniṣads interpreted to support qualified non-dualism; Brahman as personal God with attributes Dvaita Madhva Upaniṣads interpreted to support eternal distinction between God and souls Sāṅkhya Īśvarakṛṣṇa The Sāṅkhyakārikā (Kapila is the legendary founder) shares vocabulary with the Kaṭha and Śvetāśvatara (puruṣa, avyakta, guṇas); the direction of influence is debated Yoga Patañjali Shares the Upaniṣadic ideal of meditative withdrawal (cf. Kaṭha 2.3.10–11; Śvetāśvatara 2.8–15), set out in the eightfold (aṣṭāṅga) framework Buddhism Siddhārtha Gautama Rejects a permanent self (anātman); shares the vocabulary of karma, rebirth and liberation with the Upaniṣads; the extent of direct influence is debated Jainism Mahāvīra An independent śramaṇa tradition; shares with the Upaniṣads the themes of karma, rebirth and liberation

docs.title: 1.19 The Upaniṣads and World Philosophy
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads reached Europe through a Persian route. In 1657 the Mughal prince Dārā Shikōh had some fifty Upaniṣads translated into Persian as the Sirr-i Akbar (“The Great Secret”); A.-H. Anquetil-Duperron rendered this Persian version into Latin as the Oupnek’hat (1801–02) (Section 12.3.1). The German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer read the Oupnek’hat and wrote in his Parerga and Paralipomena (1851) that it had been the consolation of his life and would be the consolation of his death.

The American Transcendentalists, especially Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau, read Upaniṣadic and other Indian texts in translation, and the physicist Erwin Schrödinger expressed personal sympathy for the Vedāntic idea of a single consciousness in the epilogue to What Is Life? (1944) and in Mind and Matter (1958). These were philosophical affinities of individual readers, not evidence that the Upaniṣads anticipated modern science (see Chapter 12).

docs.title: 1.20 The Plan of This Volume
docs.text:
This volume is organised into twelve chapters, moving from the texts to their doctrines, their later companions and their interpreters:

  1. Introduction — the present chapter, including the relative chronology of the principal Upaniṣads

  2. The Mukhya Upaniṣads, Part I: Īśā, Kena, Kaṭha, Praśna

  3. The Mukhya Upaniṣads, Part II: Muṇḍaka (with its cosmic images), Māṇḍūkya (with Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā), Taittirīya, Aitareya

  4. The Mukhya Upaniṣads, Part III: Chāndogya, Bṛhadāraṇyaka and their ritual meditations (vidyās), the women philosophers, the social world of kings, brahmins and patrons, the Śvetāśvatara, and a note on the Kauṣītaki and the Maitrī

  5. The Mahāvākyas — the four great sayings, the Advaita theory of how they give knowledge, and the theistic objections

  6. Core Philosophical Doctrines: Brahman, Ātman, creation and causation, māyā, karma and liberation; the three bodies; the Buddhist and Jain critiques of the Ātman

  7. The Yoga Upaniṣads

  8. The Sannyāsa Upaniṣads

  9. The Sectarian Upaniṣads: Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta and others, with the general Vedāntic (sāmānya-vedānta) group

  10. States of Consciousness: Jāgrat, Svapna, Suṣupti, Turīya

  11. The Commentarial Tradition: the Brahmasūtra and early Vedānta; Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Madhva and the later schools; the Tamil and regional-language reception

  12. The Contemporary Relevance of Upaniṣadic Thought

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Mukhya Upaniṣads — Part I
docs.text: This chapter reads the first four of the ten principal Upaniṣads in the traditional order: the Īśā, Kena, Kaṭha, and Praśna. Three of them are verse texts or open in verse; the Praśna is prose. All four belong, in the chronology of Chapter 1, to the later layers of the principal Upaniṣads. Each is treated in one section: its place in the Vedic corpus, its structure, its main teachings and the practices it prescribes. A last section shows how the commentators divided over them.

docs.title: 2.1.1 Overview and Vedic Affiliation
docs.text:
The Īśā Upaniṣad, also known as the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad, is the only principal Upaniṣad transmitted as part of a Saṃhitā: it forms the fortieth and last chapter of the Śukla Yajurveda Saṃhitā (Vājasaneyī Saṃhitā). As Section 1.12 explains, this position shows how the Vājasaneyins arranged their canon; it does not make the Īśā as old as the hymns before it, and its verse form places it with the later verse Upaniṣads.

Īśā Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Śukla Yajurveda (Vājasaneyī Saṃhitā 40) Verses: 18 (some recensions have 17) Metre: Mainly anuṣṭubh, with some triṣṭubh Central Theme: The Lord pervading all; synthesis of knowledge and action Key Teaching: Enjoyment through renunciation; seeing the self in all beings Ācārya Commentary: Śaṅkarācārya’s Bhāṣya

docs.title: 2.1.2 The Opening Verse
docs.text:
The Īśā opens with what is probably the most often quoted verse of the Upaniṣads:

īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvaṃ yat kiñca jagatyāṃ jagat tena tyaktena bhuñjīthā mā gṛdhaḥ kasya svid dhanam Translation: “All this — whatever moves in this moving world — is pervaded by the Lord. Therefore, enjoy through renunciation. Do not covet; for whose is wealth?” — Īśā Upaniṣad, Verse 1

The verse joins a claim and an injunction. The whole moving world (idaṃ sarvam) is pervaded, or in another reading “clothed”, by the Lord (īśā vāsyam); one should therefore enjoy (bhuñjīthāḥ) by means of what has been given up (tyaktena) and not covet. The commentators read the paradox in different ways. For Śaṅkara the verse is addressed to the renouncer, who “protects” the self by giving up the world; for many modern readers it describes a life of use without possessiveness.

docs.title: 2.1.3 The Synthesis of Vidyā and Karma
docs.text:
Verses 9–11 address the relation of knowledge (vidyā) and action (karma), a theme to which the later tradition constantly returned:

andhaṃ tamaḥ praviśanti ye’vidyām upāsate tato bhūya iva te tamo ya u vidyāyāṃ ratāḥ Translation: “Into blinding darkness enter those who worship ignorance (avidyā); into still greater darkness, as it were, enter those who delight in knowledge (vidyā) alone.” — Īśā Upaniṣad, Verse 9

This verse has been the subject of extensive commentarial debate. Verse 11 continues: “one who knows both vidyā and avidyā together, crossing death by avidyā, attains immortality by vidyā.” Śaṅkara interprets avidyā here as ritual action and vidyā as meditative knowledge of the deities (not the highest brahma-vidyā); on his reading their combination leads to a higher world, while liberation comes from knowledge of the Self alone. Many modern interpreters, by contrast, read the passage as recommending an integration of action and knowledge. Either way, the text rejects the exclusive pursuit of either one (Figure 2.1).

Figure 2.1. Vidyā and avidyā in the Īśā Upaniṣad (verses 9–11)

docs.title: 2.1.4 Structure and Teaching
docs.text:
The eighteen verses of the Īśā (Kāṇva recension) fall into thematic groups (Table 2.1). Verses 1–3 introduce the Lord’s pervasion of the world and its ethical consequences; verses 4–8 describe the Ātman, unmoving yet swifter than the mind; verses 9–14 set out the paired terms vidyā and avidyā, sambhūti and asambhūti; and verses 15–18 are prayers for the hour of death.

Table 2.1. Thematic Structure of the Īśā Upaniṣad Verses Theme Content 1–3 Ethical foundation Renunciation and enjoyment; warning against the sunless worlds (asuryā lokāḥ) 4–8 Nature of Ātman Description of Ātman as unmoving yet swifter than the mind; the reconciliation of opposites 9–11 Vidyā and avidyā Those who pursue knowledge alone and ignorance alone both enter darkness; integration is the path 12–14 Sambhūti and asambhūti A parallel pair (“becoming” and “non-becoming”, with vināśa “destruction” in v. 14); both are to be known together 15–18 Concluding prayers Prayers to Sūrya and Agni for the revelation of truth at the hour of death

Two teachings of the Īśā were especially influential. The first is the pervasion of all things by the Lord, which theistic and non-theistic readers alike took as the text’s starting point. The second is the ethical consequence drawn in verse 6: one who sees all beings in the self and the self in all beings no longer shrinks from anyone. The tradition made this verse a practice as well as a doctrine, a sustained contemplation of the Lord or the self in every being. In verse 16 the worshipper, addressing the person in the sun, says “I am he” (so ’ham asmi), a formula that later yoga texts turned into a mantra of the breath (Table 5.5).

docs.title: 2.2.1 Overview and Vedic Affiliation
docs.text:
The Kena Upaniṣad takes its name from its opening word, kena (“by whom?”). It belongs to the Sāmaveda, specifically the Talavakāra Brāhmaṇa (and is hence also known as the Talavakāra Upaniṣad). It is a compact text of four sections (khaṇḍas), the first two in verse and the latter two in prose.

Kena Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Sāmaveda (Talavakāra / Jaiminīya Śākhā) Sections: 4 khaṇḍas (2 verse + 2 prose) Verses: c. 14 verses (khaṇḍas 1–2) plus prose (khaṇḍas 3–4) Metre: Mixed: jagatī/triṣṭubh and anuṣṭubh-like lines Central Theme: Brahman as the power behind all powers Key Teaching: Brahman is the unknown behind the known

docs.title: 2.2.2 The Fundamental Question
docs.text:
The Kena opens by asking who or what sets the mind, the breath, speech, sight and hearing to work (1.1, quoted in Section 1.17). Its answer is paradoxical: Brahman is that which cannot be grasped by the mind or the senses, yet it is that by which the mind and senses themselves function. It is not an object that can be pointed to but the condition of all pointing, knowing and experiencing.

yad vācā’nabhyuditaṃ yena vāg abhyudyate tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate Translation: “That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed — know that alone to be Brahman, and not this that people worship here.” — Kena Upaniṣad 1.5

docs.title: 2.2.3 Knowing the Unknown
docs.text:
Brahman is then declared to be unknown to those who know and known to those who do not know:

yasyāmataṃ tasya mataṃ mataṃ yasya na veda saḥ avijñātaṃ vijānatāṃ vijñātam avijānatām Translation: “To whomever It is not known, to him It is known; to whomever It is known, he does not know. It is not understood by those who understand It; It is understood by those who do not understand It.” — Kena Upaniṣad 2.3

The commentators read the paradox as a distinction between objective knowledge (knowledge of something, in which Brahman would become an object of the mind) and the recognition that Brahman is the knowing subject itself. One who claims to “know” Brahman as an object has, on this reading, reduced it to a finite concept; one who sees that it transcends all objective knowledge is closer to the truth.

The Kena’s teaching invites comparison with the distinction that modern phenomenology draws between the intentional object of consciousness and consciousness itself. Just as the eye can see all objects but cannot see itself, so Brahman — being the very ground of all knowing — cannot become an object of knowledge. The same thought underlies the negative method (neti neti) of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (Section 1.16.3).

docs.title: 2.2.4 The Parable of the Yakṣa
docs.text:
The prose section of the Kena tells the story of the Yakṣa (a mysterious being). The gods (devās) had won a great victory over the demons (asuras), and they began to exult in their triumph, attributing the victory to their own power. Brahman appeared before them as a Yakṣa. One by one, Agni (Fire) and Vāyu (Wind) approached the Yakṣa, boasting of their powers — the ability to burn and blow away everything. The Yakṣa placed a blade of grass before each and challenged them: “Burn this.” “Blow this away.” Neither could move it.

Finally, Indra approached, but the Yakṣa vanished. In that very space where the Yakṣa had been, the goddess Umā Haimavatī appeared and revealed the truth: the Yakṣa was Brahman, and it was through Brahman’s power alone that the gods had achieved their victory. The word yakṣa, used in popular religion for powerful spirits often represented in early Indian sculpture, here names a wondrous being whose identity the gods cannot grasp (Figure 2.2).

Figure 2.2. A stone yakṣa figure in an Indian museum. In popular religion yakṣas were powerful spirits; the Kena uses the word for the mysterious being in which Brahman appears Photo: Prady9, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The parable makes the point of the verse section in narrative form: the powers of fire, wind, mind and speech are not their own but derive from Brahman, and the gods who forget this do not know what has given them their victory. The division of the text into a verse argument (khaṇḍas 1–2) and a prose story (khaṇḍas 3–4) thus serves its teaching: the verses state the principle, and the story (ākhyāyikā) shows even the gods failing to recognise Brahman until the goddess instructs them (Table 2.2). The practice the text implies is one of recollection: in every act of seeing, hearing or thinking one is to remember the power that makes it possible.

docs.title: 2.2.5 The Role of Umā Haimavatī
docs.text:
The appearance of Umā Haimavatī (“Umā, daughter of the Himalaya”) has been read in several ways. Śaṅkara reads her as knowledge (vidyā) personified: knowledge of Brahman comes as a revelation that the gods cannot win by their own powers. Later readers have often remarked that a female figure is here the revealer of Brahman to the king of the gods. Śākta and Śaiva readers saw in Umā, the consort of Śiva, an early sign of the theology in which the Goddess is identified with Brahman (Chapter 9); whether the original passage carried that meaning is uncertain.

Table 2.2. Key Themes of the Kena Upaniṣad: A Summary Section Key Teaching Method Khaṇḍa 1 (Verse) Who is the power behind mind and senses? Direct questioning Khaṇḍa 2 (Verse) Brahman is known by not-knowing; apophatic theology Paradox Khaṇḍa 3 (Prose) The Yakṣa parable: Agni and Vāyu humbled Narrative parable Khaṇḍa 4 (Prose) Umā reveals Brahman to Indra; fruits of this knowledge Revelation through grace

docs.title: 2.3.1 Overview and Vedic Affiliation
docs.text:
The Kaṭha Upaniṣad (also called the Kaṭhopaniṣad) has been among the most widely read of the Upaniṣads, in India and abroad. It belongs to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and is named after the Kaṭha school (śākhā) of the Yajurveda. The text is structured in two chapters (adhyāyas), each containing three sections (vallīs), for a total of six vallīs.

Kaṭha Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda (Kaṭha Śākhā) Structure: 2 adhyāyas, 6 vallīs, 119 verses Metre: Anuṣṭubh and triṣṭubh Central Theme: The nature of the Ātman; death and immortality Key Figures: Naciketas (the boy-seeker) and Yama (Lord of Death) Famous Imagery: The chariot metaphor; the inverted Aśvattha tree

docs.title: 2.3.2 The Story of Naciketas
docs.text:
The Kaṭha is framed by a narrative already known, in a ritual form, from the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (Section 1.12): the encounter of the boy Naciketas with Yama, the god of death.

Vājaśravasa, the father of Naciketas, performs a sacrifice in which he is supposed to give away all his possessions. Naciketas, observing that his father is giving away only old, barren cows, asks: “Father, to whom will you give me?” Irritated, the father snaps: “I give you to Death!” (mṛtyave tvā dadāmīti).

The boy goes to the abode of Yama, where he waits for three nights without food (for Yama is absent). When Yama returns, he is horrified that a Brāhmaṇa guest has been left without hospitality and offers Naciketas three boons in compensation.

  1. Naciketas asks that his father receive him back with a calm mind — granted.

  2. He asks for the knowledge of the sacred fire that leads to heaven — granted (Yama names this fire after Naciketas himself: the Nāciketa fire).

  3. He asks whether a man exists after death or not — and here the teaching proper begins.

The philosophical content cannot be separated from this dramatic form. The teacher is Death himself (Mṛtyu), and the question of the deathless self is raised in the presence of mortality. Yama first tests the boy by offering him every worldly substitute — long life, wealth, sons and grandsons, kingship over the earth, celestial women — and teaches the secret of the Ātman only when Naciketas has refused them all. The test dramatises what the later tradition called discrimination (viveka) and dispassion (vairāgya), the prerequisites of the knowledge of Brahman (Section 1.15).

na vittena tarpaṇīyo manuṣyo lapsyāmahe vittam adrākṣma cet tvā | jīviṣyāmo yāvad īśiṣyasi tvam varas tu me varanīyaḥ sa eva Translation: “No mortal can be satisfied by wealth. Shall we possess wealth when we have seen you (Death)? We shall live only as long as you ordain. That boon alone is to be chosen by me.” — Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.1.27

docs.title: 2.3.3 The Two Paths: Śreyas and Preyas
docs.text:
Yama’s teaching begins with the distinction between the śreyas (the good, the ultimately beneficial) and the preyas (the pleasant, the immediately gratifying):

anyac chreyo ’nyad utaiva preyas te ubhe nānārthe puruṣaṃ sinītaḥ tayoḥ śreya ādadānasya sādhu bhavati hīyate’rthād ya u preyo vṛṇīte Translation: “The good (śreyas) is one thing, and the pleasant (preyas) quite another. Both these, serving different purposes, bind a person. Of these two, it is well for the one who takes the good; the one who chooses the pleasant falls away from the true purpose.” — Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.1

The Upaniṣad presents this as a choice that every person faces, and Naciketas, who has just refused Yama’s gifts, is its example.

docs.title: 2.3.4 The Chariot Metaphor and the Hierarchy of the Person
docs.text:
The best-known image of the Kaṭha is the chariot metaphor (1.3.3–4), a model of the human person and of the discipline that governs it (Figure 2.3):

ātmānaṃ rathinaṃ viddhi śarīraṃ ratham eva tu buddhiṃ tu sārathiṃ viddhi manaḥ pragraham eva ca Translation: “Know the Self (Ātman) as the lord of the chariot, the body as the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) as the charioteer, and the mind as the reins.” — Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3

Figure 2.3. The Chariot Metaphor of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (1.3.3–4)

The next verses draw the moral. The senses are the horses and their objects the roads; for one who lacks understanding and whose mind is never held firm, the senses run out of control like vicious horses, while for one who has understanding they obey like good horses (1.3.5–6). The image distinguishes the charioteer (the intellect) from the lord of the chariot (the Ātman), and the whole soteriology of the Kaṭha rests on that distinction: the self is the experiencer, not any of the faculties that carry it.

The metaphor invites comparison with the chariot image of the soul in Plato’s Phaedrus (c. 370 BCE), probably somewhat earlier than the Kaṭha in the chronology adopted here, in which the charioteer of reason guides the two horses of spirit and appetite. No historical contact between the two is known. The Upaniṣadic version distinguishes more levels (body, senses, mind, intellect and self), and it separates the driver from the owner of the chariot, which Plato’s image does not.

A few verses later (1.3.10–11) the Kaṭha turns the image into an ascending hierarchy: beyond the senses are their objects, beyond the objects the mind, beyond the mind the intellect, beyond the intellect the “great self”, beyond that the unmanifest, and beyond the unmanifest the Person (puruṣa), beyond whom there is nothing (Figure 2.4).

Figure 2.4. The Kaṭha Upaniṣad’s Hierarchy of Being (1.3.10–11)

This scheme, with its terms mahat, avyakta and puruṣa, is close to the list of principles of later Sāṅkhya, and the Gītā restates a shorter form of it (3.42–43). Its influence on the yoga traditions is real but should not be overstated. The Kaṭha defines yoga as “the steady holding of the senses” (2.3.11) and describes a withdrawal of the senses and mind towards the self, which makes it one of the earliest texts to use the word yoga for a meditative discipline (Mallinson and Singleton 2017). Patañjali’s Yogasūtra, however, does not use the Kaṭha’s hierarchy; its account of withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and concentration (dhāraṇā) is built on a different analysis of the mind (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 2.3.5 The Nature of the Ātman
docs.text:
Yama first declares that the Self is neither born nor dies:

na jāyate mriyate vā vipaścin nāyaṃ kutaścin na babhūva kaścit ajo nityaḥ śāśvato ’yaṃ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre Translation: “The wise one is not born, nor does he die; he has not come from anywhere, nor has he become anyone. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and primeval, he is not killed when the body is killed.” — Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18

The Bhagavad Gītā (2.20) adapts this verse, replacing its first line with na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ, and the next Kaṭha verse (1.2.19, “if the killer thinks he kills”) reappears as Gītā 2.19 — two of the Gītā’s many borrowings from the Kaṭha. A little later comes the verse on the Self hidden in the heart:

aṇor aṇīyān mahato mahīyān ātmāsya jantor nihito guhāyām tam akratuḥ paśyati vītaśoko dhātuprasādān mahimānam ātmanaḥ Translation: “Subtler than the subtlest, greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the heart (guhā) of every creature. The one free from desire, whose sorrow has departed, sees the greatness of the Self through the tranquillity of the senses.” (Śaṅkara reads dhātu-prasāda as “tranquillity of the senses”; others read “the grace of the Creator”, as in the parallel verse Śvetāśvatara 3.20.) — Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.20

The verse joins the smallest and the greatest, the most inward and the most cosmic. The self is found not by outward search but by turning attention to the “cave” (guhā) of the heart. A few verses later the Kaṭha adds that the self cannot be won by instruction, intellect or much learning, but only by the one whom it chooses (1.2.23), a verse the theistic schools read as a teaching of grace.

docs.title: 2.3.6 The Inverted Aśvattha Tree
docs.text:
The Kaṭha (2.3.1) presents another image — the inverted fig tree (aśvattha), with its roots above and branches below:

ūrdhvamūlo’vākśākha eṣo’śvatthaḥ sanātanaḥ tad eva śukraṃ tad brahma tad evāmṛtam ucyate Translation: “This eternal Aśvattha tree has its roots above and branches below. That is the Pure, that is Brahman, that indeed is called the Immortal.” — Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3.1

The image, later elaborated in the Bhagavad Gītā (15.1–4), represents the cosmic tree of saṃsāra. Its roots are “above” in Brahman, the transcendent source, while its branches spread “below” into the phenomenal world; what ordinary experience takes as the ground is in this image the derivative part.

docs.title: 2.3.7 The Kaṭha’s Later Influence
docs.text:
The Kaṭha was quoted and adapted more than most Upaniṣads (Table 2.3). Its question about death reached modern literature as well: Somerset Maugham took the title and epigraph of The Razor’s Edge (1944) from Kaṭha 1.3.14, which likens the path to the sharp edge of a razor.

Table 2.3. Influence of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad on Later Texts Kaṭha Teaching Later Development Text Hierarchy of senses, mind, intellect and Self (1.3.10–11) Restated in condensed form Bhagavad Gītā 3.42–43 Inverted Aśvattha (2.3.1) Extended metaphor of the cosmic tree Bhagavad Gītā 15.1–4 Terms mahat, avyakta, puruṣa (1.3.10–11) Vocabulary shared with later Sāṅkhya Sāṅkhya Kārikā Yoga as “steady holding of the senses” (2.3.10–11) One of the earliest uses of yoga for meditative discipline Later yoga literature Ātman beyond death Basis for the immortality of the soul doctrine All Vedāntic schools

docs.title: 2.4.1 Overview and Vedic Affiliation
docs.text:
The Praśna Upaniṣad (“The Upaniṣad of Questions”) belongs to the Atharvaveda and is associated with the Pippalāda śākhā. Six seekers approach the sage Pippalāda, and each poses one question (praśna); the sage answers each in turn. No other principal Upaniṣad is arranged so systematically.

Praśna Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Atharvaveda (Pippalāda Śākhā) Structure: 6 praśnas (questions) Style: Prose with occasional verse Central Theme: Creation, Prāṇa, Oṃ, meditation, and the Puruṣa Key Figure: Sage Pippalāda Seekers: Sukeśā Bhāradvāja, Śaibya Satyakāma, Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya, Kausalya Āśvalāyana, Bhārgava Vaidarbhi, Kabandhī Kātyāyana

docs.title: 2.4.2 The Year of Probation and the Six Questions
docs.text:
Before he will answer, Pippalāda tells the six students to live with him for another year in austerity (tapas), celibacy (brahmacarya) and faith (śraddhā) (1.2). The tradition reads the year as a purification (citta-śuddhi) that makes the student fit to receive the teaching, and it values the scene as a model of the patience and discipline that learning requires. The scene also shows how restricted that learning was. The six students are already learned men devoted to Brahman (1.1); a teacher who could set such conditions could also refuse those who did not meet them, and the tradition did refuse Śūdras and most women (Sections 1.15, 4.5 and 8.11). The six questions then move from cosmology to the life of the body, sleep, meditation and the Person (Table 2.4).

Table 2.4. The Six Questions of the Praśna Upaniṣad Q Questioner Subject Core Teaching 1 Kabandhī Origin of beings Creation arises from the dyad of Prajāpati: Rayi (Matter) and Prāṇa (Life) 2 Bhārgava Supremacy of Prāṇa Among the powers of the body, Prāṇa is supreme: when it rises to leave, all the others must follow (2.3–4) 3 Kausalya Nature of Prāṇa How Prāṇa arises, enters the body, and distributes itself into five forms 4 Gārgya States of sleep What sleeps? What wakes? Who sees dreams? Who experiences the bliss of deep sleep? 5 Satyakāma Meditation on Oṃ The fruits of meditating upon the syllable Oṃ with varying degrees of completeness 6 Sukeśā The Puruṣa of 16 parts The sixteen kalās (parts) of the Puruṣa and their dissolution into the Supreme

docs.title: 2.4.3 The Doctrine of Prāṇa
docs.text:
The Praśna’s treatment of Prāṇa (the vital breath, the life-force) takes up an old theme. In the second question, the powers that sustain the body — space, wind, fire, water, earth, speech, mind, sight and hearing — each claim to uphold it. Prāṇa then makes as if to leave: as it rises, all the others are carried off with it, and when it settles they all settle — just as, in the text’s simile, the bees all fly off when their “king” bee flies off and settle when it settles (Praśna 2.3–4). A fuller version of the contest, in which speech, sight, hearing and mind leave the body one after another and the person lives on mute, blind, deaf and witless until breath begins to leave, is told in the Chāndogya (5.1.6–12) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.1.7–13).

The third question elicits the teaching on the five forms of Prāṇa (Figure 2.5).

Figure 2.5. The Fivefold Prāṇa as Taught in the Praśna Upaniṣad

docs.title: 2.4.4 Meditation on Oṃ
docs.text:
The fifth question concerns meditation on Oṃ (oṃkāra-upāsanā), graded by the measures (mātrās) of the syllable. Meditation on its first measure leads to rebirth in the human world, meditation on two measures to the world of the moon, and meditation on the whole syllable to the world of Brahmā and to the vision of the Supreme Person (5.3–5). The Māṇḍūkya later builds a theory of consciousness on the same analysis of the syllable (Section 3.2).

yaḥ punar etaṃ trimātreṇom ity etenaivākṣareṇa paraṃ puruṣam abhidhyāyīta sa tejasi sūrye sampannaḥ Translation: “He who meditates on the Supreme Person with the three-measured Oṃ is united with the radiance of the Sun.” — Praśna Upaniṣad 5.5

docs.title: 2.4.5 The Sixteen Parts of the Puruṣa
docs.text:
The sixth and final question addresses the nature of the Puruṣa (Person, Self) with sixteen kalās (parts). Pippalāda teaches that just as rivers flowing into the ocean lose their individual names and forms, so too the sixteen parts of the Puruṣa merge into the Supreme Self upon liberation:

sa yathemā nadyaḥ syandamānāḥ samudrāyaṇāḥ samudraṃ prāpyāstaṃ gacchanti bhidyete tāsāṃ nāmarūpe samudra ity evaṃ procyate Translation: “Just as these rivers, flowing towards the ocean, upon reaching the ocean, disappear — their name and form are dissolved, and they are simply called ‘the ocean’ — so too the sixteen parts of the all-seeing Puruṣa…” — Praśna Upaniṣad 6.5

docs.title: 2.5 The Commentators on These Four Upaniṣads
docs.text:
Śaṅkara and Madhva both wrote commentaries on the principal Upaniṣads. Rāmānuja himself did not; the Viśiṣṭādvaita readings of these texts are those of later commentators of his school such as Raṅgarāmānuja (16th century), who applied the doctrine of the Śrībhāṣya to them. Table 2.5 is illustrative. It does not quote the commentaries but shows how each school’s general doctrine (Chapter 11) bears on three verses discussed in this chapter.

Table 2.5. Illustrative: How the Three Schools’ Doctrines Bear on Three Verses Passage Advaita (Śaṅkara) Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja’s school) Dvaita (Madhva) Īśā 1: īśā vāsyam The Lord pervades as the inner Self; the world is mithyā The Lord pervades as the inner controller; the world is real, his body The Lord (for Madhva, Viṣṇu) controls all; the world is real and distinct from him Kena 1.5: Brahman as the unknown Brahman transcends all objectification Brahman exceeds finite description but is known in devotion Brahman is never fully comprehended by any finite knower Kaṭha 1.2.20: aṇor aṇīyān The Ātman is identical with Brahman, indwelling in all The supreme Self dwells within the (atomic) individual self as its inner controller The Lord dwells in the heart, both minute and vast; the self remains distinct and dependent

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: Chapter 3: The Mukhya Upaniṣads — Part II
docs.text: This chapter reads four more of the principal Upaniṣads: the Muṇḍaka, Māṇḍūkya, Taittirīya, and Aitareya. Two are late texts of the Atharvaveda, one in verse and one in prose; the other two are prose sections of the Āraṇyakas of the Black Yajurveda and the Ṛgveda, and belong to the early prose layer. The Māṇḍūkya is read together with the verse commentary of Gauḍapāda, without which its later history cannot be understood.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Overview and Vedic Affiliation
docs.text:
The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad belongs to the Atharvaveda. Its name has been explained either from the root muṇḍ (to shave), as the text that “shaves away” ignorance, or from muṇḍaka (shaven-headed), referring to the renouncers for whom its teaching is said to be intended; at its close (3.2.10) it says that the teaching should be given only to those who have performed the “vow of the head” (śirovrata). It is known for its distinction between higher and lower knowledge and for its images of the relation between Brahman and the world.

Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Atharvaveda (Śaunaka Śākhā) Structure: 3 muṇḍakas, 6 khaṇḍas, 64 mantras Style: Metrical (verse) Central Theme: Parā and Aparā Vidyā; Brahman as the target Key Figures: Śaunaka and Aṅgiras Famous Imagery: Two birds; spider’s web; sparks; bow-and-arrow

docs.title: 3.1.2 Parā and Aparā Vidyā: Higher and Lower Knowledge
docs.text:
The Muṇḍaka divides all knowledge into two kinds:

dve vidye veditavye iti ha sma yad brahmavido vadanti, parā caivāparā ca Translation: “Two kinds of knowledge are to be known — thus, indeed, the knowers of Brahman declare — the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā).” — Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.4

Figure 3.1. The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad’s Classification of Knowledge

The Muṇḍaka (1.1.5) classifies the four Vedas themselves, together with the six auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), as aparā vidyā, lower knowledge. This does not make them worthless; it means that scriptural learning that does not lead to the knowledge of Brahman remains “lower”. Only the knowledge “by which the imperishable (akṣara) is grasped” is parā vidyā. The next verse (1.1.6) describes that imperishable: “that which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage or colour, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet; eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, most subtle; that undecaying one whom the wise perceive as the womb of beings” (yat tad adreśyam agrāhyam agotram avarṇam … yad bhūtayoniṃ paripaśyanti dhīrāḥ) (Figure 3.1). The same text calls the sacrifices “unsteady boats” (1.2.7) and sends the seeker who has seen the limits of ritual to a teacher, “fuel in hand” (1.2.12; Section 1.15).

docs.title: 3.1.3 Spider, Sparks and the Cause of the World
docs.text:
The Muṇḍaka explains the relation between Brahman and the world through a series of images:

yathorṇanābhiḥ sṛjate gṛhṇate ca yathā pṛthivyām oṣadhayaḥ sambhavanti yathā sataḥ puruṣāt keśalomāni tathā’kṣarāt sambhavatīha viśvam Translation: “As a spider sends forth and draws in its web; as herbs grow on the earth; as hair grows on the head and body of a living person — so from the Imperishable (Akṣara) arises this universe.” — Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7

A later verse adds the image of sparks flying from a blazing fire (2.1.1). Each image brings out a different aspect of the relation (Table 3.1).

Table 3.1. The Muṇḍaka’s Creation Metaphors Analysed Metaphor Aspect Illustrated Philosophical Implication Spider and web Creation from the creator’s own substance The material cause (upādāna kāraṇa) and the efficient cause (nimitta kāraṇa) are one and the same Herbs from earth Spontaneous emergence from an underlying ground The world arises naturally from Brahman without external agency Hair from a person Effortless, unconscious production Creation does not diminish or alter the creator Sparks from fire (2.1.1) Multiplicity from unity The many beings are like sparks from a single fire; they share the fire’s nature

The spider image answered a question that later Vedānta made central: if the world needs both a material cause and an efficient cause, are they two different things? The spider is both the maker and the material of its web, and so, the Vedāntins concluded, Brahman is both the intelligent and the material cause of the world (abhinna-nimitta-upādāna-kāraṇa). Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita accept this doctrine; Madhva’s Dvaita, by contrast, treats God as the efficient cause only. The cosmogonies of the Upaniṣads as a whole are compared in Section 6.4.

docs.title: 3.1.4 The Two Birds
docs.text:
The Muṇḍaka’s best-known image is that of the two birds:

dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā samānaṃ vṛkṣaṃ pariṣasvajāte tayor anyaḥ pippalaṃ svādv atty anaśnann anyo abhicākaśīti Translation: “Two birds, inseparable companions, perch upon the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating.” — Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1 (= Ṛgveda 1.164.20; also Śvetāśvatara 4.6)

The verse is borrowed from the Ṛgveda’s riddle hymn, where its meaning is obscure; in the Upaniṣad the two birds represent the jīvātman (the individual self, who “eats” the fruits of action, experiencing pleasure and pain) and the Lord or Supreme Self, the silent witness who merely observes. The tree is the body, or more broadly, the field of saṃsāra. The following verse (3.1.2) says that the bird sunk in grief on the same tree is freed from sorrow when it sees “the other, the Lord” and his greatness. Advaitins read this seeing as the recognition of identity; Viśiṣṭādvaitins and Dvaitins cite the same image as scriptural proof that the individual self and the Lord are distinct.

docs.title: 3.1.5 The Bow-and-Arrow Metaphor
docs.text:
The Muṇḍaka also gives an image of meditative practice:

praṇavo dhanuḥ śaro hy ātmā brahma tal lakṣyam ucyate apramattena veddhavyaṃ śaravat tanmayo bhavet Translation: “Oṃ is the bow; the self (ātman) is the arrow; Brahman is said to be the target. It is to be hit by one who is undistracted. One should become one with It, as the arrow becomes one with the target.” — Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.4

docs.title: 3.2.1 Overview and Significance
docs.text:
The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad is the shortest of the principal Upaniṣads, consisting of twelve prose mantras. Its later importance is out of proportion to its length, because Gauḍapāda composed a verse treatise (Kārikā) upon it, and Śaṅkarācārya (or a commentator of his school) commented on both the Upaniṣad and the Kārikā.

The late Muktikā Upaniṣad (1.26) claims that māṇḍūkyam ekam evālaṃ mumukṣūṇāṃ vimuktaye — “The Māṇḍūkya alone is sufficient for the liberation of seekers.” Its date is debated: Olivelle places it around the turn of the Common Era, while some scholars have argued that it is later than, or contemporary with, Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā (c. 6th century CE).

Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Atharvaveda Mantras: 12 (the shortest principal Upaniṣad) Style: Prose Central Theme: Oṃ and the four states of consciousness Key Teaching: Ātman = Brahman = Oṃ; the fourth state (Turīya) Associated Text: Gauḍapāda’s Māṇḍūkya Kārikā

docs.title: 3.2.2 The Opening Declaration
docs.text:
The Māṇḍūkya begins by identifying the syllable Oṃ with all that exists:
