om ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvaṃ / tasyopavyākhyānam / bhūtaṃ bhavad bhaviṣyad iti sarvam oṅkāra eva / yac cānyat trikālātītaṃ tad apy oṅkāra eva Translation: “Oṃ — this syllable is all this. Its explanation is: all that is past, present, and future is verily Oṃ. And whatever transcends the three divisions of time — that too is Oṃ.” — Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, Mantra 1

docs.title: 3.2.3 The Four Pādas (Quarters) of the Ātman
docs.text:
The Māṇḍūkya’s central teaching is the analysis of the Ātman into four pādas (quarters), corresponding to the three states of consciousness plus the transcendent fourth (Figure 3.2 and Table 3.2). Mantras 8–12 then match the quarters to the parts of the syllable Oṃ, justifying each correspondence by word-play: A from “obtaining” and “being first”, U from “exaltation” and “being in between”, M from “measuring” and “merging”. The fourth is “without measure” (amātra, mantra 12), which the commentators explain as the silence in which the syllable ends. The states themselves are examined in Chapter 10.

Figure 3.2. The Four Pādas of the Ātman in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad Table 3.2. Correspondence between Oṃ, States of Consciousness, and Aspects of Self (the fourth is “without measure”, amātra) Letter State Name Realm Characteristics A Waking (jāgrat) Vaiśvānara Gross Outward-facing; experiences external objects; 7 limbs, 19 mouths U Dream (svapna) Taijasa Subtle Inward-facing; experiences internal impressions; luminous M Deep Sleep (suṣupti) Prājña Causal Unified mass of consciousness; seed state; blissful — Turīya Ātman Beyond Neither inward nor outward; beyond duality; pure awareness

docs.title: 3.2.4 The Description of Turīya
docs.text:
The Māṇḍūkya describes the fourth quarter (mantra 7) entirely by negation:

nāntaḥprajñaṃ na bahiṣprajñaṃ nobhayataḥprajñaṃ na prajñānaghanaṃ na prajñaṃ nāprajñam adṛṣṭam avyavahāryam agrāhyam alakṣaṇam acintyam avyapadeśyam ekātmapratyayasāraṃ prapañcopaśamaṃ śāntaṃ śivam advaitam caturthaṃ manyante sa ātmā sa vijñeyaḥ Translation: “Not inwardly conscious, not outwardly conscious, not conscious both ways, not a mass of consciousness, not conscious, not unconscious — unseen, beyond transaction, ungraspable, without characteristics, unthinkable, unnameable, the essence of the awareness of the one Self, the cessation of the phenomenal world, tranquil, auspicious, non-dual — that is the Fourth. That is the Ātman. That is to be known.” — Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, Mantra 7

The passage is a classic via negativa: the Fourth is described by negation because, in the text’s view, it lies beyond all categories of discursive thought. Advaita reads it as the non-dual self that underlies the three states. Madhva, who treated the verses of Gauḍapāda’s first chapter as part of the Upaniṣad itself, read the four quarters instead as four forms of Viṣṇu presiding over the states of the soul.

docs.title: 3.2.5 Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā
docs.text:
Gauḍapāda (c. 6th century CE), regarded by tradition as the paramaguru (teacher’s teacher) of Śaṅkara, composed 215 verses (kārikās), also called the Āgamaśāstra, in four chapters (prakaraṇas). They develop the Māṇḍūkya’s twelve mantras into the earliest surviving systematic statement of non-dualist Vedānta (Mahadevan 1952; Bhattacharya 1943).

  1. Āgama Prakaraṇa (29 verses): an exegesis of the Upaniṣad, setting out the correspondence between A-U-M and the three states and pointing to the measureless fourth as Turīya.

  2. Vaitathya Prakaraṇa (38 verses): the chapter on “unreality”. Gauḍapāda argues that the waking state is, in its essential structure, no different from dream. Dream objects are real within the dream but dissolve upon waking; so the objects of waking experience are real within the waking state but dissolve upon the “awakening” to Turīya.

  3. Advaita Prakaraṇa (48 verses): the chapter on non-duality. Its central teaching is ajāti-vāda, the doctrine that nothing has ever been born, because birth would imply a change in a reality that is unchanging.

  4. Alātaśānti Prakaraṇa (100 verses): “The Quenching of the Firebrand”, the longest and most technical chapter. A firebrand (alāta) whirled in a circle produces the appearance of a ring of fire; so the phenomenal world is the appearance produced by the “movement” of consciousness, which is itself unborn and unmoving.

na nirodho na cotpattir na baddho na ca sādhakaḥ na mumukṣur na vai mukta ity eṣā paramārthatā Translation: “There is no dissolution, no origination; no one in bondage, no one practising spiritual discipline; no one seeking liberation, no one liberated. This is the ultimate truth.” — Māṇḍūkya Kārikā 2.32

docs.title: The argument from dream
docs.text:
Gauḍapāda’s best-known argument, in the second chapter, is the analogy between dream and waking. Both present objects that appear external and real; both involve a perceiving subject and perceived objects; and both are contradicted by a subsequent state (dream by waking, waking by the higher awareness of Turīya). If dream objects are admitted to be unreal, then, by parity of reasoning, so are waking objects.

ādāv ante ca yan nāsti vartamāne ’pi tat tathā | vitathaiḥ sadṛśāḥ santo ’vitathā iva lakṣitāḥ Translation: “What does not exist at the beginning and at the end is equally non-existent in the middle. Though resembling the unreal, they appear as if real.” — Gauḍapāda Kārikā 2.6

The argument is often compared with Descartes’ method of doubt, but the comparison is instructive in its limits: Descartes uses the dream argument to reach a secure foundation in the cogito; Gauḍapāda uses it to dissolve objectivity altogether, leaving only the non-dual awareness (Turīya) beyond the duality of subject and object.

Scholarly Note: Gauḍapāda and Buddhist thought

The relationship of Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā to Buddhist philosophy, particularly Mādhyamaka and Yogācāra, has been much debated. Vidhushekhara Bhattacharya argued for direct Buddhist influence (Bhattacharya 1943); T.M.P. Mahadevan maintained that while Gauḍapāda engages with Buddhist arguments, his conclusions are grounded in the Upaniṣadic tradition (Mahadevan 1952). The fourth chapter shares vocabulary and images with Buddhist texts (the firebrand-circle, the language of “non-origination”). It opens (4.1) with homage to the “best of bipeds” (dvipadāṃ vara), whom many readers take to be the Buddha, and near its end (4.99) declares that this teaching “was not spoken by the Buddha” (naitad buddhena bhāṣitam) — at minimum, evidence of close and deliberate engagement with Buddhist thought.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Overview and Vedic Affiliation
docs.text:
The Taittirīya Upaniṣad belongs to the early prose layer of the principal Upaniṣads and to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda (Taittirīya Śākhā), forming books 7–9 of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka. It is divided into three sections called vallīs (literally, “creepers”):

Taittirīya Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda (Taittirīya Śākhā) Structure: 3 vallīs: Śikṣā, Ānanda, and Bhṛgu Style: Prose Central Theme: The five sheaths; Brahman as bliss Key Teaching: Pañca-kośa (five sheaths) doctrine Famous Declaration: satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma

docs.title: 3.3.2 The Śikṣā Vallī: Phonetics, Correspondences and Ethics
docs.text:
The first section, the Śikṣā Vallī, begins with phonetics (śikṣā), the science of correct recitation, and with meditations that show the logic of correspondence on which the oldest Upaniṣads rest. In the meditation on the “great combinations” (mahāsaṃhitā, 1.3), the phonetic junction of two sounds becomes a model for five domains: of the worlds, earth is the first form, heaven the last, space their junction and wind their link; of the lights, fire and sun are joined by water and lightning; and so on through knowledge, offspring and the self. The ritual and the cosmos are bound by such equivalences (bandhu, Section 1.1). The section also teaches meditation on the sacred utterances bhūr, bhuvaḥ, suvaḥ and a fourth, mahaḥ, identified with Brahman (1.5).

The section ends with the instruction the teacher gives the pupil at the close of his study (1.11), often called the “convocation address”:

satyaṃ vada / dharmaṃ cara / svādhyāyān mā pramadaḥ mātṛdevo bhava / pitṛdevo bhava / ācāryadevo bhava / atithidevo bhava Translation: “Speak the truth. Follow dharma. Do not neglect self-study. Let your mother be a god to you. Let your father be a god to you. Let your teacher be a god to you. Let your guest be a god to you.” — Taittirīya Upaniṣad, Śikṣā Vallī 11

docs.title: 3.3.3 The Ānanda Vallī: The Five Sheaths (Pañca-Kośa)
docs.text:
The second section, the Ānanda Vallī, opens with the definition of Brahman that the Vedāntins quoted more than any other, and goes on to describe the five “selves” that later Vedānta called sheaths (pañca-kośa).

satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma / yo veda nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ parame vyoman / so’śnute sarvān kāmān saha / brahmaṇā vipaścitā Translation: “Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinity. He who knows It as existing in the cave (of the heart), in the highest space — he enjoys all desires together with the omniscient Brahman.” — Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1

Śaṅkara’s analysis of the three terms — that they define Brahman’s own nature by excluding their opposites rather than attributing properties to it — is discussed in Section 6.2. The text then describes a cosmogony in which space, wind, fire, water and earth emerge in turn from the self (2.1), and a series of five selves, each within the last (Figure 3.3).

Figure 3.3. The Five Sheaths (Pañca-Kośa) of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, as later Vedānta pictured them Table 3.3. The Five Sheaths: Summary (with the later Advaita correlation to the three bodies) Kośa (Sheath) Nature Body Description Annamaya Food/Physical Gross (Sthūla) The physical body, made of and sustained by food Prāṇamaya Vital/Energy Subtle (Sūkṣma) The life-force; the five prāṇas Manomaya Mental Subtle The mind and its operations; thinking, doubting, etc. Vijñānamaya Intellectual Subtle The discriminating intellect (buddhi); the sense of “I” Ānandamaya Blissful Causal (Kāraṇa) The sheath of bliss experienced in deep sleep

The Taittirīya itself describes each “self” (ātman) as filling the previous one and having the same human shape; it does not use the word kośa (“sheath”), which comes from later Vedānta. The correlation of the sheaths with the gross, subtle and causal bodies shown in Table 3.3, and the practice of “discriminating the five sheaths” (pañca-kośa-viveka), are likewise later Advaita developments, found for example in Vidyāraṇya’s Pañcadaśī. In Advaita the Ātman is none of these five sheaths: one recognises in turn “I am not the body”, “I am not the vital breath” and so on, arriving at the witness of all five. Śaṅkara’s commentary on Brahmasūtra 1.1.12–19 accordingly argues that even the “self made of bliss” (ānandamaya) is not Brahman itself. Other Vedāntins read the same sūtras the other way: Rāmānuja, and the earlier commentators whose view Śaṅkara reports, take the self made of bliss to be Brahman. Contemporary yoga therapy has adopted the five-sheath model as a framework for organising interventions at the level of body, breath, mind, understanding and meditative absorption; this is a modern adaptation, distinct from the Upaniṣad’s own purpose of leading the student to Brahman, and not evidence of therapeutic efficacy.

docs.title: 3.3.4 The Scale of Bliss (Ānanda-Mīmāṃsā)
docs.text:
The Ānanda Vallī (2.8) also contains an ascending scale of bliss (ānanda-mīmāṃsā), a “calculus” of the grades of happiness (Table 3.4).

Table 3.4. The Ascending Scale of Bliss in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad Level Being Measure of Bliss 1 A blessed human youth, learned, healthy, strong, possessing the whole earth 1 unit of human bliss 2 Human Gandharvas 100 \(\times\) human bliss 3 Divine Gandharvas 100 \(\times\) level 2 4 Pitṛs (Ancestors in their eternal world) 100 \(\times\) level 3 5 Devas born in the Ājāna heaven 100 \(\times\) level 4 6 Karma Devas (gods by merit) 100 \(\times\) level 5 7 Devas (the gods proper) 100 \(\times\) level 6 8 Indra (king of gods) 100 \(\times\) level 7 9 Bṛhaspati (preceptor of gods) 100 \(\times\) level 8 10 Prajāpati (the Creator) 100 \(\times\) level 9 11 Brahman 100 \(\times\) level 10; and, in the next section (2.9), the bliss of Brahman “from which words turn back, together with the mind”

By making each level a hundredfold greater than the previous one, the Upaniṣad builds a scale that rises through astronomical magnitudes: ten hundredfold steps make the bliss at the top \(100^{10}\) (\(10^{20}\)) times the bliss of the ideal human. A refrain adds that each grade of bliss is also enjoyed by “a man learned in the Veda who is free from desire” (śrotriyasya cākāmahatasya): the point is that freedom from desire gives access to what no worldly achievement can. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.3.32–33) states a similar idea and a similar scale: “on a mere fraction of this very bliss other creatures live.” Advaita commentators explain all pleasure as Brahman’s bliss filtered through the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of body, mind and senses.

docs.title: 3.3.5 The Bhṛgu Vallī: The Seeker’s Journey
docs.text:
The third section, the Bhṛgu Vallī, narrates the story of Bhṛgu, son of Varuṇa, who is instructed by his father to discover Brahman through tapas (austerity, contemplation). Bhṛgu meditates and successively identifies Brahman with food, then with prāṇa, then with mind, then with vijñāna, and finally with ānanda (bliss). Each identification is deeper than the previous one, and the narrative mirrors the five selves of the Ānanda Vallī. It culminates in the sentence:

ānando brahmeti vyajānāt Translation: “He understood: Bliss (ānanda) is Brahman!” — Taittirīya Upaniṣad, Bhṛgu Vallī 6

docs.title: 3.4.1 Overview and Vedic Affiliation
docs.text:
The Aitareya Upaniṣad belongs to the Ṛgveda (Aitareya Āraṇyaka) and is the only mukhya Upaniṣad from the Ṛgveda upon which Śaṅkara wrote a commentary. It comprises three chapters dealing with creation, the nature of the Self, and the identity of the Self with Brahman.

Aitareya Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Ṛgveda (Śākala Śākhā, Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.4–6) Chapters: 3 (dealing with creation, birth, and the Self) Style: Prose Central Theme: Creation; the Self as pure consciousness Key Teaching: Prajñānaṃ Brahma (Consciousness is Brahman)

docs.title: 3.4.2 The Creation Narrative
docs.text:
The Aitareya opens with a creation narrative:

ātmā vā idam eka evāgra āsīt / nānyat kiñcana miṣat / sa īkṣata lokān nu sṛjā iti Translation: “In the beginning, the Ātman alone existed. Nothing else was there. He thought: ‘Let me create the worlds.’ ” — Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1.1

He created the worlds of the celestial waters (ambhas), the light-particles (marīci), the mortal world (mara) and the waters below (āpaḥ). Then the cosmic Person (Puruṣa) was fashioned, and from this Person the organs of perception and action and their deities emerged. Finally the self, asking how this body could exist without it, split open the suture of the skull (sīman) and entered through that door, called vidṛti (1.3.12). Creation thus follows an act of reflection (īkṣaṇa, “he thought”), and Vedāntins later cited the passage as evidence that the first cause is conscious.

docs.title: 3.4.3 The Threefold Birth
docs.text:
The Aitareya’s second chapter presents a teaching on the threefold birth of a man (2.1.1–4):

  1. The first birth is when the man deposits his semen, his own “essence”, in the woman.

  2. The second birth is the delivery of the child, who then takes the father’s place in performing meritorious works.

  3. The third birth is the father’s rebirth after death, when he departs from this world and is born again.

The chapter closes by citing the Ṛg-Vedic seer Vāmadeva, who, already knowing this while still in the womb, broke free of his “hundred iron fortresses” and became immortal (2.1.5–6).

docs.title: 3.4.4 Prajñānaṃ Brahma
docs.text:
The third chapter asks “Who is this self?” and answers with one of the sentences later counted among the four Mahāvākyas (Great Sayings):

prajñānaṃ brahma Translation: “Consciousness is Brahman.” (or “Intelligence is Brahman.”) — Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.1.3

Before this declaration, the text lists the forms of knowing and willing — sensation, perception, discrimination, intelligence, insight, resolution, thought, understanding, impulse, memory, purpose, life, desire and control — and calls them all “names of prajñāna” (3.1.2). Gods, elements and every kind of creature are then said to be “guided by prajñāna” and “established in prajñāna” (Figure 3.4).

Figure 3.4. Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.1.2: the mental and vital functions it lists, all “names of prajñāna”

The Vedāntic commentators reconstruct the Aitareya as an argument in three stages. In the cosmological stage, the self creates the world by an act of seeing (īkṣaṇa), so that consciousness comes before the material world. In the anthropological stage, the same self that creates the cosmos enters each body and animates it. In the epistemological stage, every cognitive function is a name of one prajñāna, the single thread running through cognitive diversity. On this reading the Aitareya treats consciousness as prior to and more basic than matter, and Advaita reads it as a statement that consciousness is the only reality (Chapter 5). The text itself is a creation story followed by an identification; it does not argue against any rival view of the world, and the theistic schools read its prajñāna as the knowing Lord rather than as attributeless consciousness.

Modern Relevance: The Aitareya and Contemporary Philosophy of Mind

Modern readers often compare the Vedāntic reading of the Aitareya with positions in contemporary philosophy of mind. The “hard problem of consciousness” formulated by David Chalmers (why is there subjective experience at all?) is most pressing for a framework that takes matter as fundamental and consciousness as something to be explained; the Vedāntic reading reverses that order of explanation. The “panpsychist” views of philosophers such as Galen Strawson and Philip Goff, which hold that consciousness is a fundamental feature of reality, are a closer parallel, though Advaita goes further in making consciousness the only fundamental reality. Such comparisons are analogies between frameworks, not claims about what the text’s authors intended.

docs.title: 3.5 Reading the Upaniṣads Together: Apparent Contradictions
docs.text:
The texts read in this chapter and the last do not say the same thing. Some passages seem to support monism, others a distinction between God and the soul; some describe creation, others (in Gauḍapāda’s reading) deny it; some describe a personal Lord, others an impersonal Absolute. Modern scholars generally take these differences as evidence of several strands of speculation composed over several centuries. The traditional response is the principle of samanvaya (harmonisation) on which the Brahmasūtra of Bādarāyaṇa is built (Section 11.2): the Upaniṣads are taken to teach one coherent doctrine, and apparent conflicts are resolved by rules of interpretation. Each school harmonises the texts differently. Table 3.5 gives the Advaita solution; Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita resolve the same tensions in favour of real difference, taking the texts of identity to express the soul’s dependence on or inseparability from God (Chapter 11).

Table 3.5. Apparent Contradictions and Their Harmonisation in Advaita Apparent Position A Apparent Position B Harmonisation (Samanvaya) Brahman creates the world (Taittirīya) Nothing is ever created (Māṇḍūkya Kārikā) Creation is provisionally described for pedagogical purposes; ultimately, Brahman alone exists Ātman is described with attributes (Chāndogya) Ātman is beyond all description (Bṛhadāraṇyaka) Attributes describe the conditioned Brahman (saguṇa); the unconditioned Brahman (nirguṇa) is beyond predication Individual soul is distinct from Brahman (Muṇḍaka 3.1.1–2) Individual soul is identical with Brahman (Chāndogya 6.8.7) The distinction is apparent, caused by ignorance; the identity is the ultimate truth

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: Chapter 4: The Mukhya Upaniṣads — Part III
docs.text:
In the beginning, dear boy, this was Being alone, one only without a second. It thought, “Let me become many. Let me bring forth.” — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1–3

This chapter reads the two oldest and longest Upaniṣads, the Chāndogya and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, and the latest of the eleven usually counted as principal, the Śvetāśvatara. Most of the doctrines that later Vedānta systematised are first found in these texts. Because the two oldest Upaniṣads are also our best evidence for the world in which the teaching began, three sections follow them: on their ritual meditations, on the women who appear in them, and on the kings, brahmins and patrons among whom they were taught. The chapter closes with two further early Upaniṣads outside the ten-text canon, the Kauṣītaki and the Maitrī.

docs.title: 4.1.1 Overview and Vedic Affiliation
docs.text:
The Chāndogya Upaniṣad is one of the two oldest and most extensive Upaniṣads (alongside the Bṛhadāraṇyaka). It belongs to the Sāmaveda, specifically the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa. The name derives from the chandoga priests who chant the hymns of the Sāmaveda.

Chāndogya Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Sāmaveda Structure: 8 prapāṭhakas (chapters) Style: Prose with embedded verses Length: One of the longest Upaniṣads Central Themes: Tat tvam asi; Sad-Vidyā; meditations on Oṃ and Sāman Key Figures: Uddālaka Āruṇi and Śvetaketu; Sanatkumāra and Nārada

docs.title: 4.1.2 The Sad-Vidyā: The Teaching of Being
docs.text:
The sixth chapter contains the Sad-Vidyā (the Knowledge of Sat, Being), taught by Uddālaka Āruṇi to his son Śvetaketu. For the Vedānta schools it became the central text on the relation between the self and the ground of the world, and it is the locus classicus of Upaniṣadic teaching method.

The young Śvetaketu, sent away for Vedic study at the age of twelve, returns home at twenty-four, “conceited, considering himself learned, and arrogant” (6.1.2). His father asks:

uta tam ādeśam aprākṣyaḥ yenāśrutaṃ śrutaṃ bhavaty amataṃ matam avijñātaṃ vijñātam iti Translation: “Have you asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known?” — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3

Śvetaketu, humbled, asks his father to teach him. Uddālaka begins with three illustrations: by knowing a lump of clay, all things made of clay are known, “the modification being a verbal handle, a mere name”; so too with copper and iron (6.1.4–6; Section 6.4.2). He then teaches that in the beginning there was Sat (Being) alone, one without a second. Being thought, “Let me become many”, and the world emerged through a process of differentiation — first heat (tejas), then water (ap), then food (anna).

Each section of the teaching that follows concludes with a refrain:

tat tvam asi, Śvetaketo Translation: “That thou art, O Śvetaketu!” — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7 et seq.

The sentence is repeated nine times in the sixth chapter, each time after a different illustration (Table 4.1). The repetition drives the teaching home from several sides, and the meaning of the refrain, which the schools later disputed, is examined in Section 5.4.

Table 4.1. The Nine Contexts of the Refrain Tat Tvam Asi in Chāndogya 6.8–16 No. Analogy Teaching 1 (6.8) Sleep, hunger and thirst In deep sleep one “merges with Being”; Being is the root of food, water and heat 2 (6.9) Bees and honey Nectar from many trees becomes one honey; creatures merging in Being do not know “I am this one” 3 (6.10) Rivers and ocean Rivers become one in the ocean and no longer know “I am this river” 4 (6.11) A great tree and its sap The tree lives while pervaded by life (jīva); the body dies, but life does not 5 (6.12) The banyan fruit and seed Cutting the seed, one sees nothing; from that subtle essence the great tree grows 6 (6.13) Salt in water Invisible, the salt is tasted everywhere in the water 7 (6.14) A man blindfolded and left far from Gandhāra Directed by others, he finds his way home; so one who has a teacher knows 8 (6.15) A dying man surrounded by relatives His speech merges into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat, heat into the highest deity 9 (6.16) The accused man and the heated axe The truthful man is not burned; the untruthful is

The method is as instructive as the doctrine.

Uddālaka’s Method of Teaching

  1. Concrete before abstract: each principle is first illustrated by a tangible, observable phenomenon before it is stated in general terms.

  2. Question-driven learning: Śvetaketu’s requests for further instruction drive the dialogue forward.

  3. Repetition with variation: the refrain is repeated in nine different contexts, so that the teaching is approached from several sides.

  4. Demonstration: the pupil is asked to perform simple experiments — fasting for fifteen days to observe the dependence of mind on food (6.7), splitting the banyan seed (6.12), dissolving salt in water (6.13) — rather than accept the doctrine on authority alone.

docs.title: 4.1.3 Other Notable Teachings
docs.text:
Beyond the Sad-Vidyā, the Chāndogya contains:

  • The Bhūman Vidyā (Chapter 7): Nārada approaches Sanatkumāra and progressively learns that behind name, speech, mind, will, thought, contemplation, understanding, strength, food, water, fire, space, memory, hope, and life — there is the Bhūman (the Infinite), which alone is true happiness.

  • The Dāhara Vidyā (Chapter 8): Meditation on the tiny space (dāhara ākāśa) within the heart, which contains within itself the entire universe; and the instruction of Indra by Prajāpati, who leads him from the body through the dreaming and sleeping self to the self beyond them (8.7–12).

  • The Pañcāgni Vidyā (Chapter 5): The doctrine of the five fires, explaining the process of rebirth through a cosmic sacrificial framework (Section 6.6.2).

  • The story of Satyakāma Jābāla (4.4): A boy who does not know who his father is reports truthfully what his mother told him; the teacher Hāridrumata Gautama concludes that “no non-Brāhmaṇa could speak thus” and accepts him. Modern readers often cite the story as valuing character over birth; within the text, however, truthfulness is treated as a sign of Brāhmaṇa birth, so the story confirms rather than abolishes the varṇa criterion for Vedic study.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Overview and Vedic Affiliation
docs.text:
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (bṛhat = great, āraṇyaka = forest text) is the longest of the Upaniṣads and covers more ground than any other. It belongs to the Śukla Yajurveda and forms the concluding portion of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (book 14). It survives in two recensions, the Kāṇva and the Mādhyandina; Śaṅkara commented on the Kāṇva.

Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Śukla Yajurveda (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 14) Structure: 6 adhyāyas in 3 sections (kāṇḍas) Length: The longest of all Upaniṣads Style: Prose with embedded verses Central Themes: Aham Brahmāsmi; nature of Ātman; Yājñavalkya’s teachings Key Figures: Yājñavalkya, Maitreyī, Gārgī, Janaka

docs.title: 4.2.2 The Three Sections (Kāṇḍas)
docs.text:
Table 4.2 sets out the structure of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka in its three sections.

Table 4.2. Structure of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Kāṇḍa Chapters Content Madhu Kāṇḍa 1–2 The “Honey” section: the Aśvamedha allegory; the Madhu Vidyā; Aham Brahmāsmi Yājñavalkya (or Muni) Kāṇḍa 3–4 Yājñavalkya’s debates at Janaka’s court; dialogue with Maitreyī Khila Kāṇḍa 5–6 Supplementary teachings; meditations; lineage of teachers

docs.title: 4.2.3 Yājñavalkya
docs.text: The central figure of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka is Yājñavalkya, the most fully drawn philosophical personality of the Upaniṣads. The text presents him in three settings: the debate at Janaka’s court (chapter 3), the private instruction of Janaka (chapter 4), and the dialogue with his wife Maitreyī (2.4 and 4.5).

docs.title: The debate at Janaka’s court
docs.text:
King Janaka of Videha announces a prize of a thousand cows with gold tied to their horns for the most learned Brāhmaṇa. Yājñavalkya tells his pupil to drive the cows home before the contest has begun, and then answers his challengers one by one at the assembly (brahmodya) convened by the king (3.1–9). The questions move from the sacrifice to death, the inner self, the “thread” and the “inner controller” of the world, and the imperishable, so that the answers build a cumulative case about the Ātman (Table 4.3). The social setting of the contest is examined in Section 4.5.

Table 4.3. Yājñavalkya’s Challengers and Their Questions (Bṛhadāraṇyaka III) Challenger Question Yājñavalkya’s Answer Aśvala (3.1) How does the sacrificer escape death and time? Through the priests, identified with speech/fire, sight/sun, breath/wind and mind/moon Ārtabhāga (3.2) What happens to a person after death? The faculties merge into their cosmic counterparts; taking Ārtabhāga aside, Yājñavalkya says privately: “one becomes good by good action, bad by bad action” Bhujyu (3.3) Where have the descendants of Parikṣit gone? To where the performers of the horse sacrifice go, at the edge of the world Uṣasta (3.4) What is the Brahman that is directly perceived, the Self within all? “The one who breathes in with your breath … is your self, which is within all”; the seer of seeing cannot be seen Kahola (3.5) The same question The Self that transcends hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age and death Gārgī (3.6) On what is everything woven? Through water, wind, the intermediate region and the higher worlds to the worlds of Brahman; then silenced with a warning Uddālaka Āruṇi (3.7) What is the thread (sūtra) and the inner controller (antaryāmin)? Wind is the thread; the inner controller is “your self, the immortal” Gārgī (3.8) On what is space woven? On the imperishable (akṣara), at whose command sun and moon, heaven and earth stand apart Śākalya (3.9) How many gods are there? From 3,306, through progressive reductions, to one — breath (prāṇa), called Brahman

The contest ends violently. After the long exchange on the number of the gods, Yājñavalkya turns the tables and asks Śākalya about “the person taught in the Upaniṣads”, warning that his head will shatter if he cannot answer; Śākalya cannot, and his head shatters (3.9.26). The same threat had been used earlier to silence Gārgī (3.6). The motif belongs to the older brahmodya contests, in which failure to answer a riddle was believed to carry real danger (Black 2007). Later readers took it as a warning that ultimate questions are not mere debating points; read historically, it also shows how much was at stake, in prestige and in wealth, for the brahmins who competed.

docs.title: Maitreyī
docs.text:
In the dialogue with Maitreyī (2.4 and 4.5), Yājñavalkya, preparing to leave the household, offers to divide his wealth between his two wives. Maitreyī asks: “If the whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would I be immortal thereby?” Yājñavalkya replies: “No. Your life would be like that of the wealthy. There is no hope of immortality through wealth.” Maitreyī answers: “What should I do with that by which I do not become immortal? Teach me, Sir, what you know.”

na vā are patyuḥ kāmāya patiḥ priyo bhavaty ātmanas tu kāmāya patiḥ priyo bhavati Translation: “Verily, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear, but for the sake of the Self that the husband is dear…” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5

Yājñavalkya goes on to teach that all love and desire derive from the Ātman, which is therefore to be seen, heard, reflected on and contemplated (2.4.5; Section 5.9).

docs.title: 4.2.4 The Neti Neti Teaching
docs.text:
Yājñavalkya’s description of the Ātman is the negation neti neti (“not this, not this”; Figure 4.1):

sa eṣa neti nety ātmā / agṛhyo na hi gṛhyate / aśīryo na hi śīryate / asaṅgo na hi sajyate / asito na vyathate na riṣyati Translation: “This Self is (described as) ‘not this, not this.’ It is incomprehensible, for it cannot be comprehended; indestructible, for it cannot be destroyed; unattached, for it does not attach itself; unfettered, it does not suffer, it is not injured.” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26

Figure 4.1. Yājñavalkya’s Neti Neti: a schematic illustration of the apophatic method (the negations shown are illustrative, not quoted)

docs.title: 4.2.5 The Prayer of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka
docs.text:
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka also contains a prayer that is still recited widely. In the text it is a formula (abhyāroha) muttered by the sacrificer during the chanting of the pavamāna hymns, and the Upaniṣad itself explains each line (1.3.28):

asato mā sad gamaya tamaso mā jyotir gamaya mṛtyor māmṛtaṃ gamaya Translation: “From the unreal, lead me to the Real. From darkness, lead me to Light. From death, lead me to Immortality.” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.28

docs.title: 4.3 Ritual, Correspondence and Meditation: The Vidyās
docs.text:
A reader who knows the Chāndogya and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka only from the passages quoted so far will be surprised by the rest of them. Much of both texts is about ritual: the meaning of the chants, the hidden identities of the sacrificial horse, the correct offering into the breaths, rites for wealth and for the conception of a son. Olivelle stresses in the introduction to his translation that these concerns are not a preface to the philosophy but the setting from which it grew (Olivelle 1998, 1996). The Upaniṣads continue the Brāhmaṇas’ search for the hidden connections (bandhu, upaniṣad; Section 1.1) between three domains: the ritual (adhiyajña), the cosmos and its deities (adhidaivata), and the human person (adhyātma). To know the connection is to command what it connects.

The opening of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.1) is typical. The horse of the royal horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) is identified, limb by limb, with the universe: the dawn is its head, the sun its eye, the wind its breath, the year its body. The Chāndogya begins (1.1–2.24) with meditations on the chanted portion of the Sāman, the udgītha, identified with Oṃ. A chain of essences leads from the beings to the earth, the waters, the plants, man, speech, the verse and the chant, and the udgītha is declared the essence of essences (1.1.2–3). The “fivefold” and “sevenfold” Sāman are then correlated with the worlds, the rains, the seasons, the animals and the breaths. In the Chāndogya’s own “honey doctrine” (3.1–11) the sun is the honey of the gods, produced from the hymns of the four Vedas as bees make honey from flowers. A person’s life is interpreted as a soma sacrifice, its three periods as the three pressings (3.16–17). In the “fire-offering in the breath” (prāṇāgnihotra, 5.19–24) the first five mouthfuls of a meal are offered to the five breaths, an internalised form of the daily fire-offering. The supplementary chapters of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (5–6) contain short meditations, among them the thunder’s “da da da” read as the injunctions to self-restraint, giving and compassion (5.2), the meditation on the Gāyatrī (5.14), a “stirred drink” (mantha) rite for attaining greatness (6.3; compare Chāndogya 5.2), and the procreative rites of 6.4.

These meditations are called vidyās or upāsanās: in each the worshipper contemplates one thing as another, the chant as Oṃ, the breath as the sacrificial fire, Brahman as the space in the heart (Table 4.4). The third chapter of the Brahmasūtra later set out to decide which vidyās taught in different texts are one and the same and may be combined (Section 11.2). Interpreters have placed this material in very different ways. In Advaita the upāsanās are meditations on the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman; they purify the mind and may lead after death, by the path of the gods, to gradual liberation (krama-mukti), but the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman alone liberates directly. The theistic schools give meditation and worship a more central place. Historians, for their part, read the ritual correspondences as the matrix of the philosophy: the doctrine that the self within the heart is the essence of the whole world (Chāndogya 3.14) is the last term of a long search for the essence (rasa) and the hidden link.

Table 4.4. Principal Vidyās (Sacred Meditations) in the Chāndogya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Vidyā Source Nature and Object of Meditation Udgītha Vidyā Chānd. 1.1–9 Meditation on the udgītha (the chanted Oṃ of the Sāman) as the essence of all things Madhu Vidyā Chānd. 3.1–11; Bṛhad. 2.5 The sun as the honey of the gods (Chāndogya); the mutual dependence of all things, each “honey” to the others (Bṛhadāraṇyaka) Śāṇḍilya Vidyā Chānd. 3.14 Meditation on Brahman as the Self within the heart, “greater than the great” Pañcāgni Vidyā Chānd. 5.3–10; Bṛhad. 6.2 The five cosmic fires; the cycle of rebirth; the two paths (Devāyana, Pitṛyāna) Vaiśvānara Vidyā Chānd. 5.11–24 Meditation on the cosmic Self as the universal fire, ending in the fire-offering in the breath Sad-Vidyā Chānd. 6 Meditation on Being (Sat) as the sole reality; Tat tvam asi Bhūman Vidyā Chānd. 7 Progressive meditation from name through speech, mind, will, etc., to the Infinite Dāhara Vidyā Chānd. 8.1 Meditation on the tiny space within the heart as containing the entire universe Gāyatrī Vidyā Bṛhad. 5.14 Meditation on the Gāyatrī verse and its feet as the worlds, the Vedas and the breaths

docs.title: 4.4 Women Philosophers in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
docs.text: The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad features the two best-known women thinkers of the Vedic tradition: Gārgī Vācaknavī and Maitreyī. Their presence matters for the history of women in early Indian intellectual life, and it needs to be read carefully, neither inflated nor dismissed.

docs.title: 4.4.1 Gārgī Vācaknavī: The Philosopher-Debater
docs.text:
Gārgī, the daughter of Vacaknu, is one of the challengers of Yājñavalkya at King Janaka’s philosophical assembly (Bṛhad. 3.6 and 3.8). She presses her questions further than any other challenger, asking: “On what is space (ākāśa) woven, like warp and woof?” Yājñavalkya responds with the concept of the Akṣara (the Imperishable):

etad vai tad akṣaraṃ gārgi brāhmaṇā abhivadanty asthūlam anaṇv ahrasvam adīrgham Translation: “That, O Gārgī, which the knowers of Brahman call the Imperishable (Akṣara), is neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long…” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8

Gārgī is the only woman among Yājñavalkya’s challengers and the only one who questions him twice. She is portrayed not as a passive listener but as a formidable dialectician; on her first round Yājñavalkya silences her with the warning “do not question too much, lest your head shatter” (3.6), and on her second she frames her questions as two arrows aimed at him (3.8.2) before acknowledging his victory.

docs.title: 4.4.2 Maitreyī: The Seeker of Immortality
docs.text:
The Maitreyī dialogue (Bṛhad. 2.4 and 4.5), summarised above, presents her as the seeker who prefers the knowledge of immortality to wealth. The later version (4.5.1) introduces her with a telling contrast: of Yājñavalkya’s two wives, “Maitreyī was a discourser on Brahman (brahmavādinī), while Kātyāyanī had only a woman’s understanding (strīprajñā).”

Reading the Evidence on Women

Gārgī and Maitreyī show that at least some women of the late Vedic period could take part in philosophical discussion and be remembered for it; later tradition honours them as brahmavādinīs. The evidence is nonetheless thin and exceptional. They are two named women among dozens of male teachers; the phrase “a woman’s understanding” presupposes that ordinary women were not expected to engage in such enquiry; and the same Upaniṣad (6.4) contains procreative rites that treat the wife largely as an object of ritual control. The later Dharmasūtras and Manusmṛti (c. 2nd century CE) restricted women’s access to Vedic study and initiation further. It is therefore more accurate to say that the Upaniṣads preserve memorable exceptions within a patriarchal society than that they describe an age of equality later lost (Black 2007).

docs.title: 4.5 Kings, Brahmins and Patrons: The Social World of the Early Upaniṣads
docs.text: The dialogues of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya are set in a recognisable society. They take place at royal courts, at sacrifices and in the households of teachers, in the late Vedic kingdoms of northern India: the Kuru-Pañcāla country, Kāśī, Videha and, in the north-west, Kekaya. Brahmins travel to compete for patronage, kings sponsor sacrifices and contests, and wealth is counted in cattle and gold. Reading the narrative frames together with the doctrine shows who taught, who learned, who paid and who was left outside the circle (Black 2007).

docs.title: 4.5.1 Courts, Contests and Cattle
docs.text:
The great debate of Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3 (Section 4.2.3) begins with a sacrifice. Janaka of Videha performs it with lavish fees (bahudakṣiṇa), and the brahmins of the Kuru-Pañcāla country assemble for it. Wishing to know which of them is the most learned, the king sets apart a thousand cows with ten measures (pāda) of gold tied to the horns of each (3.1.1). No one dares to claim them until Yājñavalkya tells his own pupil to drive them home. When the angry brahmins ask whether he really thinks himself the most learned, he replies that he bows to the most learned but simply wants the cows (3.1.2). The scene takes three things for granted: that knowledge of Brahman can be tested in public, that it is rewarded in wealth, and that the king who supplies the wealth presides over the contest.

The private instruction of Janaka in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4 follows the same pattern of royal patronage:

  • Janaka reports what six earlier teachers had told him. Each had identified Brahman with a single faculty: speech, breath, sight, hearing, mind or heart. Two of these teachers, Satyakāma Jābāla and Vidagdha Śākalya, are known from other passages. Yājñavalkya calls each answer only “one leg” of Brahman.

  • After each answer the king offers a thousand cows with a bull as big as an elephant. Each time Yājñavalkya declines, saying that his father held that one should not take a fee without having fully instructed (4.1.2–7).

  • The teaching on dream, deep sleep and death that follows (4.3–4.4) is given to a king. The text notes that at one point Yājñavalkya grew afraid that this clever king would drive him from every position he held (4.3.33).

  • At the end Janaka gives the people of Videha, and himself with them, to Yājñavalkya as his servants (4.4.23).

Kings competed for the prestige such patronage brought. When Ajātaśatru of Kāśī is offered a teaching, he promises a thousand cows for the mere offer and remarks that people run about crying “Janaka! Janaka!” (2.1.1). A king’s fame as a patron of learning was something a rival king wanted for himself.

docs.title: 4.5.2 Kings Who Teach Brahmins
docs.text:
In several dialogues the usual roles are reversed, and a king instructs brahmins.

  • Ajātaśatru and Bālāki (Bṛhad. 2.1; Kauṣītaki 4). The proud brahmin Gārgya Bālāki offers a dozen formulations of Brahman: the person in the sun, in the moon, in lightning, in space and so on. The king answers each by saying that he already venerates that person under a better name. When Bālāki falls silent, Ajātaśatru observes that it is against the natural order (pratiloma) for a brahmin to come to a kṣatriya expecting to be taught about Brahman, but that he will make him understand all the same (2.1.15). He takes him by the hand to a sleeping man. He wakes the man and asks where the person consisting of consciousness was during sleep and from where it returned. The answer is that it rests in the space within the heart, and that from this self all breaths, worlds, gods and beings issue like sparks from a fire (2.1.20).

  • Pravāhaṇa Jaivali (Chānd. 5.3–10; Bṛhad. 6.2). The Pañcāla king puts five questions to the young Śvetaketu, who cannot answer them. His father, Gautama Āruṇi, goes to the king himself. Refusing the wealth the king offers, he asks for the teaching and becomes his pupil by declaration alone, as men of earlier times are said to have done (Bṛhad. 6.2.7). Before teaching him the five fires and the two paths of the dead (Section 6.6.2), the king says that this knowledge had never before gone to brahmins. That, he adds, is why rule in all the worlds has belonged to the kṣatriya alone (Chānd. 5.3.7; compare Bṛhad. 6.2.8).

  • Aśvapati Kaikeya (Chānd. 5.11–24). Five wealthy and learned householders, among them Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava and Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, ask themselves “What is our self? What is Brahman?” They turn to Uddālaka Āruṇi, who doubts that he can answer and leads them to Aśvapati, king of the Kekayas. The king offers them gifts. When they hesitate, he assures them that his kingdom harbours no thief, no miser, no drunkard, no one without a sacrificial fire, no unlearned man and no adulterer, still less an adulteress (5.11.5). The next morning they come to him “fuel in hand” as pupils, and he teaches them without performing the rite of initiation (anupanīya, 5.11.7). The teaching is the self as Vaiśvānara, the universal fire, of which each of them had worshipped only a part.

The Kauṣītaki’s Citra Gāṅgyāyani, who teaches Āruṇi the journey of the dead, belongs to the same series (Section 4.7.1).

These scenes once supported a “kṣatriya thesis”, proposed around 1900 by Richard Garbe and others and surveyed by Black (Black 2007). On this view the doctrines of the self and of rebirth arose among warriors and were later taken over by the priests. The objections are serious:

  • The dialogues were composed and transmitted by brahmins, inside the ritual texts of brahmin schools.

  • Ajātaśatru’s own remark about the natural order presupposes the brahmin norm it momentarily reverses.

  • The reversal has a literary function: it marks a teaching as new, as something the ritual expert does not yet possess, and it lends that teaching the prestige of royal authority.

Brian Black reads these dialogues as negotiating a relationship of mutual need. Brahmins needed royal patrons, and kings needed the legitimacy that brahmin knowledge conferred. The ideal Upaniṣadic king is therefore one who both rewards and understands the teaching (Black 2007). It remains possible that some ideas did circulate first among the court elite, but the texts do not allow us to trace a separate “warrior philosophy”.

docs.title: 4.5.3 Teachers, Pupils and the Limits of the Circle
docs.text:
Within this world the transmission of knowledge followed set forms. The pupil approached a teacher with fuel for the teacher’s fire in his hands (samitpāṇi; Muṇḍ. 1.2.12), lived in his household, tended his cattle and served him for years. Śvetaketu left at twelve and returned at twenty-four, having learned all the Vedas (Chānd. 6.1.2). Satyakāma Jābāla drove his teacher’s four hundred cows away and did not return until they had become a thousand (4.4–9). In the Chāndogya’s story, Indra lived as a student with Prajāpati for a hundred and one years before he was taught the self (8.7–12).

The teaching was regarded as a possession to be guarded. A father may impart the doctrine of Brahman to his eldest son or to a worthy resident pupil and to no one else. He must not part with it even for the whole earth surrounded by water and filled with treasure (Chānd. 3.11.5–6).

The story of Raikva shows the boundaries of this circle being tested and redrawn (Chānd. 4.1–2):

  • King Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, a generous donor who had rest-houses built everywhere so that people would eat his food, overhears two geese. They mock his merit beside that of “Raikva with the cart”.

  • He finds Raikva sitting under a cart, scratching his sores. He offers him six hundred cows, a gold necklace and a chariot drawn by mules. Raikva sends him away, calling him “śūdra”.

  • Jānaśruti returns with a thousand cows and his daughter, and Raikva relents. He receives the villages that came to bear his name in the Mahāvṛṣa country (4.2.5) and teaches the king the doctrine of the “absorbers” (saṃvarga): wind in the cosmos and breath in the person.

A kṣatriya addressed as a śūdra was a problem for later exegesis. The Brahmasūtra (1.3.34) explains the word by a folk etymology, which Śaṅkara spells out in his commentary: the king “ran to grief” (śuc) on hearing the geese, so the word does not describe his birth. On this basis Śaṅkara, commenting on 1.3.34–38, concludes that the passage gives no warrant for teaching the Veda to śūdras (Section 1.15).

The circle was narrow. The teachers named in the older Upaniṣads are almost all brahmin or kṣatriya men. Gārgī, who questions Yājñavalkya in open debate, and Maitreyī, who receives his teaching, are remembered as exceptions (Section 4.4), and Satyakāma’s acceptance confirms the varṇa criterion rather than abolishing it (Section 4.1). The whole enterprise rested on agrarian and pastoral wealth that kings could command and give away. None of this diminishes the philosophy. It does show that the claim that the self lies beyond every social distinction was first made inside a society that kept those distinctions firmly in place, and the later debate over who may hear the Upaniṣads, traced in Chapters 8 and 11, begins here.

docs.title: 4.6.1 Overview and Vedic Affiliation
docs.text:
The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad belongs to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and is named after the sage Śvetāśvatara. It stands apart from the older principal Upaniṣads in combining several strands of thought: Upaniṣadic monism with devotional theism, Sāṅkhya-like enumerations with yoga practice, and abstract doctrine with personal devotion to a supreme Lord, named Rudra and Śiva (Table 4.5). Its verses are shared with the Kaṭha, the Muṇḍaka and the Vedic hymns (Table 1.7), and it is generally placed late among the verse Upaniṣads.

Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad — Quick Reference

Veda: Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Structure: 6 adhyāyas, 113 verses Style: Metrical (verse) Central Themes: Personal God (Īśvara); the triad of God, self, and matter Distinctive Feature: Synthesis of monism and theism; proto-Śaiva elements Key Imagery: The spider; the fire hidden in wood; the Lord as the cosmic magician

docs.title: 4.6.2 The Opening Questions
docs.text:
The Śvetāśvatara opens with a series of questions about the first cause:

kiṃ kāraṇaṃ brahma kutaḥ sma jātā jīvāma kena kva ca saṃpratiṣṭhāḥ adhiṣṭhitāḥ kena sukhetareṣu / vartāmahe brahmavido vyavasthām Translation: “What is the cause — is it Brahman? Whence were we born? By what do we live? And on what are we established? Governed by whom, O knowers of Brahman, do we live in pleasure and pain, each in our respective situation?” — Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.1

The next verse lists the candidates of the day — time, inherent nature (svabhāva), necessity, chance, the elements, the womb, the person — and rejects them all in favour of the power of God (1.2–3).

docs.title: 4.6.3 The Theistic Dimension
docs.text:
What distinguishes the Śvetāśvatara from most other Upaniṣads is its theistic character. While the older Upaniṣads speak primarily of an impersonal Brahman, the Śvetāśvatara speaks of a personal Lord (Īśvara) who is the cause of the universe, the ruler of all and the refuge of the devotee. This Lord is not opposed to Brahman: he is Brahman, approached as a personal reality.

eko devaḥ sarvabhūteṣu gūḍhaḥ sarvavyapī sarvabhūtāntarātmā karmādhyakṣaḥ sarvabhūtādhivāsaḥ sākṣī cetā kevalo nirguṇaś ca Translation: “The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings, the overseer of karma, dwelling in all beings, the witness, the consciousness, the alone, beyond the guṇas…” — Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11

docs.title: 4.6.4 The Spider, the Triad and Māyā
docs.text:
The Śvetāśvatara takes up the spider of the Muṇḍaka (1.1.7):

yas tantunābha iva tantubhiḥ pradhānajaiḥ svabhāvataḥ deva ekaḥ svam āvṛṇoti sa no dadhād brahmāpyayam Translation: “The one God who, like a spider, covers himself by his own nature with threads produced from primal matter (pradhāna) — may he grant us entry into Brahman.” — Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.10

It gives the image a theistic and Sāṅkhya colouring: the one God veils himself in the threads of primal matter, so that the world is at once his own self-concealment and the field from which the seeker asks to be led into Brahman. The same text uses Sāṅkhya terminology — puruṣa, prakṛti, the three guṇas — within a theistic framework. It identifies primal matter with māyā and calls the Lord the māyin, its wielder (4.9–10; Section 6.5). And it sets out a triad — the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment and the impeller (bhoktā bhogyaṃ preritāraṃ ca, 1.12; cf. 1.9) — that later Viśiṣṭādvaitins took up as their doctrine of three realities (tattva-traya) (Figure 4.2).

Figure 4.2. The Triad of Īśvara, Jīva, and Prakṛti in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad

docs.title: 4.6.5 Yoga Teachings
docs.text:
The Śvetāśvatara also contains one of the earliest descriptions of yoga practice in the Upaniṣadic corpus:

trirunnataṃ sthāpya samaṃ śarīraṃ hṛdīndriyāṇi manasā saṃniveśya Translation: “Holding the body with its three parts (head, neck, chest) erect and even, and directing the senses together with the mind into the heart…” — Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.8

The passage (2.8–15) describes the posture, the control of breath, the subduing of the senses, a suitable place for practice and the visual signs of progress. Composed in the last centuries BCE, it predates Patañjali’s Yogasūtra (c. 325–425 CE) by several centuries.

docs.title: 4.6.6 From Jñāna to Bhakti
docs.text:
The Śvetāśvatara stands historically between the impersonal monism of the older Upaniṣads and the personal theism of the Bhagavad Gītā, the Purāṇas and the later devotional movements. It develops the idea, already present in Kaṭha 1.2.23, that the self is attained through divine favour: it says that the sage Śvetāśvatara taught “by the power of his austerity and by the grace of God” (tapaḥprabhāvād devaprasādāc ca, 6.21). Alongside grace it insists on knowledge:

tam eva viditvāti mṛtyum eti nānyaḥ panthā vidyate ’yanāya Translation: “Only by knowing Him does one cross over death; there is no other path for liberation.” — Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8

The Upaniṣad closes with a verse on devotion:

yasya deve parā bhaktir yathā deve tathā gurau tasyaite kathitā hy arthāḥ prakāśante mahātmanaḥ Translation: “To one who has supreme devotion to God, and devotion to the Guru as to God, to that great soul these truths become manifest.” — Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23

This final verse contains one of the earliest occurrences of the word bhakti in Sanskrit literature and joins two ideas that would become pillars of later Indian religion: parā bhakti (supreme devotion) to God and devotion to the teacher. Some scholars regard the closing verses (6.22–23) as a later appendix, but theistic Vedāntins from Rāmānuja onward cite the verse as scriptural support for devotion as a means to liberation (Figure 4.3).

Figure 4.3. The Śvetāśvatara as a Bridge Between Impersonal Monism and Personal Theism Table 4.5. Philosophical Strands Combined in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad Philosophical Strand Source Tradition Form in the Śvetāśvatara Non-dual Brahman Older Upaniṣads The one God hidden in all beings, the inner Self of all (6.11; cf. 3.2, “Rudra is one; they did not stand for a second”) Personal God (Īśvara) Proto-theistic tradition Brahman is addressed as Rudra/Śiva, the compassionate Lord (3.2–4) Prakṛti and Puruṣa Sāṅkhya The text uses Sāṅkhya categories but subordinates them to a theistic framework (4.5–10) Yogic practice Yoga tradition Specific instructions on posture, breath, and withdrawal of senses (2.8–15) Māyā doctrine Vedāntic cosmology The Lord’s creative power (māyā) projects the manifold world (4.9–10) Devotion (bhakti) Devotional tradition The grace of God (6.21) and the seeker’s devotion to God and teacher (6.23)

The later schools read this combination very differently. For the theistic Vedāntins and for Śaiva Siddhānta (Section 11.13), it shows that knowledge of Brahman and love of God are complementary, the personal Lord being the highest reality. For Advaita, the personal Lord (Īśvara) is real at the empirical level but is finally transcended in the knowledge of attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman. The text itself supports both emphases, which is one reason it became so important to all of them.

docs.title: 4.7 Two Further Early Upaniṣads: the Kauṣītaki and the Maitrī
docs.text: R. E. Hume’s “thirteen principal Upaniṣads” (Section 1.6) include two texts that stand outside the ten-text canon because Śaṅkara did not comment on them: the Kauṣītaki and the Maitrī. Both matter for the history of Upaniṣadic thought, and a short account of each follows (Hume 1921; Olivelle 1998).

docs.title: 4.7.1 The Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad
docs.text:
The Kauṣītaki (also called the Kauṣītaki-Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad) belongs to the Ṛgveda and forms chapters 3–6 of the Kauṣītaki or Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka. It is a prose text of four chapters, which Olivelle places with the Taittirīya and Aitareya among the early prose Upaniṣads (Table 1.6). The four chapters are only loosely connected:

  1. The journey after death (chapter 1). Uddālaka Āruṇi, unable to answer a question that the king Citra Gāṅgyāyani had put to his son Śvetaketu, goes to the king “fuel in hand” as a pupil — another of the Upaniṣadic scenes in which a Brāhmaṇa learns from a Kṣatriya. Citra teaches that all who depart this world go first to the moon, which questions them; those who answer rightly travel on by the path of the gods to the world of Brahman, described in vivid mythical detail (the ageless river Vijarā, the tree Ilya, the unconquered palace Aparājita), until Brahman himself asks the newcomer, “Who are you?” The chapter elaborates the two paths of Chāndogya 5.10 and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.2 (Section 6.6.2).

  2. Breath as Brahman (chapter 2). Teachings ascribed to Kauṣītaki and Paiṅgya identify breath (prāṇa) with Brahman. The chapter also preserves domestic rites, among them the “transfer” (saṃpratti) in which a dying father hands over his speech, breath, sight and other faculties to his son.

  3. Indra and Pratardana (chapter 3). Indra tells King Pratardana that he is breath, the self made of intelligence (prajñātman). The faculties and their objects depend on one another as the rim of a wheel rests on the spokes and the spokes on the hub; the self of intelligence is the hub. Indra also claims that one who knows him is harmed by no deed, a passage the commentators found hard to reconcile with ordinary ethics. The account of dreamless sleep in this chapter (3.3) is discussed in Section 10.5.

  4. Bālāki and Ajātaśatru (chapter 4). The Brāhmaṇa Bālāki Gārgya offers to teach King Ajātaśatru of Kāśī about Brahman and ends by being taught by him — a fuller version of the dialogue in Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.1.

The Kauṣītaki is thus an important witness to the identification of breath with the conscious self and to an early analysis of the relation between the knowing faculties and what they know.

docs.title: 4.7.2 The Maitrī Upaniṣad
docs.text:
The Maitrī (or Maitrāyaṇīya) Upaniṣad belongs to the Maitrāyaṇīya school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It is mainly prose with verses interspersed and is usually printed in seven chapters, the last two of which appear to be supplements. It is generally regarded as the latest of Hume’s thirteen, later than the Śvetāśvatara and probably than the early Buddhist literature; Olivelle does not include it among the early Upaniṣads. Śaṅkara did not comment on it, though there is a later Advaita commentary by Rāmatīrtha.

Its frame story tells how King Bṛhadratha, having installed his eldest son on the throne, withdraws to the forest, practises austerities and asks the sage Śākāyanya to teach him the Self; Śākāyanya passes on what Prajāpati once taught the Vālakhilya sages. Several features make the text historically important:

  • a strongly world-weary tone: the king describes the body as a foul-smelling, insubstantial compound and asks what use the enjoyment of desires can be in it, language close to the śramaṇa critiques of desire;

  • a distinction between the “elemental self” (bhūtātman), bound by the fruits of action and overpowered by the guṇas, and the higher self that remains untouched, set out in terms close to Sāṅkhya;

  • a “sixfold yoga” (ṣaḍaṅga yoga) of breath control, withdrawal of the senses, meditation, concentration, reflection (tarka) and absorption (6.18) — one of the earliest lists of the limbs of yoga, differing from Patañjali’s eight (compare the Amṛtanāda, Section 7.3);

  • meditation on Oṃ and on the two forms of Brahman, “with sound” and “without sound” (6.22);

  • the treatment of Rudra, Viṣṇu and other deities as forms of the one Brahman, and a polemic against false teachers (7.8–10) that some scholars take to be aimed at heterodox groups.

The Maitrī thus stands between the classical Upaniṣads and the later Yoga and sectarian Upaniṣads of Chapters 7–9, and it shows how Upaniṣadic, Sāṅkhya and yogic ideas were being combined in the early centuries of the Common Era.

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: Chapter 5: The Mahāvākyas — The Four Great Sayings
5.1 Introduction to the Mahāvākyas
docs.text:
Among the vast number of Upaniṣadic utterances, the Advaita tradition singled out four sentences as possessing supreme philosophical and spiritual significance. These are the Mahāvākyas — the “Great Sayings” — one drawn from an Upaniṣad of each of the four Vedas. The grouping is post-Upaniṣadic: Śaṅkara already treats sentences such as tat tvam asi as “great sayings” that convey the identity of Self and Brahman, but the canonical set of four, with its correlation to the four Vedas, is expounded in later Advaita works such as the fifth chapter (Mahāvākya-viveka) of Vidyāraṇya’s Pañcadaśī (14th century). Theistic Vedāntins accept the sentences as scripture but deny that they teach identity.

In the Advaita tradition the Mahāvākyas are more than propositions to be debated; they serve as the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) through which the prepared student attains aparokṣa-jñāna (direct, unmediated knowledge of Brahman) (Figure 5.1). Because the very idea of four “great sayings” belongs to Advaita, this chapter sets out the Advaita account first; the theistic readings, which deny that the sentences teach identity, are given in Sections 5.8 and 5.13 and in Chapter 11.

Figure 5.1. The Four Mahāvākyas — One from Each Veda

docs.title: 5.2 The Fourfold Function of the Mahāvākyas
docs.text:
Modern Advaita teaching often assigns a specific function to each Mahāvākya (Table 5.1).

Table 5.1. The Functions of the Four Mahāvākyas in Modern Advaita Teaching Mahāvākya Veda Function Explanation Prajñānaṃ Brahma Ṛgveda Lakṣaṇa vākya (Definition) Defines the nature of Brahman as consciousness Tat tvam asi Sāmaveda Upadeśa vākya (Teaching) The Guru’s instruction to the student Ahaṃ Brahmāsmi Yajurveda Anubhava vākya (Experience) The student’s own realisation Ayaṃ Ātmā Brahma Atharvaveda Anusandhāna vākya (Contemplation) Continuous meditative contemplation

Read in sequence, the four functions describe a course of instruction: the nature of reality is defined; the teacher instructs the student in the identity of self and Brahman; the student realises that identity; and the realised student maintains the awareness through continuous contemplation. The scheme should be treated with caution. It is not in the Upaniṣads, which do not rank these sentences or group them as four, and although Vidyāraṇya’s Mahāvākya-viveka explains the four sentences one after another, the editor has not been able to trace the complete fourfold scheme of functions to a classical Advaita text. It is best understood as a teaching device of the modern Advaita tradition, not as a doctrine of the Upaniṣads.

docs.title: 5.3.1 Source and Context
docs.text:
This Mahāvākya appears in the Aitareya Upaniṣad (3.1.3) of the Ṛgveda. The Aitareya first lists the cognitive and vital functions — sensation, perception, discrimination, intelligence, insight, steadfastness, thought, impulse, memory, resolution, purpose, life, desire and control — and calls them all names of a single reality, prajñāna (consciousness) (Section 3.4 and Figure 3.4).

eṣa brahmā eṣa indraḥ eṣa prajāpatiḥ / ete sarve devā imāni ca pañca mahābhūtāni…/ sarvaṃ tat prajñānetram / prajñāne pratiṣṭhitam / prajñānetro lokaḥ / prajñā pratiṣṭhā / prajñānaṃ brahma Translation: “This is Brahmā, this is Indra, this is Prajāpati; all these gods and the five great elements…all this is guided by consciousness, is established in consciousness. The world is guided by consciousness. Consciousness is the foundation. Consciousness is Brahman.” — Aitareya Upaniṣad 3.1.3

docs.title: 5.3.2 Philosophical Analysis
docs.text:
The equation Prajñānaṃ = Brahma, read in the Advaita way, claims that consciousness is not a by-product of matter, but is itself the ultimate reality. Western philosophers would class such a position as a form of idealism. In the modern Advaita scheme the sentence is the “definitional sentence” (lakṣaṇa-vākya) because it states the essential nature (svarūpa) of Brahman: not a distant deity or an abstract principle, but the consciousness by which anything at all is known.

The point of the passage is that all these functions are treated as names of a single reality, prajñāna. On the Vedāntic reading consciousness is not one function among many but the light by which all functions are illumined.

Consciousness as Substrate

The Aitareya’s argument structure may be formalised thus: (1) Every cognitive function presupposes a knowing capacity. (2) This knowing capacity is invariant across all functions — it is the same “light” whether it manifests as memory, desire, or intelligence. (3) This invariant knowing capacity is prajñāna. (4) Since Brahman is defined as the ultimate substrate of all reality, and prajñāna is the ultimate substrate of all cognition, prajñānaṃ brahma. This reconstruction (a modern one, not the text’s own wording) invites comparison with Kant’s “transcendental unity of apperception” — the necessary unity of consciousness that underlies all experience.

docs.title: 5.3.3 The Three Schools on Prajñānaṃ Brahma
docs.text:
The three Vedāntic schools interpret this Mahāvākya in characteristically different ways. Rāmānuja did not comment on the Aitareya, and Table 5.2 is illustrative: it applies each school’s general doctrine of consciousness, as set out in Chapter 11, to the sentence rather than quoting a commentary on it.

Table 5.2. Illustrative: Three Vedāntic Readings of Prajñānaṃ Brahma School Interpretation Advaita (Śaṅkara) Consciousness is the very essence of Brahman; Brahman is consciousness, not merely possesses it. All apparent multiplicity of cognitive functions is superimposed upon the one non-dual consciousness. Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja) Consciousness is the defining attribute (dharma-bhūta-jñāna) of Brahman (Nārāyaṇa). Brahman possesses consciousness as an essential quality, but is not reducible to consciousness alone. Dvaita (Madhva) Consciousness characterises both God and individual souls, but God’s consciousness is independent (svatantra) while the soul’s consciousness is dependent (paratantra). The sentence defines Brahman’s supreme attribute, not identity with the jīva.

docs.title: 5.4 Tat Tvam Asi — That Thou Art
5.4.1 Source and Context
docs.text: This, the most often discussed of the Mahāvākyas, appears in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.8.7 and following) as the culminating declaration of the Sad-Vidyā teaching of Uddālaka Āruṇi to his son Śvetaketu.

docs.title: 5.4.2 The Three Words Analysed
docs.text:
The sentence Tat tvam asi consists of three words, each of which the schools analysed closely (Figure 5.2).

Figure 5.2. Analysis of the Three Words of Tat Tvam Asi (Advaita reading)

docs.title: 5.4.3 The Method of Jahad-Ajahad Lakṣaṇā
docs.text:
Advaita holds that the identity asserted by Tat tvam asi is not a crude equation of the individual empirical self (with all its limitations) with the cosmic Lord (with all his powers). Śaṅkara and his pupil Sureśvara analyse the sentence as one in which two words with different connotations refer to the same thing; later manuals such as Sadānanda’s Vedāntasāra systematise this as jahad-ajahad lakṣaṇā (also called bhāga-tyāga lakṣaṇā) — the method of “partially retaining and partially abandoning” the literal meanings (Table 5.3).

Table 5.3. The Method of Jahad-Ajahad Lakṣaṇā Applied to Tat Tvam Asi Word Literal Meaning (Vācyārtha) To be Abandoned To be Retained (Lakṣyārtha) Tat (That) Īśvara: omniscient, omnipotent creator Attributes of omniscience, omnipotence, creatorship Pure Consciousness (Cit) Tvam (Thou) Jīva: limited, ignorant, suffering Attributes of limitation, ignorance, suffering Pure Consciousness (Cit) Asi (Art) Identity — Absolute identity of the Cit in both

A classic illustration is offered: “This is that Devadatta.” When we say, “This Devadatta (seen here and now, old and grey) is that Devadatta (seen there, years ago, young and dark),” we abandon the contradictory attributes (youth/age, there/here) and retain the identical referent — the person Devadatta. Similarly, Tat tvam asi abandons the contradictory attributes of Īśvara and jīva but retains the identical referent: pure Consciousness.

docs.title: 5.4.4 The Refrain in Its Context
docs.text:
Uddālaka does not assert the identity once; he gives nine successive illustrations (Section 4.1 and Table 4.1), each followed by the refrain “sa ya eṣo ’ṇimaitadātmyam idaṃ sarvaṃ, tat satyaṃ, sa ātmā, tat tvam asi, śvetaketo” (“That which is the finest essence — the whole world has that as its Self. That is the True. That is the Self. That thou art, O Śvetaketu.”).

Each illustration brings out a different side of the teaching: the pervasiveness of Being (salt in water), the invisibility of the ultimate cause (banyan seed), the dependence of all particulars on the universal (rivers and ocean), and the role of the teacher in removing ignorance (the blindfolded man). The setting matters too: the saying is addressed to a student who has returned from twelve years of Vedic study “conceited, considering himself learned, and arrogant” (mahāmanā anūcānamānī stabdhaḥ, Chāndogya 6.1.2), and it answers his father’s question about the one teaching by which the unknown becomes known (6.1.3; see Section 4.1).

docs.title: 5.4.5 The Three Types of Lakṣaṇā
docs.text:
The Advaita analysis of Tat tvam asi draws on the three types of lakṣaṇā (secondary or indicative meaning) recognised by the Indian theorists of language:

  1. Jahad-lakṣaṇā (Exclusive Indication): The literal meaning is entirely abandoned in favour of the secondary meaning. Example: “The village is on the Gaṅgā” — the village is not literally on the river but on its bank.

  2. Ajahad-lakṣaṇā (Inclusive Indication): The literal meaning is entirely retained but supplemented. Example: “The red one is running” — the redness is retained and supplemented by identifying a specific red object (a horse).

  3. Jahad-ajahad lakṣaṇā (Partial Indication): Part of the literal meaning is abandoned and part is retained. This is the method applied to Tat tvam asi: the contradictory attributes of Īśvara (omniscience, creatorship) and jīva (limitation, ignorance) are abandoned, while the common referent — pure Consciousness — is retained.

Advaita teachers treat this analysis as a contemplative practice as well as a rule of interpretation: the student is to abandon the identification with the limited body and mind (the contradictory attributes of tvam) and retain the awareness that is their common referent.

docs.title: 5.5.1 Source and Context
docs.text:
This Mahāvākya appears in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (1.4.10). The context is the primordial Self’s act of self-recognition:

brahma vā idam agra āsīt / tad ātmānam evāvet — ahaṃ brahmāsmīti / tasmāt tat sarvam abhavat Translation: “In the beginning, this was Brahman alone. It knew only Itself, (saying) ‘I am Brahman.’ Therefore, It became all.” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10

docs.title: 5.5.2 Philosophical Significance
docs.text:
While Tat tvam asi is the guru’s teaching to the student (second person: “Thou art That”), Ahaṃ Brahmāsmi is the student’s own realisation expressed in the first person: “I am Brahman.” This is not an assertion of the ego; it is the dissolution of the ego in the recognition of one’s true nature as infinite consciousness.

The text immediately adds: tasmāt tat sarvam abhavat — “Therefore, It became all.” It goes on to say that whoever knows “I am Brahman” becomes this whole world; in the Advaita reading such a person does not become something new but recognises that he has always been Brahman. Even the gods cannot prevent this, for, as the text says, such a person becomes the Self of the gods themselves.

In Advaita teaching the passage from Tat tvam asi (the teacher’s instruction) to Ahaṃ Brahmāsmi (the student’s own recognition) marks the point at which hearing (śravaṇa), reflection (manana) and contemplation (nididhyāsana) have issued in direct knowledge. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka itself the sentence is spoken first by Brahman in a creation narrative, not by a student.

docs.title: 5.6 Ayaṃ Ātmā Brahma — This Self is Brahman
5.6.1 Source and Context
docs.text:
The fourth Mahāvākya is found in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad (Mantra 2):

sarvaṃ hy etad brahma / ayam ātmā brahma / so’yam ātmā catuṣpāt Translation: “All this is indeed Brahman. This Self is Brahman. This Self has four quarters.” — Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, Mantra 2

docs.title: 5.6.2 The Demonstrative “This” (Ayam)
docs.text: The commentators attach weight to the demonstrative pronoun ayam (“this”). In their reading it points to the self as immediately present and directly experienced — not a distant, transcendent entity, but the awareness that is now reading, thinking and experiencing — and declares that this self is Brahman.

docs.title: 5.7 The Mahāvākyas in Sannyāsa Dīkṣā
docs.text:
In the living tradition, the Mahāvākyas play a concrete liturgical role. When a person takes sannyāsa (formal renunciation) in the Daśanāmī order associated with Śaṅkara, the guru imparts one of the Mahāvākyas to the initiate, which then becomes a lifelong object of contemplation. According to the Maṭhāmnāya tradition, each of the four principal monasteries (maṭhas), whose foundation is traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara, is associated with one Veda and its Mahāvākya; in practice the saying imparted depends on the lineage into which one is initiated. Historians regard the four-maṭha organisation as a later, probably second-millennium, development projected back onto Śaṅkara (Table 5.4).

Table 5.4. The Mahāvākyas, the Vedas and the four Maṭhas (traditional scheme) Veda Mahāvākya Source; associated Maṭha Ṛgveda Prajñānaṃ Brahma Aitareya; Govardhana Maṭha, Purī Yajurveda Ahaṃ Brahmāsmi Bṛhadāraṇyaka; Śāradā Pīṭha, Śṛṅgerī Sāmaveda Tat Tvam Asi Chāndogya; Śāradā Maṭha, Dvārakā Atharvaveda Ayaṃ Ātmā Brahma Māṇḍūkya; Jyotir Maṭha, Jośīmaṭh

docs.title: 5.8 Divergent Interpretations of the Mahāvākyas
docs.text:
The three principal schools of Vedānta interpret the Mahāvākyas very differently (Figure 5.3):

  1. Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): The Mahāvākyas assert absolute identity (abheda) between Ātman and Brahman. The apparent difference between the individual self and the Absolute is due to avidyā (ignorance) and is sublated upon realisation.

  2. Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta (Rāmānuja): The Mahāvākyas assert qualified identity — the individual self is a part or mode of Brahman, not absolutely identical. Rāmānuja reads “Tat tvam asi” as co-reference: both “That” and “thou” ultimately denote Brahman, the first as cause of the world and the second as the inner controller who has the individual self as his body. The relationship is one of inseparable distinction (apṛthak-siddhi).

  3. Dvaita Vedānta (Madhva): The Mahāvākyas do not assert identity at all — the individual self is eternally distinct from Brahman, though wholly dependent upon Him. Madhva and his followers interpret the sentence as expressing similarity or dependence (“you belong to That”, “you are like That”), and some divide the preceding words of Chāndogya 6.8.7 (sa ātmā tat tvam asi) so as to read sa ātmātat tvam asi, “you are not That”.

Figure 5.3. The Three Vedāntic Interpretations of the Mahāvākyas

docs.title: 5.9 The Transformative Power of the Mahāvākyas
docs.text:
In the Advaita framework the Mahāvākyas are meant to transform the hearer, not only to be analysed, and they do so through a threefold process:

  1. Śravaṇa (Hearing): The aspirant first hears the Mahāvākya from a qualified teacher in the proper context of guru-śiṣya paramparā.

  2. Manana (Reflection): The aspirant then reflects upon the meaning, resolving all doubts through reasoning, analogies, and the study of the commentaries.

  3. Nididhyāsana (Contemplative Meditation): Finally, the aspirant engages in sustained contemplative meditation upon the truth of the Mahāvākya until the realisation becomes one’s own direct, unshakeable experience (aparokṣa jñāna).

ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ Translation: “The Self, verily, is to be seen, to be heard, to be reflected upon, and to be contemplated upon.” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5

For Advaita, to understand even one of these sentences fully is to attain mokṣa, liberation from the cycle of birth and death. For the theistic schools the same sentences are true and important but do not by themselves liberate: they describe the soul’s relation to the Lord, and liberation comes through devotion and grace (Section 5.13).

docs.title: 5.10 Secondary Mahāvākyas and Supporting Sentences
docs.text:
While the tradition singles out four principal Mahāvākyas, the Upaniṣads contain numerous other sentences of comparable philosophical weight, and later Vedāntic literature added summary formulas of its own. Table 5.5 distinguishes the two:

Table 5.5. Secondary Mahāvākyas of the Upaniṣads Vākya Source Significance Sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma Chāndogya 3.14.1 “All this is indeed Brahman” — affirms the non-dual nature of all existence Ekam evādvītīyam Chāndogya 6.2.1 “One only, without a second” — the most concise statement of non-duality So ’ham asmi Īśā 16 “I am He” — the worshipper’s identification with the person in the sun; later yogic texts make so ’ham the mantra of the breath Neti neti Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.3.6 “Not this, not this” — the apophatic definition of Brahman Brahma satyaṃ jagan mithyā Vivekacūḍāmaṇi 20; Brahmajñānāvalīmālā 20 (not Upaniṣadic; numbering varies by edition) “Brahman is real; the world is appearance” — a later Advaita summary formula, popularly attributed to Śaṅkara; the second work adds jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ (Section 11.4) Satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma Taittirīya 2.1.1 “Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinity” — definitional description (quoted in Section 3.3) Ānando brahmeti vyajānāt Taittirīya 3.6 “He knew: Bliss is Brahman” — identifies Brahman with bliss

docs.title: 5.11 The Mahāvākyas as Instruments of Knowledge
docs.text:
How can a sentence produce knowledge of Brahman? The Upaniṣads do not set out a theory of the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇas) in the manner of the later Nyāya or Mīmāṃsā schools, but they make claims that the Vedāntins worked into one. The Muṇḍaka places all Vedic learning below the knowledge “by which the imperishable is grasped” (Section 3.1), and the Kena says that Brahman is “not understood by those who understand” (Section 2.2), because it is the knowing subject and cannot be an object.
