Advaita concluded that perception and inference, which deal with objects, cannot reveal Brahman, and that the only means of knowing it is scripture, verbal testimony (śabda-pramāṇa), above all the Mahāvākyas (Table 5.6). Anantanand Rambachan has argued that for Śaṅkara the sentences of the Upaniṣads are themselves the means of liberating knowledge, not a preparation for some further experience (Rambachan 1991); Wilhelm Halbfass discusses the place of reason beside revelation in Śaṅkara (Halbfass 1991). Direct, immediate knowledge (aparokṣa-jñāna) is on this view not a separate pramāṇa but the result that śabda produces in a prepared mind.

Table 5.6. The Means of Knowledge and Brahman in Advaita Means Sanskrit Term Role in the Knowledge of Brahman Perception Pratyakṣa Limited to empirical objects; cannot reveal Brahman directly Inference Anumāna Useful in reflection (manana) to remove doubts, but cannot by itself establish Brahman Testimony Śabda The Upaniṣadic sentences, above all the mahāvākyas: the only pramāṇa for Brahman Result (not a pramāṇa) Aparokṣa-jñāna Immediate knowledge of the self, produced by śabda in a prepared mind

Śaṅkarācārya explains that the Mahāvākyas do not create the identity of Ātman and Brahman (which is eternally the case); they remove the ignorance that conceals it. Just as the sentence “This is not a snake; it is a rope” does not create the rope but removes the false perception, so “Tat tvam asi” does not create the identity but destroys the error of duality (Figure 5.4).

Figure 5.4. How the Mahāvākya Operates as an Instrument of Knowledge

docs.title: 5.12 The Mahāvākyas in Meditation Practice
docs.text:
In Advaita practice the Mahāvākyas are also objects of contemplation (nididhyāsana). Teachers in the tradition describe four stages:

  1. Vākya-śravaṇa: Repeated, attentive listening to the guru’s exposition of the Mahāvākya, with all its implications explored through the method of anvaya-vyatireka (co-presence and co-absence) and lakṣaṇā (indicative meaning).

  2. Vākya-manana: Systematic reflection to remove all intellectual doubts (saṃśaya). The student examines each word of the sentence, considers objections, studies the commentaries, and arrives at firm conviction (niścaya).

  3. Vākya-nididhyāsana: Sustained, one-pointed contemplation on the meaning of the sentence. The practitioner sits in a meditative posture, steadies the mind through prāṇāyāma, and then holds the meaning of “Ahaṃ Brahmāsmi” or “Tat tvam asi” in unwavering awareness, allowing the truth to permeate the entire being.

  4. Sahaja-sthiti: The natural, effortless abidance in the truth of the Mahāvākya that follows the dawn of aparokṣa jñāna. At this stage, contemplation is no longer a practice; it is the practitioner’s very nature.

Philosophical Note

Here doctrine (siddhānta) and discipline (sādhana) meet. For the tradition, to hear “Tat tvam asi” with a prepared mind, from a teacher, is not merely to learn a proposition but to undergo a transformation of identity.

docs.title: 5.13 Philosophical Objections and Responses
docs.text:
The Advaita doctrine of the Mahāvākyas was criticised by the other Indian schools, and the exchange produced some of the most sustained arguments in Indian philosophy (Table 5.7). The table gives the Advaitin replies; the theistic schools’ own positions are set out in Chapter 11.

Table 5.7. Major Objections to the Mahāvākya Doctrine and Advaitin Responses School Objection Advaitin Response Dvaita (Madhva) Identity of finite soul with infinite God is logically impossible The identity is of essence (svarūpa), not of accidental properties; through lakṣaṇā, contradictions are resolved Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja) “Tat tvam asi” means the soul is a part of Brahman, not identical The Upaniṣads explicitly negate all division in Brahman; “parthood” reintroduces duality Buddhism There is no permanent Ātman to be identical with anything The denial of Ātman contradicts direct experience; the very act of denial presupposes a conscious denier Pūrva Mīmāṃsā The Vedas prescribe action, not identity-knowledge The Upaniṣads are a distinct section (jñāna-kāṇḍa) whose purpose is knowledge, not ritual

Philosophical Note

The debate over the interpretation of the Mahāvākyas had direct consequences for practice. If “Tat tvam asi” means absolute identity (as Advaita holds), then liberation consists in the direct realisation of this identity through knowledge alone. If it means qualified identity (as Viśiṣṭādvaita holds), then liberation requires devotion and divine grace in addition to knowledge. If it means eternal difference (as Dvaita holds), then liberation is perpetual loving service to a God who always remains distinct from the soul. The interpretation of three words thus determines the entire structure of one’s spiritual life.

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: 6.1 Introduction: The Doctrines and Their Systematisers
docs.text: The Upaniṣads do not present a single doctrine but a set of interconnected and sometimes divergent teachings. Later Vedānta drew from them five central doctrines: Brahman (the ultimate reality), Ātman (the self), māyā (the power by which the one appears as many), karma (action and its consequences), and mokṣa (liberation). Two cautions are needed. First, these doctrines are developed unevenly in the Upaniṣads themselves: Brahman, Ātman, karma and liberation are pervasive, whereas māyā occurs only a few times, chiefly in the Śvetāśvatara. Second, the systematic shape given to them below is largely that of Advaita Vedānta, the school that did most to systematise them; where Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita differ, this is noted in each section, and their positions are treated as wholes in Chapter 11. The chapter ends with the earliest and sharpest critics of the Upaniṣadic self, the Buddhists and the Jains.

docs.title: 6.2.1 The Concept of Brahman
docs.text:
The word Brahman is usually derived from the root bṛh (to grow, to expand). In the older Vedic texts it means the sacred formula and its power; in the Upaniṣads it becomes the name of the ground of all that exists. The Upaniṣads describe Brahman as that from which the world arises, in which it lives and into which it dissolves, and in many passages as one, without a second, all-pervading and self-luminous. Whether Brahman is an impersonal reality or a personal Lord is the question on which the later schools divided.

yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante / yena jātāni jīvanti / yat prayanty abhisaṃviśanti / tad vijijñāsasva / tad brahma Translation: “That from which all beings are born, that by which, once born, they live, and that into which, upon departing, they enter — seek to know That. That is Brahman.” — Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1

docs.title: 6.2.2 Nirguṇa and Saguṇa Brahman
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads describe Brahman both with and without attributes. Advaita systematised this as a distinction between Nirguṇa Brahman (Brahman without attributes) and Saguṇa Brahman (Brahman with attributes) (Table 6.1 and Figure 6.1). Rāmānuja and Madhva reject the distinction as Advaita draws it: for them the texts that deny qualities to Brahman deny only bad or limiting qualities, and Brahman is the Lord with infinite auspicious attributes.

Table 6.1. Nirguṇa and Saguṇa Brahman as distinguished in Advaita Aspect Nirguṇa Brahman Saguṇa Brahman Nature Without qualities; transcendent With qualities; accessible to devotion Description Neti neti (not this, not this) Omniscient, omnipotent, all-compassionate Knowledge type Parā vidyā (higher knowledge) Aparā vidyā (lower knowledge) Approach Jñāna (knowledge), nididhyāsana Bhakti (devotion), Upāsanā (meditation) Upaniṣadic ref. Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.9.26 Chāndogya 3.14.2 Result Sadyo-mukti (immediate liberation) Krama-mukti (gradual liberation) Figure 6.1. Nirguṇa and Saguṇa: Two Aspects of the One Brahman

docs.title: 6.2.3 Brahman as Sat-Cit-Ānanda
docs.text:
The compound Sat-Cit-Ānanda (Being-Consciousness-Bliss) does not appear as a single phrase in the principal Upaniṣads. It is a later formula assembled from Upaniṣadic passages: sat from the Chāndogya’s “in the beginning, Being alone was, one without a second” (sad eva somyedam agra āsīd ekam evādvītīyam, 6.2.1); cit from the Aitareya’s “consciousness is Brahman” (prajñānaṃ brahma, 3.1.3); and ānanda from the Taittirīya’s “he understood: bliss is Brahman” (ānando brahmeti vyajānāt, 3.6).

The identification of Brahman with bliss had several consequences in Vedāntic thought. If bliss is the nature (svarūpa) of reality rather than a passing emotion, then the goal of life is not to acquire happiness from outside but to discover the bliss that is already one’s nature; the Taittirīya’s scale of bliss (Section 3.3.4) makes every lesser happiness a fraction of it. And if all beings share in the same bliss, then harming any being is, in the end, harming oneself, a metaphysical ground that later teachers gave for non-violence (ahiṃsā). Western philosophy offers partial parallels — Plato’s Form of the Good, Plotinus’s union with the One, Spinoza’s beatitudo — but none quite makes the claim that bliss is the nature of reality itself.

docs.title: 6.2.4 The Apophatic Method: Neti Neti
docs.text:
Alongside these positive descriptions stands the negative method of Yājñavalkya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.3.6; Section 1.16.3). Since Brahman transcends all conceptual categories, it cannot be described by any finite predicate, and the seeker proceeds by negating everything that Brahman is not:

athāta ādeśo neti neti / na hy etasmād iti nety anyat param asti Translation: “Now therefore the description (of Brahman): ‘Not this, not this.’ For there is nothing else beyond this ‘not this.’ ” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6

In Advaita the method is not a denial of Brahman’s existence but an affirmation of its transcendence. As Śaṅkara explains in his commentary, the negation applies only to the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) superimposed on the Ātman — body, mind, intellect, ego, the world of the senses and of dreams — not to the Ātman itself. When all superimpositions have been negated, what remains is not nothing but the self-luminous witness-consciousness that was present all along.

Apophatic and Cataphatic Approaches Compared

The Upaniṣads describe Brahman both positively (the cataphatic way) — as sat, cit, ānanda, as truth, knowledge and infinity — and negatively (the apophatic way), by neti neti. The commentators take the two as complementary: the positive terms point to what Brahman is in its own nature, and the negations show that Brahman is not limited to any conceptual description.

docs.title: 6.2.5 The Taittirīya’s Definition of Brahman
docs.text:
The Taittirīya’s definition — satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma, “Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinity” (2.1.1, quoted in full in Section 3.3) — became a test case for the schools. Śaṅkara’s commentary explains that the three words, though grammatically qualifiers (viśeṣaṇas), do not here add properties to Brahman: their purpose is definition (lakṣaṇa), pointing to Brahman’s own nature (later Advaita calls this a svarūpa-lakṣaṇa). Each word distinguishes Brahman from what it is not:

  1. Satyam (Truth/Reality) — distinguishes Brahman from everything unreal or illusory

  2. Jñānam (Knowledge/Consciousness) — distinguishes Brahman from all insentient matter

  3. Anantam (Infinity) — distinguishes Brahman from everything finite and limited

Rāmānuja, discussing the same sentence in the Śrībhāṣya, draws the opposite conclusion. Words with different meanings that refer to one thing (sāmānādhikaraṇya) show that the one Brahman really possesses several attributes; a sentence made of words that all meant the same bare essence would convey nothing.

docs.title: 6.3.1 The Concept of Ātman
docs.text:
While Brahman refers to the ultimate reality viewed cosmically, as the ground of the universe, Ātman refers to the self viewed individually, as the innermost essence of each being. The central claim of many Upaniṣadic passages is that the two are one: “this self is Brahman” (ayam ātmā brahma, Māṇḍūkya 2; Section 5.6). Advaita takes the claim as strict identity; the theistic schools take it as the inseparable relation of the self to the Lord who dwells within it.

The Ātman is described as:

  • Self-luminous (svayaṃjyotiḥ): It shines by its own light; it is not illumined by anything external (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.9).

  • The Witness (sākṣin): It is the witness of all experience — waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

  • Unchanging (nityam): While the body, mind, and intellect undergo constant change, the Ātman remains ever the same.

  • Unaffected (asaṅga): Untouched by the experiences of the body-mind complex. The Chāndogya (4.14.3) uses the image of water that does not cling to a lotus leaf: “so evil action does not cling to one who knows this” (Figure 6.2).

Figure 6.2. A lotus leaf (Nelumbo nucifera) on which water stands in drops and does not wet the surface: the image the Chāndogya (4.14.3) uses for the knower whom evil action does not touch Photo: H. Zell, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Taittirīya’s model of the five “selves” or sheaths (pañca-kośa), through which the student is led inward from the body to bliss, was discussed in Section 3.3. In Advaita the Ātman is none of the five sheaths, nor their sum, but the witness (sākṣin) that illumines each of them.

docs.title: 6.3.2 The Ātman in Yājñavalkya’s Teaching
docs.text:
The most extended discussion of the Ātman in the Upaniṣads is in Yājñavalkya’s teachings in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, particularly in his dialogues with Maitreyī (2.4 and 4.5) and with King Janaka (4.3–4.4). To Maitreyī he gives the image of a lump of salt dissolved in water:

sa yathā saindhavakhilya udake prāsta udakam evānuvilīyeta / na hāsyodgrahaṇāyeva syāt / yato yatas tv ādadīta lavaṇam eva / evaṃ vā ara idaṃ mahad bhūtam anantam apāraṃ vijñānaghana eva Translation: “As a lump of salt thrown into water dissolves and cannot be taken out again, yet wherever one tastes the water it is salty — even so, this great being, infinite and boundless, is a mass of consciousness alone.” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12

This analogy conveys that the Ātman is not located in any particular part of the body or experience; it pervades the entire field of experience, just as salt pervades the water. It cannot be extracted as a separate object because it is the very medium in which all experience occurs.

docs.title: 6.4.1 The Upaniṣadic Cosmogonies
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads give several accounts of the origin of the world. Historically they reflect different strands of speculation, some inherited from the Vedic hymns and Brāhmaṇas. Later Vedānta, and Advaita in particular, read them as complementary teaching devices that lead the student from a dualistic picture of creation towards the recognition that there is only the one Brahman appearing as the many (Table 6.2).

In the Muṇḍaka (1.1.8–9) Brahman “grows” by tapas — literally heat, and austerity — and from it come food, breath, mind and the worlds; the text itself adds that the omniscient one’s tapas “consists of knowledge” (1.1.9), which is why the commentators read the word as the concentrated power of consciousness. In the Aitareya (1.1.1–2; Section 3.4) and the Chāndogya (6.2.3) creation follows an act of thought or will (īkṣaṇa): the self, or Being, “thought, let me create the worlds”, “let me become many”. In the Śvetāśvatara (4.9–10) the Lord is the wielder of māyā, the creative power through which the manifold world appears; Advaita later read this as illusory projection. The Taittirīya (2.1) describes a sequence of emanation: from the self came space (ākāśa), from space wind, from wind fire, from fire water, from water earth. This scheme of the five elements was taken up throughout later Indian cosmology. Finally Gauḍapāda, in his Kārikā on the Māṇḍūkya, declares that no creation has ever occurred (ajāti-vāda): the appearance of creation is like the apparent circle traced by a whirling firebrand (Section 3.2.5).

Table 6.2. Upaniṣadic Cosmogonic Models Compared Model Source Mechanism Status in Advaita Tapas model Muṇḍaka Heat or austerity, read as the power of knowledge Provisional (vyāvahārika) Volitional model Aitareya, Chāndogya The self’s thought or intention (īkṣaṇa) Provisional Māyā model Śvetāśvatara The Lord’s creative power (māyā); read as illusory projection in Advaita Explanatory Emanation model Taittirīya Sequential emergence of elements Provisional Non-origination Māṇḍūkya Kārikā No creation; appearance only Ultimate (pāramārthika)

Śaṅkara reconciles these accounts through the distinction between two standpoints. At the empirical level (vyāvahārika), creation appears real and can be described through various models; at the ultimate level (pāramārthika), there is no creation, no destruction, no bondage and no liberation — only the non-dual Brahman. The creation stories are thus provisional attribution (adhyāropa) followed by negation (apavāda) (Section 11.4.3). For Rāmānuja and Madhva, by contrast, creation is real: the world is either the body of Brahman, transformed from a subtle to a gross state, or a real product of God’s will distinct from him.

docs.title: 6.4.2 The Doctrine of Causation: Sat-Kārya-Vāda
docs.text:
The Chāndogya (6.1) states what later philosophers called sat-kārya-vāda — the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause:

yathā somyaikena mṛtpiṇḍena sarvaṃ mṛnmayaṃ vijñātaṃ syāt / vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ / mṛttikety eva satyaṃ Translation: “Just as by knowing one lump of clay, all things made of clay are known — the modification being a mere verbal distinction, a name — the clay alone is real.” — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4

The passage makes three claims: the cause alone is ultimately real, the effects being modifications (vikāras) that are mere names (nāmadheyam); by knowing the cause (Brahman), all effects (the manifold world) are known; and the diversity of the world is vācārambhaṇam, a verbal handle, dependent on language and naming.

Scholarly Note

The three analogies employed by Uddālaka in Chāndogya 6.1.4–6 — a lump of clay and things of clay, a copper trinket (lohamaṇi, which Śaṅkara takes as gold) and things of copper, a nail-cutter and things of iron — became the starting point of every later Vedāntic discussion of causation. Advaita, especially after Śaṅkara, developed it into vivarta-vāda, the doctrine that the effect is an apparent transformation of the cause, not a real change in it. Rāmānuja understood it as a real transformation (pariṇāma) of Brahman’s body, the world of souls and matter, with Brahman’s own nature unchanged. The same passage thus supports a whole spectrum of positions.

docs.title: 6.5.1 From Vedic Power to Vedāntic Appearance
docs.text:
The word māyā has a long history before Advaita. In the Ṛgveda it means wondrous power or magical creative ability, often the power to take on many forms, which could be used to deceive (Indra “goes about in many forms by his māyās”, Ṛgveda 6.47.18), but not yet the illusoriness of the world. In the Upaniṣads the term appears in a verse of the Śvetāśvatara:

māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyān māyinaṃ tu maheśvaram Translation: “Know that Prakṛti (Nature) is Māyā, and the great Lord is the wielder of Māyā.” — Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10

Here māyā is the Lord’s creative power, identified with primal matter (prakṛti). In Śaṅkara and his successors it becomes the principle of apparent duality in a non-dual reality (Table 6.3).

Table 6.3. Evolution of the Concept of Māyā Period Text/Thinker Meaning of Māyā Vedic Ṛgveda Wondrous, shape-changing power of the gods (and demons), sometimes used to deceive Upaniṣadic Śvetāśvatara The Lord’s creative power (śakti) that projects the world Systematic Vedānta Śaṅkara and successors The beginningless principle of cosmic ignorance; neither real nor unreal (the equation of māyā with avidyā is made explicit by Śaṅkara’s successors) Post-Śaṅkara Later Advaita Distinguished into mūlāvidyā (root ignorance) and tūlāvidyā (derivative ignorance)

Śaṅkara describes name-and-form as “indeterminable as either identical with or different from” Brahman (tattvānyatvābhyām anirvacanīya, commentary on Brahmasūtra 2.1.14); his successors made indeterminability (anirvacanīyatā) the defining mark of māyā. On this view māyā is neither real, since it is contradicted by the knowledge of Brahman, nor unreal, since it produces the appearance of the world; the world is accordingly mithyā, “false” in the technical sense of being neither real nor unreal.

docs.title: 6.5.2 What Māyā Means in Advaita
docs.text:
The Advaita doctrine is often misunderstood, and Table 6.4 sets out what it does and does not claim. Later Vedāntic philosophy also distinguished two powers of māyā, one that veils and one that projects (Figure 6.3).

Table 6.4. Clarifying the Concept of Māyā in Advaita Māyā Does NOT Mean… Māyā DOES Mean… The world is a mere hallucination The world is a real appearance with no ultimate substance Nothing exists The phenomenal world exists at the empirical level (vyavahārika) but not at the absolute level (pāramārthika) Life is meaningless illusion The world is the creative play (līlā) of Brahman Passive nihilism Active engagement in the world with the understanding that Brahman alone is ultimately real Figure 6.3. The Two Powers of Māyā

The theistic schools rejected the Advaita doctrine. Rāmānuja’s Śrībhāṣya sets out a series of objections to an ignorance that is neither real nor unreal — on what does it rest, what does it conceal, how can it be removed — and reads the Śvetāśvatara’s māyā as the Lord’s real and wonderful power of creation. Madhva holds the world to be fully real. The doctrine of māyā is therefore a reading of the Upaniṣads, not a teaching that all their interpreters found in them.

docs.title: 6.6.1 Karma in the Upaniṣadic Framework
docs.text:
The oldest Upaniṣads contain the earliest extended statements in Indian literature of the doctrine that a person is reborn according to his actions; the Ṛgveda knows an afterlife but not a cycle of rebirth governed by moral causation. Whether these passages are older than the Buddha, and whether the doctrine arose within the Brahmanical tradition, is debated (Section 1.12). The Bṛhadāraṇyaka roots action in desire: “a person consists of desire; as is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the action he performs; and as is the action he performs, so does he become” (4.4.5). Later Indian philosophy added the vocabulary of latent impressions (saṃskāras, vāsanās) to explain how actions bind the individual to the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra); Figure 6.4 combines the Upaniṣadic core with that later vocabulary.

yathākārī yathācārī tathā bhavati / sādhukārī sādhur bhavati / pāpakārī pāpo bhavati / puṇyaḥ puṇyena karmaṇā bhavati / pāpaḥ pāpena Translation: “As one acts, as one behaves, so does one become. The doer of good becomes good; the doer of evil becomes evil. One becomes virtuous by virtuous action, sinful by sinful action.” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5

Figure 6.4. The Cycle of Karma and Saṃsāra, and Liberation Through Knowledge

Later Vedānta distinguishes three types of karma: the accumulated store of past actions from earlier births (sañcita); the portion of it that has begun to bear fruit in the present life (prārabdha); and the new actions performed in the present life (āgāmī or kriyamāṇa).

docs.title: 6.6.2 The Two Paths After Death: Devāyana and Pitṛyāna
docs.text:
The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5.10) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (6.2) describe two paths that the soul may take after death, taught by the king Pravāhaṇa Jaivali (Section 4.5):

  1. The Path of the Gods (Devāyana): For those who have attained knowledge (vidyā) and practised meditation (upāsanā). This path leads progressively through the realms of fire, day, bright fortnight, the six months of the northern course of the sun, the year, the sun, the moon, and lightning, until the soul reaches Brahman and does not return.

  2. The Path of the Ancestors (Pitṛyāna): For those who have performed sacrificial rites and charitable acts but have not attained knowledge. This path leads through smoke, night, dark fortnight, the six months of the southern course of the sun, and the world of the ancestors, to the moon. After enjoying the fruits of their meritorious actions, they return to earthly existence through space, wind, rain, plants and food, and are reborn.

Those who know neither path, the Chāndogya adds, are born again and again as small creatures (5.10.8). Later Vedānta adds a further possibility: the one who knows Brahman here is liberated without travelling either path (Figure 6.5). The doctrine of the two paths has a clear consequence for practice: meritorious action leads to rebirth in good circumstances, but it does not end the cycle of birth and death; only knowledge does. This is the basis of the Upaniṣadic preference for the path of knowledge over the path of ritual action — not because action is worthless, but because action without knowledge cannot end the cycle of becoming.

Figure 6.5. The Two Post-Mortem Paths and Direct Liberation

docs.title: 6.7.1 The Goal
docs.text:
Mokṣa (liberation, release) is the highest goal (parama-puruṣārtha) that the Upaniṣads hold out: freedom from the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) through knowledge of the self. The texts describe it in several ways — as going to Brahman by the path of the gods, as becoming Brahman, as union with the Lord — and the schools built on different descriptions. For Advaita, liberation is not a future event but the recognition of a truth that has always been the case: the Ātman has never been bound and only appears bound through ignorance (avidyā), so liberation is the removal of a false cognition rather than the production of a new state. For Rāmānuja and Madhva it is a real change in the soul’s condition, given by the Lord’s grace, in which the soul enjoys the presence of God for ever (Table 6.5).

sa yo ha vai tat paramaṃ brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati Translation: “Whoever truly knows that supreme Brahman, becomes Brahman indeed.” — Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9

Table 6.5. Types of Liberation in Upaniṣadic and Vedāntic Thought Type Sanskrit Term Description Liberation while living Jīvanmukti The individual realises Brahman while still embodied; actions continue but create no new bondage Liberation at death Videhamukti The body falls away at the exhaustion of prārabdha karma; no further rebirth occurs Gradual liberation Krama-mukti The soul attains the world of Brahmā through the Devāyana path and is eventually liberated there Immediate liberation Sadyo-mukti Instantaneous liberation upon the dawn of knowledge; characteristic of the Advaita tradition

docs.title: 6.7.2 Jīvanmukti: Liberation While Living
docs.text:
The idea of jīvanmukti — liberation attained while still living in the body, not after death — is one of the most distinctive of the Vedāntic tradition. The term itself does not occur in the principal Upaniṣads; it was developed in the Advaita tradition, culminating in Vidyāraṇya’s Jīvanmuktiviveka (14th century). The idea draws on passages such as Kaṭha 2.3.14 (= Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.7): “When all the desires that dwell in the heart are cast away, then a mortal becomes immortal and attains Brahman here.”

bhidyate hṛdaya-granthiś chidyante sarva-saṃśayāḥ | kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare Translation: “The knot of the heart is cut asunder, all doubts are destroyed, and all karmas perish when That which is both the higher and the lower is seen.” — Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8

The jīvanmukta continues to live in the world until the karma that produced the present body is exhausted, like a potter’s wheel that goes on spinning after the potter has stopped turning it — an image best known from the Sāṅkhyakārikā (67) and adopted by Advaita. Drawing on these passages and on the Gītā’s portrait of the person of steady wisdom (sthita-prajña, BG 2.55–72), later Vedānta describes the liberated person as free from desire, since nothing is lacking to one who has realised the fullness of the self; as even-minded in pleasure and pain, praise and blame; as acting for the welfare of all beings (sarva-bhūta-hita), because the same self is seen in all; and as acting rightly from that understanding rather than from external rule. Modern readers have compared this ideal with virtue ethics and with humanistic psychology’s “self-actualisation”; the Vedāntic version differs in grounding compassion not in empathy but in the recognition that all beings share a single self.

Scholarly Note: Mokṣa in Cross-Cultural Perspective

Comparisons between mokṣa and “salvation” in the Abrahamic religions are often drawn too sharply. It is true that Advaita understands liberation as the result of knowledge, as the transcendence of individual identity and as achievable in this life, whereas mainstream Christian and Islamic theology speak of salvation through divine grace with the individual preserved in the hereafter. But each side contains the other’s emphasis: the theistic Vedānta of Rāmānuja and Madhva, and the bhakti traditions generally, stress grace and the eternal individuality of the liberated soul, while Christian mysticism and Sufism speak of union with or annihilation in God. The real contrast lies as much within the traditions as between them.

docs.title: 6.8 The Doctrine of the Three Bodies (Tri-Śarīra)
6.8.1 The Gross, Subtle, and Causal Bodies
docs.text:
Building upon the pañca-kośa model of the Taittirīya, the later Vedāntic tradition — drawing on passages from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Māṇḍūkya, and other Upaniṣads — developed the doctrine of the three bodies (tri-śarīra), which provides a systematic framework for understanding the relationship between the Ātman and its apparent embodiments.

The sthūla śarīra (gross body) is the physical body composed of the five gross elements (pañca-mahābhūtas). It is the vehicle of waking-state experience and is subject to birth, growth, disease, decay, and death. The sūkṣma śarīra (subtle body) consists of the five vital breaths, the five sense organs, the five organs of action, the mind, and the intellect — seventeen components in all. It is the vehicle of dream-state experience and persists through the cycle of rebirth, carrying the individual’s karmic impressions (saṃskāras) from one life to the next. The kāraṇa śarīra (causal body) is the formless seed-state of ignorance (avidyā) that is the root cause of both the subtle and gross bodies. It is the vehicle of deep-sleep experience (Table 6.6).

Table 6.6. The Three Bodies and Their Relationship to the Five Sheaths and Four States Body Kośas included State Characteristics Sthūla (Gross) Annamaya Jāgrat (Waking) Physical body; subject to birth and death; composed of food Sūkṣma (Subtle) Prāṇamaya, Manomaya, Vijñānamaya Svapna (Dream) 17 components; carries saṃskāras; transmigrates between births Kāraṇa (Causal) Ānandamaya Suṣupti (Deep Sleep) Root ignorance (avidyā); beginningless; destroyed only by knowledge Ātman (Beyond) None — witness of all Turīya (The Fourth) Self-luminous; unborn; the real identity of the individual

docs.title: 6.8.2 The Three States and the Three Bodies
docs.text:
In this framework each state of consciousness is correlated with a body: waking consciousness operates through the gross body, dream consciousness through the subtle body, and deep-sleep consciousness through the causal body. The Fourth (Turīya) is the Ātman itself, the witness of all three bodies and all three states but identical with none of them. The ordinary person identifies with whichever body is active — “I am this body” in waking, “I am this dreamer” in dream. For Advaita this identification is an error (adhyāsa); one’s true identity is the witnessing awareness that remains constant through all states and all bodies. The scheme is an Advaita systematisation; the theistic schools do not accept a “causal body” made of ignorance in the Advaita sense.

The Concept of Adhyāsa (Superimposition) in Śaṅkara’s Philosophy

Śaṅkara’s introduction (adhyāsa-bhāṣya) to his commentary on the Brahma Sūtras identifies adhyāsa (superimposition) as the fundamental error that underlies all human suffering and bondage. Adhyāsa is defined as the apparent presentation, in the form of memory, of something previously experienced in something else — specifically, the mutual superimposition of the Self (Ātman) and the not-Self (body, mind, ego).

This superimposition operates in two directions:

  • Superimposition of the not-Self on the Self: One attributes to the Ātman the properties of the body — “I am fat,” “I am old,” “I am a man/woman.”

  • Superimposition of the Self on the not-Self: One attributes to the body the properties of the Ātman — “This body is conscious,” “This mind is the knower.”

All worldly transactions (vyāvahāra), including moral conduct, religious ritual, and even the study of the Vedas, presuppose this mutual superimposition. Liberation consists in the cessation of superimposition through the direct knowledge of the distinction between Self and not-Self (ātma-anātma-viveka).

docs.title: 6.9 The Five Doctrines in the Advaita System
docs.text:
In the Advaita systematisation the five doctrines form one structure. Brahman is the sole reality. The Ātman is Brahman known from within the individual. Māyā is the indeterminable power that makes Brahman appear as the manifold world and the Ātman as a limited individual. Karma is the mechanism by which the self, deluded by māyā, is entangled in birth and death. And liberation is the recognition that the self was always Brahman, accomplished by knowledge, which dissolves māyā and exhausts karma. Table 6.7 relates the doctrines to the three levels of reality of post-Śaṅkara Advaita. This is the account Advaita reads out of the Upaniṣads; the theistic schools tell it differently, with the individual self and the world real and dependent on the Lord, and liberation as communion with him.

Table 6.7. The three levels of reality of post-Śaṅkara Advaita and the five doctrines Level What Appears Relevant Doctrines Pāramārthika (Absolute) Brahman/Ātman alone Brahman, Ātman (identical); Mokṣa as recognition Vyāvahārika (Empirical) The manifold world of name and form Māyā (veiling and projecting), Karma (action-consequence cycle) Prātibhāsika (Illusory) Snake on a rope; silver in a shell Māyā at its most distorted; error of perception

docs.title: 6.10 The Upaniṣadic Ātman and Its Śramaṇa Critics
docs.text: The Upaniṣadic teaching on the self met its most searching critic in the Buddha, and the exchange between the two traditions lasted more than a thousand years. Buddhist doctrine is set out in Volume 4 (Buddha–Jina Prabhā), which gives the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta in full, and the philosophical debate between the schools in Volume 3 (Darśana Darpaṇa). This section asks a narrower question: which Upaniṣadic ideas do the early Buddhist texts appear to address, and how did the Vedāntins answer? On the chronology adopted in this volume, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya are older than the Buddha, and the verse Upaniṣads were taking shape while Buddhism spread (Section 1.12).

docs.title: 6.10.1 What the Early Buddhist Texts Knew
docs.text:
The Tevijja Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 13) is the Pali canon’s most direct engagement with Vedic teachers. Two young brahmins, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, dispute which path leads to union with Brahmā (brahmasahabyatā). Each school of brahmins (Adhvaryu, Taittirīya, Chandoga, Bahvṛca) claims that its own path leads there. The Buddha asks whether any brahmin learned in the three Vedas, or any teacher of theirs back to the seventh generation, has seen Brahmā face to face. When the answer is no, he compares their teaching to a file of blind men, each holding on to the one in front and none of them able to see. He then teaches the four “divine abidings” (brahmavihāra). In these the mind is made to pervade every direction with friendliness, compassion, sympathetic joy and equanimity, and this, he says, is the way to companionship with Brahmā. Richard Gombrich reads the sutta as a deliberate ethical reinterpretation of the Brahmanical language of union with brahman (Gombrich 2009). The sutta speaks of a personal god, Brahmā, not of the neuter brahman of the Upaniṣads. This suggests that its authors knew the Upaniṣadic idea at some remove, or chose to treat it in theistic form.

The Alagaddūpama Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 22) lists among the “standpoints for views” that a disciple must reject the view that “the world is the self”, and that after death one will become that, permanent, stable and eternal. Scholars have often compared this with Śāṇḍilya’s teaching in the Chāndogya (3.14.4). There the self within the heart is declared to be Brahman, the whole of what exists, and the meditator resolves that on departing from here he will merge into it. The Pali names no source, but the structure of the two claims is the same: the self is identified with the all, and union with it is expected after death.

The Kaṭha offers a third point of contact. Naciketas asks Death about the doubt whether a man exists after he has died, “some say he does, others that he does not” (1.1.20). Whether the Tathāgata exists after death is one of the questions the Buddha set aside as undetermined (avyākṛta). Yama answers Naciketas by teaching the unborn, undying self (1.2.18). The Buddha declines to answer, holding the question itself to be wrongly posed.

docs.title: 6.10.2 The Not-Self Argument and the Upaniṣadic Self
docs.text:
In the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.59) the Buddha examines the five aggregates of the person: form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. None of them is the self. If one of them were, it would not lead to affliction, and one could command it to be thus and not otherwise. Each is impermanent, and what is impermanent is unsatisfactory. What is impermanent and unsatisfactory is not fit to be regarded as “this is mine, this I am, this is my self”.

The argument accepts a definition of what a self would have to be, namely permanent, free from suffering and in control, and then shows that nothing in experience meets it. That definition corresponds closely to the Upaniṣadic ātman:

  • it is unborn and undying (Kaṭha 1.2.18);

  • it is beyond hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, old age and death (Bṛhad. 3.5.1);

  • it is the immortal inner controller (antaryāmin) of all things, apart from which, Yājñavalkya adds, “everything else is afflicted” (ārta; Bṛhad. 3.7.23).

Steven Collins accordingly reads the not-self teaching in this Brahmanical setting, as directed against such a conception of the self (Collins 1982).

The method also has an Upaniṣadic precedent. Yājñavalkya too refuses to identify the self with anything that can be pointed to. It is “not this, not this” (Bṛhad. 3.9.26; Section 1.16.3), and one cannot see the seer of seeing (3.4.2). Some modern interpreters have therefore argued that the Buddha denied only that the aggregates are the self, leaving a transcendent self unmentioned rather than rejected.

The conclusions, however, diverge. Yājñavalkya ends with an unseen seer (3.7.23). The Buddhist tradition ends with conditioned processes and no subject behind them. The mainstream of Buddhist scholasticism, from the Abhidharma to Vasubandhu’s refutation of the person in the ninth chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, and most modern scholars, read anattā as excluding any permanent self whatever.

The doctrine of karma shows the same pattern of shared ground and divergence. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka already traces action back to the inner life. As one acts, so one becomes; a person consists of desire; as is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the deed he does; and the deed he does, that he attains (4.4.5; compare Yājñavalkya’s private teaching to Ārtabhāga, 3.2.13). The Buddha’s saying that “intention is karma” (Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.63; Volume 4) carries the internalisation further, placing the moral weight of an act entirely in the intention behind it. Gombrich argues that the Buddha thus completed the “ethicisation” of a concept that had begun as ritual action (Gombrich 2009). He also argues, following Joanna Jurewicz (Jurewicz 2000), that the chain of dependent origination answers the Vedic cosmogonies. In place of a story of how a primal being created the world through desire, mind and heat (as in Bṛhad. 1.2), it gives an account of how suffering arises in each person.

The difference returns at the point of liberation. For the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, the man without desire, whose only desire is the self, does not depart at death but, being Brahman, goes to Brahman (4.4.6). For the Buddha there is no self to be free; there is only the ending of craving.

docs.title: 6.10.3 The Later Debate
docs.text:
The exchange continued in the scholastic literature of both sides:

  • Bhāviveka (6th century) devoted the eighth chapter of his Madhya­maka­hṛdaya­kārikā, the “Ascertainment of the Truth of Vedānta” (Vedāntatattvaviniścaya), to the Vedāntin doctrine of a single, all-pervading self, and answered it from the Madhyamaka standpoint. This is one of the earliest datable accounts of Vedānta by an outsider (Qvarnström 1989).

  • Śāntarakṣita’s Tattvasaṅgraha (8th century) includes, in its examination of theories of the self, a section on the self of the “followers of the Upaniṣads” (aupaniṣadika). It argues that a single, eternal consciousness cannot account for the variety and succession of actual cognitions.

  • On the Vedāntin side, Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā engages Buddhist arguments closely (Section 3.2.5).

  • Śaṅkara refutes the Buddhist realists and idealists, and dismisses the doctrine of emptiness, in his commentary on Brahmasūtra 2.2.18–32. His central reply to the denial of the self comes elsewhere, under 2.3.7. The self cannot be refuted, because it is the ground of every act of knowing, including the act of refutation; “the one who denies it is its very nature”.

Later Vaiṣṇava and Sāṅkhya critics nevertheless called Advaita “Buddhism in disguise” (pracchanna-bauddha). The charge shows how close the two negative methods looked from outside. The Advaitin’s reply is that the Buddhist negation leaves nothing behind, whereas the Upaniṣadic negation leaves the witness that performs it (compare Table 5.7). The debate sharpened both sides. The Vedāntins had to say what kind of self survives the analysis of the aggregates: not an object among objects, but the awareness to which all objects appear. The Buddhists had to explain memory, responsibility and rebirth without a self, a task that occupied their philosophers for centuries (Volume 3). Jonardon Ganeri’s study of Indian theories of the self follows these arguments on both sides as philosophy rather than as doxography (Ganeri 2007).

docs.title: 6.10.4 Jain Conceptions of the Self
docs.text:
The Jains, the other great śramaṇa tradition, agreed with the Upaniṣads against the Buddhists that there is a self, but disagreed about almost everything else (Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā) (Dundas 2002). For the Jain canon and its systematisers, souls (jīva) are infinite in number. Each is eternal and conscious by nature, endowed with infinite knowledge, perception, bliss and energy that karma obscures. Karma is not, as in the Upaniṣads, the deed and its unseen result, but a subtle kind of matter that flows into the soul through activity and binds it. Liberation comes when restraint and austerity stop the inflow and wear away what has accumulated; the freed soul rises to the summit of the universe and remains there for ever, individual and omniscient. In embodiment the soul is the size of its body, contracting and expanding as the light of a lamp fills a small or a large room, an image the Jain systematisers use. The Jains reject the authority of the Veda and the idea of a creator God.

The Jain texts also argue against the Upaniṣadic doctrine directly. The Sūtrakṛtāṅga, one of the oldest books of the Śvetāmbara canon, lists among the wrong views of other teachers the doctrine that a single self appears as the whole world, as one heap of earth appears in many forms (Jacobi 1895). Later Jain philosophers, among them the Digambara Samantabhadra (whose date is disputed), criticised the “one-sided” (ekānta) doctrine of non-duality from the standpoint of their own doctrine of many-sidedness (anekāntavāda). A reality that is only one and only unchanging, they argued, leaves no room for bondage and release, for action and its fruit, or for the difference between teacher and pupil. The Jain view thus stands between the two positions examined above: with the Upaniṣads it affirms a permanent self, against them it makes that self plural and individual, and with the Buddhists it holds that liberation is won by one’s own discipline rather than by knowing one’s identity with the all.

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: 7.1 Introduction: The Yoga Upaniṣads in Context
docs.text: Among the 108 Upaniṣads enumerated in the Muktikā canon, twenty are classified as Yoga Upaniṣads. While the mukhya Upaniṣads focus primarily on the metaphysical identity of Ātman and Brahman, the Yoga Upaniṣads give practical instructions on how that identity is to be realised through psycho-physical disciplines: posture, breath control, the subtle channels and centres of the body, inner sound and light, and meditative absorption. They thus represent the sādhana (practice) dimension of the Vedāntic teaching.

docs.title: 7.1.1 Date and Composition
docs.text:
It is essential to be clear about the date of these texts, because they are often presented as ancient sources of yoga. They are not. Apart from a few short and comparatively early works (such as the Amṛtabindu, Amṛtanāda, Kṣurikā and Tejobindu, which may go back to the first millennium CE), the Yoga Upaniṣads are medieval and early modern compositions. Their vocabulary — kuṇḍalinī, a system of cakras, the three bandhas, khecarī and vajrolī mudrā — is that of the Haṭha Yoga literature of the eleventh to fifteenth centuries, and of the Nātha tradition associated with Gorakṣanātha.

The decisive study is Christian Bouy’s Les Nātha-yogin et les Upaniṣads (Bouy 1994). Bouy showed that the Yoga Upaniṣads survive in two forms: shorter versions, current in North India, and much longer versions transmitted in South India, which are the versions found in the 108-Upaniṣad collection and commented on by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin in the eighteenth century. The longer South Indian versions were expanded, probably in the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries, by incorporating verses taken wholesale from Haṭha Yoga works such as the Haṭhayogapradīpikā (15th century), the Yogabīja, the Vivekamārtaṇḍa and the Khecarīvidyā; the second chapter of the Yogakuṇḍalī Upaniṣad, for example, is drawn from the Khecarīvidyā (Mallinson 2007). In other words, the direction of borrowing generally runs from the Haṭha texts to the Yoga Upaniṣads, not the reverse. Giving these teachings the name “Upaniṣad” brought Haṭha Yoga within the authority of the Veda and reconciled it with Advaita Vedānta, which is the doctrinal frame of most of these texts.

None of this lessens the interest of the texts. They document how yogic practice and Vedāntic theology were brought together, and they preserve an important stage in the history of Indian contemplative techniques (Mallinson and Singleton 2017). But they should be read as late witnesses to the yoga traditions, not as their source, and as later than both Patañjali’s Yogasūtra (c. 325–425 CE) and the earliest Haṭha texts (Table 7.1).

Table 7.1. The Twenty Yoga Upaniṣads of the Muktikā Canon (Veda affiliations as given in that list) No. Upaniṣad Veda Primary Focus 1 Advaya-Tāraka Śukla Yajurveda Tāraka Yoga; inner light phenomena 2 Amṛta-Bindu Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Mind control; Oṃ meditation 3 Amṛta-Nāda Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda The six limbs of Yoga 4 Dhyāna-Bindu Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Meditation; inner sounds 5 Haṃsa Śukla Yajurveda Haṃsa mantra; Ajapā Gāyatrī 6 Kṣurikā Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Yoga as the “knife” (kṣurikā) cutting bondage 7 Mahāvākya Atharvaveda Great sayings in Yogic context 8 Maṇḍala-Brāhmaṇa Śukla Yajurveda Eight-limbed Yoga 9 Nāda-Bindu Ṛgveda Inner sound (nāda) meditation 10 Paśupata-Brahma Atharvaveda Śaiva Yoga 11 Śāṇḍilya Atharvaveda Comprehensive eight-limbed Yoga 12 Tejo-Bindu Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Fifteen-limbed Yoga; Brahma-Vidyā 13 Triśikhi-Brāhmaṇa Śukla Yajurveda Yoga postures; prāṇāyāma; meditation 14 Varāha Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Tattva-jñāna through Yoga 15 Yoga-Cūḍāmaṇi Sāmaveda Kuṇḍalinī Yoga 16 Yoga-Kuṇḍalī Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Kuṇḍalinī and Cakras 17 Brahmavidyā Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Oṃ and the haṃsa meditation 18 Yoga-Śikhā Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Fire of Yoga; Kuṇḍalinī 19 Yoga-Tattva Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Comprehensive Yoga tattvas 20 Darśana Sāmaveda Yoga postures and āsanas

Cross-Reference: Volume 5, Yoga Taraṅgiṇī

The practices that the Yoga Upaniṣads share with Haṭha Yoga — prāṇāyāma, the nāḍīs and cakras, Kuṇḍalinī, mudrās and bandhas — and Patañjali’s Yogasūtra are treated in detail in Volume 5 of this series, Yoga Taraṅgiṇī. This chapter summarises them only so far as is needed to show what the Yoga Upaniṣads themselves contribute and how they relate to the older Upaniṣads and to the yoga traditions.

docs.title: 7.2 Key Themes of the Yoga Upaniṣads
docs.text: The Yoga Upaniṣads share a small set of themes, each taken up in the sections that follow: breath control (prāṇāyāma), the subtle channels and centres (nāḍīs and cakras), the coiled power (kuṇḍalinī), the inner sound (nāda), the bodily seals and locks (mudrās and bandhas), and meditation (dhyāna) leading to absorption (samādhi).

docs.title: 7.3 The Aṣṭāṅga Yoga in the Yoga Upaniṣads
docs.text: Several Yoga Upaniṣads present their own versions of the eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) Yoga path — yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna and samādhi — which they take over from Patañjali’s formulation, often reinterpreting the limbs in Vedāntic terms (the Śāṇḍilya and Darśana, for example, list ten yamas and ten niyamas). Others give different numbers of limbs: the Amṛtanāda has six, the Tejobindu fifteen (Section 7.8).

docs.title: 7.4 Prāṇāyāma, Nāḍīs and Cakras
docs.text:
The Yoga Upaniṣads give extensive attention to prāṇāyāma (breath control), which they regard as the pivotal practice linking the gross body to the subtle mind. The Yoga-Tattva, Śāṇḍilya and Triśikhi-Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣads give the most detailed instructions. Each round has three phases — inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), regarded as the most important, and exhalation (recaka) — and in the purification of the channels (nāḍī-śodhana) the breath is drawn in through one nostril and let out through the other, alternately. The texts prescribe proportions such as 1:4:2 for the three phases and grade practice by its bodily signs: perspiration at the lowest level, trembling at the middle, and at the highest a “rising” (utthāna) of the body, which is a traditional claim.

Health and Safety Note

This chapter describes practices as the texts present them; it is not a manual. Prolonged breath retention (kumbhaka), forceful breathing, inverted postures and techniques such as khecarī (which traditionally involves cutting the frenulum of the tongue) and vajrolī can cause injury and are unsuitable for people with heart disease, high blood pressure, epilepsy, glaucoma, respiratory illness or pregnancy. The Haṭha texts themselves warn that breath control practised wrongly produces disease (Haṭhayogapradīpikā 2.16). The texts’ claims that these practices cure illness, conquer ageing or produce levitation are traditional claims, not established facts. Anyone wishing to practise should seek qualified instruction and medical advice.

Modern Relevance: Breath Control and Modern Research

Laboratory studies of slow, regular breathing report measurable effects on heart-rate variability, autonomic balance and subjective calm; a systematic review is given by Zaccaro et al. (2018). Such findings are consistent with the texts’ general claim that breath control “steadies the mind”, but they do not validate the specific ratios, the subtle-body physiology, or the claims of longevity and supernatural powers, and many of the underlying studies are small.

docs.title: 7.4.1 The Nāḍīs
docs.text:
The Yoga Upaniṣads describe a system of subtle channels (nāḍīs) and centres (cakras) within the body. This is a map of the body as experienced in meditation and ritual (the “subtle body”), not an anatomical description, and the individual texts do not agree with one another on the number, location or names of the centres. The figure of 72,000 channels goes back to the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (2.1.19), where they are the paths of the self in sleep. The Yoga Upaniṣads adopt it and single out three channels as of paramount importance (Table 7.2).

Table 7.2. The Three Principal Nāḍīs Nāḍī Position Quality Function Iḍā Left side Lunar, cooling Associated with the left nostril and the moon Piṅgalā Right side Solar, heating Associated with the right nostril and the sun Suṣumṇā Central — The channel through which breath and Kuṇḍalinī rise in yogic practice

docs.title: 7.4.2 The Cakras
docs.text: The scheme of six cakras along the central channel — mūlādhāra, svādhiṣṭhāna, maṇipūra, anāhata, viśuddha and ājñā, with the thousand-petalled sahasrāra above — that is familiar today is only one of several. It was popularised by Pūrṇānanda’s Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa (1577) and, in the West, by Arthur Avalon’s The Serpent Power (1919); the Yoga Upaniṣads themselves give varying lists.

docs.title: 7.5 Kuṇḍalinī: The Coiled Power
docs.text:
The concept of Kuṇḍalinī — the dormant power coiled at the base of the spine — entered yoga from the Śaiva and Śākta Tantras and the Haṭha texts, and is a central theme in several Yoga Upaniṣads, particularly the Yoga-Kuṇḍalī, the Yoga-Cūḍāmaṇi, the Yoga-Śikhā, the Yoga-Tattva and the Darśana. It does not occur in the principal Upaniṣads. As these texts describe it, the process of awakening involves:

  1. Purification of the nāḍīs through prāṇāyāma

  2. Arousal of the dormant energy through specific practices (bandhas, mudrās, mantras)

  3. Gradual ascent of the energy through the suṣumṇā nāḍī, piercing each cakra in succession

  4. Union with Śiva at the sahasrāra

Several texts add that the rising power must pierce three “knots” (granthis) named after Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Rudra. Their locations differ from text to text (the Haṭhayogapradīpikā, 4.69–77, connects them with stages of inner sound at the heart, the throat and between the eyebrows); modern teachers often explain them psychologically as attachment to the body, to persons and to the sense of doership, but that interpretation is modern.

The Yoga Upaniṣads insist that these practices must be learned from a qualified teacher and not from textual study alone, and they warn of physical and mental disturbance when they are practised prematurely or wrongly. In this they continue the older Upaniṣadic view that the highest teaching is transmitted personally, from teacher to pupil (Section 1.15).

docs.title: 7.6 Nāda Yoga: The Yoga of Inner Sound
docs.text:
The Nāda-Bindu Upaniṣad and the Dhyāna-Bindu Upaniṣad describe a distinctive meditative practice based on the perception of inner sounds (nāda). The practitioner, seated in a specific posture with the ears closed (using the ṣaṇmukhī mudrā), progressively hears subtler and subtler sounds — from the roaring of an ocean to the sound of a bell, a flute, a lute, the buzzing of a bee, and finally the subtlest sound of all, which leads to absorption in the Absolute (Table 7.3).

Table 7.3. Progressive Stages of Nāda Perception (a composite summary; the texts differ in the number and order of the sounds) Stage Sound Perceived Significance 1 Ocean / Thunder Gross stage; initial practice 2 Drum / Waterfall Attention begins to stabilise 3 Bell / Conch Intermediate stage; mind becomes absorbed 4 Flute / Vīṇā Subtle stage; deep concentration 5 Bee / Humming Very subtle; approaching samādhi 6 Silence / Unstruck Sound The anāhata nāda; absorption in Brahman

docs.title: 7.7 The Haṃsa Upaniṣad: The Swan of the Self
docs.text:
The Haṃsa Upaniṣad presents one of the most elegant teachings in the Yoga Upaniṣadic corpus. The word haṃsa (swan, or more precisely, the bar-headed goose) is traditionally explained as the natural sound of breathing: ha on exhalation and sa on inhalation. Reversed, it gives so ’ham, “I am He” (saḥ aham). Texts such as the Yogacūḍāmaṇi add that every being thus repeats this mantra 21,600 times in a day and a night — a traditional figure, not a physiological measurement.

This is called the Ajapā Gāyatrī — the “un-chanted” Gāyatrī — because it occurs naturally with every breath, whether one is aware of it or not. The practice of Haṃsa Yoga consists in becoming conscious of this natural mantra and thereby transforming every breath into an act of Self-remembrance.

docs.title: 7.8 The Tejo-Bindu Upaniṣad: The Fifteen-limbed Yoga
docs.text: The Tejo-Bindu Upaniṣad presents a fifteen-limbed Yoga, going far beyond the standard eight limbs. The additional limbs include subtle practices aimed at the dissolution of the mind (mano-nāśa) and the exhaustion of latent tendencies (vāsanā-kṣaya). The fifteen are: (1) yama, (2) niyama, (3) tyāga (renunciation), (4) mauna (silence), (5) deśa (place), (6) kāla (time), (7) āsana, (8) mūlabandha, (9) dehasāmya (bodily equipoise), (10) dṛksthiti (steadiness of gaze), (11) prāṇasaṃyamana (breath control), (12) pratyāhāra, (13) dhāraṇā, (14) ātma-dhyāna (meditation on the Self) and (15) samādhi.

docs.title: 7.9 Mudrās and Bandhas
docs.text: The Yoga Upaniṣads describe a number of mudrās (seals) and bandhas (locks) that are considered essential for the arousal and control of the breath and the subtle energies. They are the same as those of the Haṭha texts: khecarī mudrā, in which the tongue, lengthened by gradual cutting of the frenulum, is turned back into the cavity above the palate; mahāmudrā; the inverted viparītakaraṇī, said to reverse the downward flow of the nectar (amṛta); vajrolī, a technique of urethral suction intended to retain bindu (semen); and the three locks — mūla bandha (contraction of the perineum), uḍḍīyāna bandha (drawing the abdomen in and up) and jālandhara bandha (chin pressed to the chest). The Yoga-Cūḍāmaṇi Upaniṣad states that when the three bandhas are applied together the breath is forced into the suṣumṇā, where it begins to ascend and awakens Kuṇḍalinī. The claims made for these practices (conquest of ageing, longevity) are traditional; see the safety note above, and Volume 5 for the techniques.

docs.title: 7.10 The Advaya-Tāraka Upaniṣad: Tāraka Yoga
docs.text:
The Advaya-Tāraka Upaniṣad presents a distinctive form of yoga called Tāraka Yoga — the “Yoga of the Deliverer” — which centres on the perception of inner light phenomena (jyotis). The text describes three types of inner vision:

  1. Antar-lakṣya (Internal Vision): Perception of coloured lights, geometric forms, and luminous patterns within the body during meditation with closed eyes

  2. Bahir-lakṣya (External Vision): Perception of subtle lights in the space before the eyes — blue, golden, and white radiances perceived with partially open eyes

  3. Madhya-lakṣya (Intermediate Vision): The vision of the bhrūmadhya (inter-brow centre), where the concentrated gaze reveals progressively subtler luminous phenomena

The text declares that through sustained practice of Tāraka Yoga, the practitioner perceives the advaya (non-dual) nature of reality and attains liberation even while living (jīvanmukti).

Tāraka as “That Which Delivers”

The word tāraka derives from the root tṛ (to cross over, to deliver). Tāraka Yoga is thus the “yoga that delivers” the practitioner across the ocean of saṃsāra. The inner light perceived in this practice is understood not as a physiological phenomenon but as the self-luminous radiance of the Ātman itself, becoming progressively visible as the veils of ignorance are thinned through practice.

docs.title: 7.11 The Varāha Upaniṣad: Tattva-Jñāna through Yoga
docs.text:
The Varāha Upaniṣad presents a comprehensive synthesis of Yoga and Vedānta. It describes the nature of the five elements (pañca-bhūtas), the nature of the jīva (individual soul), and the method of liberation through combined practice of Haṭha Yoga and Jñāna Yoga. Unusually for a Yoga Upaniṣad, the Varāha gives an extended treatment of the tattvas (principles of reality) and their transcendence through meditative insight.

The text describes the person who has attained tattva-jñāna (knowledge of reality) through yogic practice in terms familiar from the Gītā’s portrait of the person of steady wisdom; in summary:

  • Equanimity in pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour

  • Freedom from attachment to the fruits of action

  • Spontaneous compassion for all beings

  • Absence of ego-identification with the body

  • Natural abidance in the awareness “I am the Ātman”

  • Indifference to worldly acquisitions and conventional religious observances

jñātvā devaṃ sarvapāśāpāhāniḥ kṣīṇaiḥ kleśair janmamṛtyuprahāṇiḥ Translation: “Knowing the Lord, all fetters fall away, afflictions are destroyed, and birth and death cease.” — Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.11, an older verse expressing the ideal the Yoga Upaniṣads take up

docs.title: 7.12 The Relationship Between Yoga Upaniṣads and Patañjali
docs.text:
The Yoga Upaniṣads are later than Patañjali’s Yogasūtra and borrow its eight limbs, but they differ from it significantly (Table 7.4).

Table 7.4. Yoga Upaniṣads vs. Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtras Aspect Yoga Upaniṣads Patañjali’s Yoga Sūtras Date Mostly medieval to early modern (expanded versions c. 17th–18th century) c. 325–425 CE Philosophical base Vedāntic (Brahman = Ātman) Sāṅkhya-Yoga (Puruṣa \(\neq\) Prakṛti) Goal Realisation of Brahman Kaivalya (isolation of Puruṣa) Kuṇḍalinī Central concept Not mentioned Nāda Yoga Extensively described Not mentioned Cakras Detailed description Not mentioned Emphasis Haṭha practice combined with meditation and Vedāntic knowledge Eight-limbed meditative discipline (later called Rāja Yoga)

docs.title: 7.13 Samādhi: The Goal of Yogic Practice
docs.text:
The Yoga Upaniṣads describe samādhi (complete absorption) as the culmination of all yogic practice. Following Advaita usage (rather than Patañjali’s distinction between samprajñāta and asamprajñāta samādhi), they distinguish two types (Table 7.5).

Table 7.5. Two Types of Samādhi in the Yoga Upaniṣads Aspect Savikalpa Samādhi Nirvikalpa Samādhi Nature Absorption with a subtle trace of subject-object distinction Complete absorption without any distinction whatsoever Content Awareness of “I am meditating on Brahman” No awareness of meditation; only Brahman Duration Temporary; one returns to normal consciousness May be temporary or permanent (sahaja) Result Purification; strengthening of conviction Direct knowledge (aparokṣa jñāna); liberation

The Maṇḍala-Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad describes the highest samādhi in terms that echo the Māṇḍūkya’s description of Turīya: it is beyond waking, dream, and deep sleep; it is self-luminous, non-dual, and blissful. The practitioner who attains this state is described as jīvanmukta — liberated while still living in the body.

docs.title: 7.14 The Yoga Upaniṣads and Śaṅkara’s Advaita
docs.text:
The relationship between the Yoga Upaniṣads and Śaṅkara’s Advaita Vedānta is complex. Śaṅkara himself emphasised jñāna (knowledge) as the sole direct means of liberation and treated Yoga as a preparatory discipline (sādhana) for purifying the mind. The Yoga Upaniṣads, while not contradicting this position, give far greater independent weight to Yogic practice, sometimes suggesting that Samādhi itself is the means of liberation rather than merely a preparatory stage.

Key Insight

The Yoga Upaniṣads serve as a bridge between the philosophical Upaniṣads and the practical yoga traditions of India. They present the Upaniṣadic vision of Ātman-Brahman identity not as a theoretical proposition but as a state to be realised through āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna and samādhi — a synthesis that, as Section 7.1.1 showed, was achieved largely in the medieval and early modern periods.

docs.title: 7.15 The Haṭha Yoga Tradition and Its Upaniṣadic Roots
7.15.1 From Upaniṣadic Yoga to Haṭha Yoga
docs.text:
The relationship between the Yoga Upaniṣads and the Haṭha Yoga tradition is one of close textual continuity — but, as explained in Section 7.1.1, the Haṭha texts generally come first. The Haṭhayogapradīpikā of Svātmārāma (15th century) compiles material from earlier Haṭha works; the expanded South Indian Yoga Upaniṣads in turn quote the Pradīpikā and its sources, often verbatim. The Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā (c. 17th–18th century) and the Śiva Saṃhitā belong to the same late period.

The parallels listed below are therefore best read as evidence of Haṭha material being absorbed into Upaniṣadic form. Together, these texts show that later Indian traditions came to treat the trained and purified body as an instrument of liberation rather than simply an obstacle to it (Table 7.6).

Table 7.6. Parallels Between the Yoga Upaniṣads and the Haṭhayogapradīpikā Practice Yoga Upaniṣad Parallel in the Haṭhayogapradīpikā Khecarī Mudrā Yoga-Cūḍāmaṇi, Yoga-Kuṇḍalī Haṭha-Yoga-Pradīpikā 3.32–54 Nāḍī Śodhana Śāṇḍilya, Yoga-Tattva Haṭha-Yoga-Pradīpikā 2.7–10 Kuṇḍalinī awakening Yoga-Kuṇḍalī, Yoga-Śikhā Haṭha-Yoga-Pradīpikā 3.1–5 Tri-bandha Yoga-Cūḍāmaṇi Haṭha-Yoga-Pradīpikā 3.55–76 Nāda meditation Nāda-Bindu, Dhyāna-Bindu Haṭha-Yoga-Pradīpikā 4.64–102 Samādhi descriptions Maṇḍala-Brāhmaṇa Haṭha-Yoga-Pradīpikā 4.1–16

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: 8.1 Introduction: Renunciation in the Indian Tradition
docs.text:
The institution of sannyāsa (formal renunciation of worldly life in pursuit of liberation) is one of the most distinctive features of Brahmanical religion, developed in dialogue with the older ascetic orders of the Buddhists and Jains. The Sannyāsa Upaniṣads are a group of about seventeen to twenty texts in the Muktikā canon that give the rationale, ritual procedures, rules of conduct and spiritual practices of the renouncer (sannyāsin). They serve simultaneously as philosophical treatises and as manuals of conduct.

Their dates vary widely. Patrick Olivelle, whose translation is the standard scholarly treatment (Olivelle 1992), distinguishes an older group — including the Āruṇi, Laghu-Saṃnyāsa, Kaṇṭhaśruti, Paramahaṃsa, Jābāla and Brahma Upaniṣads — composed probably around the beginning of the Common Era, from a younger group composed in the medieval period, some of them (such as the Nāradapariv­rājaka) many centuries later and heavily influenced by Advaita Vedānta. They are thus considerably later than the principal Upaniṣads, which know wandering ascetics but not the formal institution described here (Table 8.1).

Table 8.1. The Principal Sannyāsa Upaniṣads No. Upaniṣad Veda Primary Focus 1 Jābāla Śukla Yajurveda Conditions for sannyāsa; the right to renounce 2 Āśrama Atharvaveda The four āśramas; transition to sannyāsa 3 Parama-Haṃsa Śukla Yajurveda The supreme renunciant; the wandering monk 4 Nāradapariv­rājaka Atharvaveda Types of sannyāsins; their duties and conduct 5 Kaṇṭhaśruti (Kaṭhaśruti) Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Ritual procedures of renunciation 6 Kuṇḍikā Sāmaveda Equipment and conduct of the sannyāsin 7 Brahma Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda The sannyāsin’s meditation on Brahman 8 Maitreya Sāmaveda Śiva’s teaching to the sage Maitreya on renunciation and the Self 9 Sannyāsa Sāmaveda Comprehensive rules of renunciation 10 Āruṇi Sāmaveda Internal vs. external sannyāsa

docs.title: 8.2 The Philosophy of Renunciation
docs.text:
The philosophical basis of sannyāsa, as the later texts present it, rests upon the Vedāntic insight that if Brahman alone is real and the phenomenal world is a superimposition (adhyāsa) upon Brahman, then attachment to worldly objects, relationships and achievements is fundamentally misplaced. Its scriptural precedent is the Bṛhadāraṇyaka’s description of those who, knowing the Self, “give up the desire for sons, wealth and worlds and live the life of a mendicant” (3.5.1; cf. 4.4.22). Sannyāsa is the natural consequence of viveka (discrimination) and vairāgya (dispassion).

yad ahar eva virajet tad ahar eva pravrajet Translation: “On that very day that dispassion (vairāgya) arises, one should renounce.” — Jābāla Upaniṣad 4

This bold declaration from the Jābāla Upaniṣad is of great significance. Having first set out the orderly sequence (student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer), the text adds that one may also renounce directly from studentship, from the household or from the forest: sannyāsa is not contingent upon completing the earlier āśramas. The question of whether this was permissible was hotly debated in Dharmaśāstra, where many authorities insisted on the sequence.

docs.title: 8.3 The Four Āśramas and the Place of Sannyāsa
docs.text:
The classical Dharmaśāstra theory organises the life of a twice-born man into four stages (āśramas). Olivelle has shown that this sequential scheme is itself a later reworking: in the earliest Dharmasūtras (c. 3rd–2nd century BCE) the āśramas were four alternative, lifelong ways of life chosen by an adult, and only later were they arranged as successive stages (Olivelle 1993). The scheme applied in theory to men of the three upper varṇas; women and Śūdras had no place in it (Figure 8.1).

Figure 8.1. The Four Āśramas and the Direct Path to Sannyāsa

docs.title: 8.4 The Parama-Haṃsa: The Supreme Renunciant
docs.text: The Parama-Haṃsa Upaniṣad describes the highest type of sannyāsin — the parama-haṃsa (literally, “supreme swan”). The swan (haṃsa) is a powerful symbol in Indian tradition: it is said to possess the ability to separate milk from water, just as the realised soul separates the Real from the unreal. The paramahaṃsa abandons the topknot and the sacred thread, the marks of Brahmanical ritual status, and lives established in Brahman alone.

docs.title: 8.4.1 Types of Sannyāsins
docs.text:
The Sannyāsa Upaniṣads classify renunciants into several categories, based on their level of realisation and their mode of life (Table 8.2).

Table 8.2. Classification of Sannyāsins According to the Sannyāsa Upaniṣads Type Meaning Description Kuṭīcaka Hut-dweller Lives in a fixed hermitage near a temple or village Bahūdaka Many-watered Wanders from place to place, begging at many doors Haṃsa Swan Wanders freely but with some minimal possessions Parama-Haṃsa Supreme Swan Utterly free; beyond all conventions; absorbed in Brahman Turīyātīta Beyond the Fourth Transcends even the four categories; beyond description Avadhūta The Shaken-off Has shaken off all worldly bonds; the most radical form

docs.title: 8.5 The Ritual of Sannyāsa Dīkṣā
docs.text:
The Kaṇṭhaśruti Upaniṣad and the Nāradapariv­rājaka Upaniṣad provide descriptions of the ritual of sannyāsa initiation (dīkṣā), which later manuals elaborated further. The ceremony involves several solemn acts:

  1. Prāyaścitta (Atonement): A final expiatory rite to absolve past transgressions

  2. Virajā Homa (Fire sacrifice): The aspirant performs a final fire sacrifice, symbolically offering into the fire all worldly attachments

  3. Prāṇāgnihotra: The internalisation of the sacrificial fire — henceforth, the renunciant’s own breath becomes the sacred fire

  4. Giving up the sacred thread (yajñopavīta): The external markers of caste identity are renounced

  5. Receiving the Mahāvākya: In later Advaita practice, the guru imparts a Great Saying to the new sannyāsin

  6. Tri-daṇḍa or Eka-daṇḍa: The renunciant receives the triple staff (controlling body, speech, and mind) or the single staff

  7. Declaration: The sannyāsin says “I have renounced” three times, then grants “fearlessness to all beings” (a vow of non-harm)

docs.title: 8.6 The Conduct of the Sannyāsin
docs.text:
The Sannyāsa Upaniṣads prescribe a detailed code of conduct for the renunciant. The Nāradapariv­rājaka Upaniṣad is particularly comprehensive:

  • Dwelling: The sannyāsin should not settle in one place, staying only briefly in any village or town (except during the rainy season, cāturmāsya)

  • Food: Only alms (bhikṣā), begged from no more than a few houses (five or seven, according to different rules)

  • Possessions: A staff (daṇḍa), a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), a loincloth (kaupīna), and an ochre-dyed cloth (kāṣāya vastra)

  • Speech: Measured, truthful, and beneficial; silence is preferred

  • Attitude: Equanimity towards honour and dishonour, praise and blame, pleasure and pain

  • Practice: Constant meditation on Brahman; study of the Upaniṣads; recitation of Oṃ

docs.title: 8.7 The Āruṇi Upaniṣad: Internal Renunciation
docs.text:
The Āruṇi Upaniṣad, one of the oldest of the group, has Āruṇi ask Prajāpati how he may give up ritual activity altogether; he is told to abandon his sons, relatives, topknot and sacred thread and to live as a mendicant devoted to the Self. Several later texts, together with the Gītā (5.3; 6.1), go further and insist that true renunciation is internal — a transformation of consciousness — rather than merely external.

The teaching implies that the essence of sannyāsa lies not in the outward trappings — the ochre robe, the shaven head, the begging bowl — but in the inner detachment from identification with the body-mind complex. A person may wear the ochre robe and yet be inwardly attached; conversely, a person may live in the world and yet be inwardly a sannyāsin.

docs.title: 8.8 The Avadhūta: The Radical Renunciant
docs.text:
The late Avadhūta Upaniṣad (attributed to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda) describes the most radical and unconventional form of sannyāsa. It explains the word avadhūta through a fourfold analysis of its syllables, each standing for a quality of the renouncer (Table 8.3).

Table 8.3. The Fourfold Etymology of Avadhūta Syllable Root Meaning Significance A Akṣaratva Being imperishable Va Vareṇyatva Being most excellent, worthy of choice Dhū Dhūta-saṃsāra-bandhana Having shaken off the bonds of worldly existence Ta Tat-tvam-asy-ādi-lakṣyatva Being the referent of sayings such as “That thou art”

The Avadhūta transcends all social conventions, all external observances, and even the normative codes of the other types of sannyāsins. Unlike the Kuṭīcaka who lives in a fixed hermitage, or the Bahūdaka who follows prescribed begging routes, the Avadhūta is utterly free — wandering without pattern, eating what comes without solicitation, wearing or not wearing clothing as the occasion arises, and remaining absorbed in Brahman regardless of external circumstances.

Philosophical Note

The figure of the Avadhūta represents the extreme logical consequence of Advaita non-dualism: if Brahman alone is real and the world is mithyā, then all social distinctions — caste, gender, propriety, convention — are ultimately without substance. Yet the texts that voice this ideal for the realised renouncer did not dismantle those distinctions in society, or even in the rules for who might renounce (see below). The divine sage Dattātreya, revered as the archetypal avadhūta and as the teacher in the Avadhūtagītā, personifies the ideal.

docs.title: 8.9 The Ethics of Renunciation
docs.text:
The Sannyāsa Upaniṣads prescribe rules, but they also ground them in an ethic: the recognition of the Ātman in all beings. The sannyāsin’s vow of abhaya-dāna (the gift of fearlessness to all beings) is of particular moral significance:

abhayaṃ sarvabhūtebhyo mattaḥ Translation: “Fearlessness to all beings from me!” — Āruṇi Upaniṣad 3, after the threefold “I have renounced” (saṃnyastaṃ mayā)

This declaration — uttered at the moment of renunciation — is an unconditional commitment to ahiṃsā (non-violence) at the most fundamental level. The sannyāsin pledges to be a source of fearlessness to every living being — not only refraining from causing harm but actively radiating the peace that comes from Self-knowledge (Table 8.4).

Table 8.4. Ethical Principles Embedded in the Sannyāsa Upaniṣads Principle Description and Source Abhaya-dāna Gift of fearlessness to all beings — the supreme ethical act of the renouncer Sama-darśana Equal vision towards all — seeing the Ātman equally in a brahmin, an outcaste, a cow, an elephant, and a dog (Bhagavad Gītā 5.18, echoing Upaniṣadic principles) Nir-dvandva Freedom from the pairs of opposites — pleasure and pain, heat and cold, honour and dishonour (Nāradapariv­rājaka) Nir-ahaṅkāra Freedom from ego-identification — acting without the sense of personal doership (Parama-Haṃsa) Satyavāditā Truthfulness in all speech and conduct (Āruṇi)

docs.title: 8.10 Sannyāsa in the Modern World
docs.text:
The institution of sannyāsa has adapted considerably in the modern era. The great reformers of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries — Svāmī Vivekānanda, Svāmī Dayānanda Sarasvatī (of the Ārya Samāj), Svāmī Śivānanda, Svāmī Chinmayānanda, and others — were all sannyāsins who brought the ancient institution into creative engagement with modernity. They established organisations, hospitals, schools, and global missions while maintaining the inner spirit of renunciation.

The modern sannyāsin faces distinctive challenges: the presence of mass media, the globalisation of culture, the expectations of institutional management, and the demands of a worldwide following. Yet the core teaching of the Sannyāsa Upaniṣads remains unchanged: true renunciation is internal. Whether one lives in a cave in Uttarakāṣī or manages a global spiritual organisation, the essence of sannyāsa is the recognition that “I am not this body, not this mind; I am the infinite Ātman.”

Scholarly Note

The historical and sociological study of Indian renunciation has produced a substantial body of modern scholarship. Patrick Olivelle’s The Āśrama System (1993) and his annotated translation of the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads (1992) are foundational academic works (Olivelle 1993, 1992), and G. S. Ghurye’s Indian Sadhus (1953) remains a useful survey of the living orders.

docs.title: 8.11 Who May Renounce? Caste and Gender
docs.text:
The ideal of renunciation proclaims that the Self is beyond all social distinctions, but the rules for entering the renunciant life were socially restrictive. Most Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads simply assume a male renouncer of the twice-born classes, and many Dharmaśāstra authorities — as well as Śaṅkara in his commentaries — held that formal renunciation was open only to Brāhmaṇa men. The rites themselves presuppose this: the renouncer gives up the sacred thread and the domestic fires, which only an initiated twice-born man possessed. In the Daśanāmī orders that trace themselves to Śaṅkara, several branches long admitted only Brāhmaṇas, while others admitted non-Brāhmaṇas.

Women appear in the Upaniṣads as seekers — Maitreyī in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka chooses the knowledge of immortality over wealth — but the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads do not provide for women’s renunciation. (The Maitreya Upaniṣad of this group is named after a male sage, not after Maitreyī.) Women ascetics are nonetheless attested throughout Indian history, from the Buddhist and Jain orders of nuns to independent female renouncers in later Hindu traditions, and in modern times several Hindu orders have instituted formal sannyāsa for women (for example the Śrī Śāradā Maṭh, founded in 1954 in the Ramakrishna tradition).
