The gap between the egalitarian metaphysics of the Self and the exclusive social rules of renunciation is one of the tensions that modern Hindu reformers have sought to resolve. The Buddhist and Jain orders, which admitted members of all classes and established orders of nuns at an early date, provide an instructive contrast.

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: 9.1 Introduction: Upaniṣads of the Devotional Traditions
docs.text:
Among the 108 Upaniṣads of the Muktikā canon, a large number are associated with particular devotional traditions (sampradāyas). These are the so-called “sectarian” Upaniṣads: texts devoted to Śiva (Śaiva Upaniṣads, about fourteen in the conventional grouping), to Viṣṇu (Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣads, also about fourteen), and to the Goddess (Śākta Upaniṣads, about eight or nine), with a few devoted to Gaṇeśa and Sūrya. The designation “sectarian” is a scholarly convention and is not meant pejoratively. These texts show how the devotional traditions claimed Upaniṣadic authority for their theologies by composing works in the Upaniṣadic form, often borrowing phrases from the principal Upaniṣads and identifying their chosen deity with Brahman.

Their dates must be kept in view. With a few exceptions — the Mahānārāyaṇa that forms the tenth book of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (a different text from the Atharvavedic Mahānārāyaṇa of the Muktikā list), and possibly the Atharvaśiras, Kaivalya and Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya, which may belong to the first millennium CE — the sectarian Upaniṣads were composed in the medieval and early modern periods, many of them between about the tenth and the seventeenth centuries. Several reflect the theology of particular medieval schools: the Rāmatāpanīya that of the Rāmānandī tradition, the Gopālatāpanī that of Kṛṣṇa devotion in Braj, and the Śākta Upaniṣads that of Śrīvidyā Tantra. The numbers and the Vedic allocations given below follow the conventional grouping of the Muktikā list, which itself varies between editions. Many of them are known in the form transmitted in the South Indian collection of the 108, and they were commented on as a body by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin in the eighteenth century (Section 11.8).

docs.title: 9.2.1 Overview
docs.text:
The Śaiva Upaniṣads identify the supreme Brahman with Śiva (Maheśvara, Rudra). Their oldest Upaniṣadic model is the Śvetāśvatara, which already names the one God Rudra and Śiva (Section 4.6); several of them also draw on the Śatarudrīya, the litany to Rudra of the Yajurveda (Table 9.1).

Table 9.1. Principal Śaiva Upaniṣads Upaniṣad Veda Key Teaching Kaivalya Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Kaivalya (liberation) through knowledge of Śiva Atharva-Śiras Atharvaveda Śiva as the supreme deity; the meaning of Rudra Atharva-Śikhā Atharvaveda Meditation on Oṃ; Śiva (Īśāna) as its object Bṛhajjābāla Atharvaveda Vibhūti (sacred ash); Rudra as Brahman Rudra-Hṛdaya Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda The heart of Rudra; Śiva-Śakti non-duality Dakṣiṇāmūrti Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Śiva as the primordial Guru Pañcabrahma Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Five faces/aspects of Śiva Akṣamālikā Ṛgveda The rosary (akṣamālā) in Śaiva worship

docs.title: 9.2.2 The Atharvaśiras and the Pāśupatas
docs.text:
The Atharvaśiras (“Head of the Atharvaveda”) is probably among the oldest of the Śaiva Upaniṣads. A text of that name is already listed among purificatory recitations in the Dharmasūtras, though whether it is the work that survives cannot be proved. It opens with the gods going to Rudra’s world and asking him, “Who are you?” Rudra answers that he alone was in the beginning, is and will be, and that there is nothing apart from him; he then identifies himself with every god, every direction, every Veda and every element. The text goes on to explain Oṃ and the names of Rudra, and closes with an observance: the worshipper smears his body with ash while reciting that fire, wind, water, earth and space are ash.

This “Pāśupata observance” (pāśupata-vrata) links the Upaniṣad with the Pāśupatas, the oldest Śaiva ascetic order known from inscriptions and texts, who traced their teaching to Lakulīśa. Alexis Sanderson, in his survey of the Śaiva traditions, places the Pāśupatas in the “outer path” (atimārga) of ascetics who sought liberation through observances of ash-bathing, chanting and deliberately provocative behaviour, as distinct from the later tantric Śaivism of initiated householders (Sanderson 1988). The Atharvaśiras shows one way in which such a tradition could claim Vedic standing: by composing an Upaniṣad in which Rudra is the Brahman of the older texts. The related Atharvaśikhā, which teaches meditation on Oṃ with Śiva (Īśāna) as its object, and the Bṛhajjābāla and Bhasmajābāla, which are largely about sacred ash, continue the same concerns.

docs.title: 9.2.3 The Kaivalya Upaniṣad
docs.text:
The Kaivalya Upaniṣad is the most widely read of the Śaiva Upaniṣads and the closest in doctrine to the classical texts. Brahmā teaches the sage Āśvalāyana that liberation (kaivalya) is attained not by works, offspring or wealth but by renunciation, faith, devotion and meditation, and that the one to be known is Śiva, identical with the Ātman within:

sa eva sarvaṃ yad bhūtaṃ yac ca bhavyaṃ sanātanam jñātvā taṃ mṛtyum atyeti nānyaḥ panthā vimuktaye Translation: “He alone is everything — what was, what will be, the eternal. Knowing Him, one crosses beyond death. There is no other path to liberation.” — Kaivalya Upaniṣad 9

The second line echoes the Śvetāśvatara (3.8; Section 4.6.6), and the text as a whole is a mosaic of phrases from the principal Upaniṣads, which is one reason Advaitins valued it.

docs.title: 9.2.4 The Dakṣiṇāmūrti Upaniṣad
docs.text:
This Upaniṣad presents Śiva in his form as Dakṣiṇāmūrti — the south-facing deity who is the primordial teacher (ādi-guru). In the iconography and hymns associated with this form (above all the Dakṣiṇāmūrti-stotra attributed to Śaṅkara), Śiva sits under the banyan tree, a young teacher surrounded by aged disciples, and teaches the highest truth through silence: the silence itself is the teaching, a statement that ultimate truth transcends verbal expression (Figure 9.1).

Figure 9.1. Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Śiva as the teacher: a South Indian stone sculpture, the god seated with one foot resting on the dwarf Apasmāra Photo: Jagat321jeet, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 9.3.1 Overview
docs.text:
The Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣads identify Brahman with Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa) or with his incarnations, particularly Nṛsiṃha, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. Several of them were used by the Śrīvaiṣṇava and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava traditions (Table 9.2). Two texts with similar names must be kept apart. The Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad of the Muktikā list is a short Kṛṣṇa Yajurvedic text. The Mahānārāyaṇa of the same list is assigned to the Atharvaveda and is identified with the later Tripādvibhūti-Mahānārāyaṇa. Both differ from the older Mahānārāyaṇa, the tenth book of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, which Deussen counted among the verse Upaniṣads (Section 1.12) and on which Rāmānuja relied (Section 11.12.2).

Table 9.2. Principal Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣads (Vedic allocation as in the Muktikā list) Upaniṣad Veda Key Teaching Nṛsiṃha-Tāpanīya (Pūrva) Atharvaveda The mantra of Nṛsiṃha, the man-lion form of Viṣṇu, and its ritual use Nṛsiṃha-Tāpanīya (Uttara) Atharvaveda Nṛsiṃha identified with the self and with Oṃ, on the model of the Māṇḍūkya Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Nārāyaṇa as the source of all; the eight-syllable mantra Mahānārāyaṇa (Tripādvibhūti-) Atharvaveda Nārāyaṇa and his transcendent world (not the Mahānārāyaṇa of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka) Rāma-Tāpanīya (Pūrva and Uttara) Atharvaveda The Rāma mantra; Rāma as Brahman Gopāla-Tāpanīya (Pūrva and Uttara) Atharvaveda Kṛṣṇa the cowherd as the supreme Brahman; the Kṛṣṇa mantra Vāsudeva Sāmaveda Vāsudeva as the all-pervading Reality Avyakta Sāmaveda The unmanifest nature of Viṣṇu

docs.title: 9.3.2 The Nṛsiṃha-Tāpanīya Upaniṣad
docs.text:
The Nṛsiṃha-Tāpanīya is historically the most important of the Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣads, because it shows a mantra-based devotional text being fused with the Advaita reading of the Māṇḍūkya. It has two parts. The Pūrva (earlier) part is devoted to the “king of mantras” (mantra-rāja) of Nṛsiṃha, a thirty-two-syllable verse in anuṣṭubh metre: its divisions, its seed syllables, the diagram in which it is to be installed and the fruits of reciting it.

The Uttara (later) part turns from ritual to doctrine. It takes up the Māṇḍūkya’s analysis of the syllable Oṃ and the four quarters of the self (Section 3.2) and declares that the self in its fourth, non-dual state is Nṛsiṃha himself. The man-lion who in myth bursts from a pillar to destroy the demon Hiraṇyakaśipu becomes the Turīya of the Māṇḍūkya, and the devotee’s mantra becomes a means to the knowledge that the self is Brahman. The text uses the non-dualist vocabulary of Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā and is generally taken to presuppose both the Māṇḍūkya and Gauḍapāda; it is therefore unlikely to be older than the second half of the first millennium CE. Deussen included both parts in his Sixty Upaniṣads (Deussen 1897). Advaitins valued the work highly, and a commentary on its first part is ascribed to Śaṅkara, though the ascription is doubted. For the history of the Upaniṣads it is a clear case of what this chapter describes: a sectarian deity identified, through the vocabulary of the principal Upaniṣads, with the Brahman they teach.

docs.title: 9.3.3 The Rāma- and Gopāla-Tāpanīya Upaniṣads
docs.text:
The Rāma-Tāpanīya, modelled on the Nṛsiṃha text, does the same for Rāma: it expounds the six-syllable Rāma mantra and identifies Rāma with Brahman and with the syllable Oṃ. It was valued in the Rāmānandī tradition of north India.

The Gopāla-Tāpanīya Upaniṣad is important for the Kṛṣṇa-bhakti traditions, particularly the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava sampradāya of Caitanya (1486–1534), whose theologians, notably Jīva Gosvāmī, quote it extensively. It identifies the cowherd Kṛṣṇa of Vṛndāvana with the Supreme Brahman and presents the eighteen-syllable Kṛṣṇa mantra. The Gauḍīya doctrine that Kṛṣṇa is not merely an incarnation of Viṣṇu but svayaṃ bhagavān, the original form of the Godhead, rests chiefly on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (1.3.28), with the Upaniṣad cited in support.

docs.title: 9.4.1 Overview
docs.text:
The Śākta Upaniṣads identify Brahman with the Goddess (Devī, Mahāśakti). Most of them belong to the Śrīvidyā tradition, the tantric worship of the Goddess as Tripurasundarī, and they give that tradition a Vedic warrant (Table 9.3). The Kena’s Umā Haimavatī, who reveals Brahman to the gods, was read by Śākta commentators as their earliest Upaniṣadic witness (Section 2.2).

Table 9.3. Principal Śākta Upaniṣads Upaniṣad Veda Key Teaching Devī Atharvaveda Devī as the Supreme; the cosmic Goddess Tripurā-Tāpinī Atharvaveda Tripurasundarī; the Śrī Vidyā tradition Saubhāgya-Lakṣmī Ṛgveda Lakṣmī as the auspicious power of Viṣṇu Sarasvatī-Rahasya Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda Sarasvatī as the power of knowledge Bhāvanā Atharvaveda Meditations on the Goddess; Śrī Cakra Sītā Atharvaveda Sītā as the Supreme Śakti Annapūrṇā Atharvaveda The Goddess as the giver of food/sustenance

docs.title: 9.4.2 The Devī Upaniṣad
docs.text:
The Devī Upaniṣad (also known as Devī Atharva-Śīrṣa), a medieval text widely recited with the Devīmāhātmya, is the best known of the Śākta Upaniṣads. It opens with the gods asking the Great Goddess: “Who are You?” — the same question the gods put to Rudra in the Atharvaśiras. She answers:

ahaṃ brahmasvarūpiṇī / mattaḥ prakṛti-puruṣātmakaṃ jagat / śūnyaṃ cāśūnyaṃ ca Translation: “I am the form of Brahman. From me (emanates) the world, composed of Prakṛti and Puruṣa — both the void and the non-void.” — Devī Upaniṣad 1–2

The Devī Upaniṣad goes on to identify the Goddess with the principal Upaniṣadic categories — Brahman, Ātman, Sat-Cit-Ānanda, the Mahāvākyas, and Oṃ. She is at once transcendent and immanent, formless and possessed of all forms.

docs.title: 9.4.3 The Tripurā-Tāpinī and the Śrīvidyā Upaniṣads
docs.text:
The Tripurā-Tāpinī Upaniṣad belongs to the Śrīvidyā tradition and centres on the worship of the Goddess Tripurasundarī. It presents her as Brahman, sets out her mantra — the Śrīvidyā of fifteen syllables — and the diagram in which she is worshipped, the Śrī Cakra or Śrī Yantra (Figure 9.2), and it gives an esoteric exegesis of Vedic material, including the Gāyatrī, in Śrīvidyā terms. It ends, like the Nṛsiṃha text, by making the worship a path to non-dual knowledge. Two shorter texts complete the picture. The Ṛgvedic Tripurā Upaniṣad expresses the tradition’s doctrine in cryptic verses, and the Bhāvanā Upaniṣad teaches an inner worship in which the practitioner identifies the parts of the Śrī Cakra with the parts and faculties of the body. Both were commented on in the eighteenth century by Bhāskararāya, the leading theologian of the Śrīvidyā, who used them to argue that his tradition was Vedic and not merely tantric. Douglas Brooks’s studies of the Śrīvidyā show how much of the tradition’s self-understanding rests on this claim (Brooks 1990).

Figure 9.2. A schematic sketch of the Śrī Cakra (Śrī Yantra): four upward-pointing (blue) and five downward-pointing (maroon) triangles nested around the central bindu, within lotuses of eight and sixteen petals and the outer square. In the true diagram the nine triangles interlock to form forty-three smaller triangles; the sketch shows only their number and orientation

docs.title: 9.5 The Gaṇapati, Sūrya and Sāvitrī Upaniṣads
docs.text:
Beyond the three major sectarian groups, the Muktikā canon includes Upaniṣads devoted to Gaṇapati (Gaṇeśa) and to the Sun (Table 9.4). The Gaṇapati Upaniṣad (also called Gaṇapati Atharva-Śīrṣa), a late text probably of the sixteenth or seventeenth century and associated with the Gāṇapatya cult of Maharashtra (Courtright 1985), identifies Gaṇapati with the non-dual Brahman: tvaṃ brahmā tvaṃ viṣṇus tvaṃ rudras tvam indras tvam agnis tvaṃ vāyus tvaṃ sūryaḥ — “Thou art Brahmā, thou art Viṣṇu, thou art Rudra, thou art Indra, thou art Agni, thou art Vāyu, thou art Sūrya.” It is today among the most widely recited devotional texts in western India. It shows that the Upaniṣadic identification of all deities with the one Brahman could be applied to any member of the pantheon: the elephant-headed god of obstacles, learning and beginnings becomes the cause of creation, preservation and dissolution.

The Sūrya Upaniṣad, also in the “Atharvaśīrṣa” form, identifies the Sun with Brahman and with the self of all that moves and is still, takes up the Gāyatrī verse addressed to Savitṛ, and gives an eight-syllable mantra of the Sun. The Sāvitrī Upaniṣad of the Sāmaveda is a short text of correspondences in the old style: Savitṛ and Sāvitrī are fire and earth, Varuṇa and the waters, wind and space, and so on through a series of male and female pairs, and the Gāyatrī (also called Sāvitrī) is interpreted through them. It closes with the two spells called Balā and Atibalā, which in the Rāmāyaṇa Viśvāmitra teaches to Rāma.

Table 9.4. The Minor Sectarian Upaniṣads: Gaṇapati and Sūrya Groups Upaniṣad Deity Key Teaching Gaṇapati Atharva-Śīrṣa Gaṇeśa Gaṇapati is the Supreme Brahman; the bīja-mantra Gaṃ as the seed of all creation Sūrya Upaniṣad Sūrya The Sun as the visible form of Brahman; the Gāyatrī mantra as the path to liberation Sāvitrī Upaniṣad Savitṛ and Sāvitrī The divine creative power; meditation on the solar deity and the Sāvitrī verse

docs.title: 9.6 Common Framework and Theological Pluralism
docs.text:
Despite their different deities, the sectarian Upaniṣads share a framework. Each identifies its chosen deity with Brahman: Śiva, Viṣṇu or the Goddess is declared to be the non-dual, all-pervading, self-luminous reality of the principal Upaniṣads, and the deity is identified with the “That” of tat tvam asi. Each joins the path of knowledge (jñāna-mārga) of the older texts with the devotion (bhakti) of its tradition. And each gives mantras, diagrams, meditations and observances (upāsanā) for the worship of its deity — in this respect the sectarian texts stand closer to the ritual meditations of the oldest Upaniṣads (Section 4.3) than the philosophical summaries usually suggest.

The existence of Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava and Śākta Upaniṣads, each declaring its deity to be the supreme Brahman, raises the question of theological pluralism, to which three answers were given:

  1. The Advaita response: all sectarian Upaniṣads teach the same non-dual Brahman under different names. The names and forms (nāma-rūpa) differ, but the reality they point to is one — an application of the Ṛg-Vedic verse ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti (“The One Being, the wise call by many names”, Ṛgveda 1.164.46). Upaniṣadbrahmayogin’s commentary on the whole collection takes this line.

  2. The sectarian response: this is the position of most of the sectarian texts themselves. Each tradition claims that its deity is truly supreme and that the other deities are subordinate manifestations. The Śaiva tradition regards Viṣṇu as a form of Śiva; the Vaiṣṇava tradition regards Śiva as a devotee of Viṣṇu.

  3. The inclusive response: the supreme reality encompasses all divine forms. Śiva, Viṣṇu and the Goddess are aspects of one undivided Absolute, as in the Purāṇic scheme in which Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Maheśvara represent creation, preservation and dissolution — three functions of one being.

docs.title: 9.7 Beyond the Sectarian Groups: The Sāmānya Vedānta Upaniṣads
docs.text:
The modern classification of the 108 (Figure 1.2) has one further group that is neither sectarian nor devoted to yoga or renunciation: the “general Vedānta” (sāmānya-vedānta) Upaniṣads. The grouping goes back to the Adyar Library editions and translations of the minor Upaniṣads published in the early twentieth century, which divided the non-principal texts of the Muktikā list into Yoga, Sannyāsa, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta and “general” volumes; later scholars, including Olivelle in his work on the Sannyāsa Upaniṣads (Olivelle 1992), have used the same divisions. The group is a residual category, and its membership varies, but it includes texts such as the Subāla, Paiṅgala, Adhyātma, Nirālamba, Sarvasāra, Mahā, Vajrasūcī and Muktikā itself. Most are medieval, and most are doctrinal summaries rather than records of dialogue.

A few of them matter beyond their group:

  • The Subāla gives a cosmogony and a long account of the self dwelling within every element and faculty, ending with the declaration that the inner self of all beings is “the one divine God, Nārāyaṇa”. Rāmānuja cites it as scripture for his doctrine that the world is the body of Brahman (Section 11.12.2).

  • The Paiṅgala, a dialogue between Yājñavalkya and his pupil Paiṅgala, is a compact manual of Advaita: the emergence of the world from māyā, the three bodies, the five sheaths, the analysis of the mahāvākyas, and the condition of the liberated. It shows the doctrines of Chapters 5 and 6 in the form of an Upaniṣad.

  • The Mahā Upaniṣad contains, in its sixth chapter, the verse that ends “for the noble-minded the whole earth is one family” (vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam), a line also found in the Hitopadeśa and much quoted today.

  • The Vajrasūcī (“Diamond Needle”) asks who is truly a Brāhmaṇa. It rejects in turn the soul, the body, birth, learning and ritual acts as the criterion, and answers that a Brāhmaṇa is one who has directly known the self. A Buddhist work of the same title, ascribed (doubtfully) to Aśvaghoṣa, attacks caste by similar arguments. The Upaniṣad redefines the highest varṇa in spiritual terms; it does not call for the abolition of caste in social life, and it should not be read as evidence that the Upaniṣadic tradition rejected caste (Sections 4.5 and 8.11).

The general Vedānta group thus shows the same process at work as the sectarian groups. In the medieval period the Upaniṣad was a living genre: teachers of every school composed texts in its form to state their doctrines with the authority of revelation, and the canon of 108 was assembled from them.

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: Chapter 10: States of Consciousness: From Waking to Turīya
10.1 Introduction: Consciousness as the Central Problem
docs.text:
The analysis of the states of consciousness is one of the most distinctive contributions of the Upaniṣads. Western philosophers from Aristotle to Descartes also reflected on dreaming, but mainly as a problem for knowledge of the external world; the Upaniṣadic teachers instead made the comparison of waking, dream and deep sleep into a method for discovering the nature of the self, and posited a further state beyond all three.

The principal texts for this analysis are the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad (with Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā), the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (particularly Yājñavalkya’s teachings in 4.3), the Chāndogya (8.7–12) and the Praśna Upaniṣad (Question 4). The Māṇḍūkya’s own text, its correlation of the states with the syllable Oṃ, and Gauḍapāda’s arguments are set out in Section 3.2; this chapter examines each state in turn. The systematic interpretation that follows is largely that of Advaita, whose teachers did most to develop it; where the theistic schools differ, this is noted.

docs.title: 10.2 The Four States: An Overview
docs.text:
Figure 10.1 arranges the four states in ascending order of subtlety, from waking to Turīya.

Figure 10.1. The Four States of Consciousness in Ascending Order of Subtlety

docs.title: 10.3.1 Description
docs.text:
In the waking state (jāgrat), consciousness is directed outward through the sense organs (indriyas) towards the objects of the external world. The self in this state is called Vaiśvānara (“relating to all people”), because this state is common to all beings; later Advaita correlates it with the gross body (sthūla śarīra).

The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad describes Vaiśvānara as having “seven limbs and nineteen mouths” (Table 10.1).

Table 10.1. The Symbolic Anatomy of Vaiśvānara Attribute Interpretation Seven Limbs Heaven (head), Sun (eye), Air (breath), Space (torso), Water (bladder), Earth (feet), Fire (mouth) — the cosmic Vaiśvānara of Chāndogya 5.18.2, to which Śaṅkara refers Nineteen Mouths 5 sense organs + 5 organs of action + 5 vital breaths + mind + intellect + ego + citta = 19 instruments of experience (Śaṅkara’s explanation)

docs.title: 10.3.2 Philosophical Significance
docs.text: The waking state, though the most familiar, is not treated as privileged. Yājñavalkya pictures the self moving between waking and dream “as a great fish moves along both banks of a river” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.18). Gauḍapāda later went much further, arguing that waking experience shares the essential characteristics of dream — subject-object duality, dependence on time, and eventual sublation (see Section 3.2.5).

docs.title: 10.4.1 Yājñavalkya’s Analysis of Dream
docs.text:
Yājñavalkya’s analysis of the dream state in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.3.9–14) is the fullest in the Upaniṣads:

na tatra rathā na rathayogā na panthāno bhavanti / atha rathān rathayogān pathaḥ sṛjate / na tatrānandā mudaḥ pramudo bhavanti / athānandān mudaḥ pramudaḥ sṛjate Translation: “There are no chariots there, no yokes, no roads — but he creates chariots, yokes, and roads. There are no joys, delights, or pleasures there — but he creates joys, delights, and pleasures.” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10

The passage makes the dreamer the source of the dream world: in the dream state, the mind itself becomes the creator, the material, and the experiencer of the dream world. The dreamer constructs entire universes from the material of his own consciousness. Later thinkers, Gauḍapāda above all, drew a startling implication: if the mind can create a convincingly real world in dream, might not the waking world also be, in some sense, a construction of consciousness? Yājñavalkya’s own concern is narrower: dream shows that the self is “its own light”.

docs.title: 10.4.2 The Self as Creator in Dream
docs.text: svayaṃ vihatya svayaṃ nirmāya svena bhāsā svena jyotiṣā prasvapiti / atrāyaṃ puruṣaḥ svayaṃjyotir bhavati Translation: “Taking (the world) apart by himself and building it by himself, he dreams by his own radiance, by his own light. Here this person becomes his own light.” — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9

docs.title: 10.5 Suṣupti: The State of Deep Sleep
10.5.1 The Paradox of Deep Sleep
docs.text:
The state of deep sleep (suṣupti) is the hardest case for the Upaniṣadic analysis. In deep sleep:

  • There is no awareness of any object — neither external (as in waking) nor internal (as in dream)

  • There is no sense of time passing

  • There is no sense of individual identity (no “I am this” or “I am that”)

  • Yet, upon waking, one reports: “I slept well; I knew nothing”

The Upaniṣadic basis for treating deep sleep as evidence of the Self is Yājñavalkya’s statement that “when he does not see, he is still seeing, though he does not see; for there is no cessation of the seeing of the seer, because it is imperishable” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.23). Later Advaitins built on this the argument from the report “I slept well; I knew nothing”: since one can report on deep sleep, a witness must have been present even then — aware, but aware of nothing in particular. The Upaniṣads also record the opposite intuition: in the Chāndogya (8.11.1) Indra objects that in dreamless sleep one does not know oneself as “I am this” and seems to have “gone to annihilation”, and Prajāpati must lead him further.

The Kauṣītaki (3.3) gives yet another account: when a sleeping man sees no dream, he becomes one with breath (prāṇa) alone, and speech with all names, sight with all forms and the other faculties enter into it, to come forth again on waking.

docs.title: 10.5.2 Deep Sleep as the Gateway to Turīya
docs.text:
The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad calls the self in deep sleep Prājña (“the knowing one”) and describes it as “a single mass of cognition” (prajñānaghana, Mantra 5). This state is characterised by:

  1. Unity: All duality dissolves; there is no subject-object distinction

  2. Bliss: The Māṇḍūkya (5) calls Prājña “made of bliss and enjoying bliss”; later Advaita correlates this state with the ānandamaya kośa

  3. Ignorance: According to Advaita, the seed of ignorance (avidyā-bīja) persists in deep sleep, which is why one wakes again into the same limited identity

It is this last feature — the persistence of ignorance even in the midst of bliss — that, for Advaita, distinguishes deep sleep from Turīya: deep sleep resembles liberation but does not bring it.

docs.title: 10.6 Turīya: The Fourth State — Pure Awareness
10.6.1 Beyond the Three States
docs.text:
For Advaita, Turīya (“the Fourth”) is not a state alongside the other three but the witness and ground of all three states. Just as a cinema screen is the unchanging substratum upon which all images appear and disappear, Turīya is the unchanging awareness in which waking, dream, and deep sleep arise, play out, and dissolve (Figure 10.2).

Figure 10.2. Turīya as the Unchanging Substratum of the Three States

docs.title: 10.6.2 The Māṇḍūkya’s Description of Turīya
docs.text: The Māṇḍūkya (Mantra 7, quoted in full in Section 3.2) describes Turīya through a series of negations: it is not inwardly conscious (like dream), not outwardly conscious (like waking), not a mass of consciousness (like deep sleep), not conscious, not unconscious — but rather the cessation of all phenomenal appearance (prapañcopaśama), tranquil (śāntam), auspicious (śivam), non-dual (advaitam).

docs.title: 10.6.3 Turīya in Advaita Teaching
docs.text:
Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā (Section 3.2.5) draws the most radical conclusion from this analysis: if waking is like dream, and both are sublated in the Fourth, then nothing has ever truly been born (ajāti-vāda), and the appearance of birth and multiplicity is like the circle traced by a whirling firebrand. Later Advaita teachers explain the relation of the Fourth to the three states with their best-known illustration.

Turīya and the Three States: The Rope-Snake Analogy

A man sees a rope in dim light and mistakes it for a snake. The snake is not real (it has no independent existence), yet it is not entirely unreal (the man genuinely experiences fear). When the rope is seen for what it is, the snake “disappears” — not because it goes anywhere, but because it was never there. Similarly, the three states of consciousness are “appearances” in Turīya; when Turīya is recognised, the three states are seen to have been the one awareness all along, appearing under different conditions of clarity and obscuration.

Some late Yoga and Sannyāsa Upaniṣads, and texts of the Nātha tradition, describe a fifth state beyond even Turīya, called Turīyātīta (“beyond the Fourth”): the state in which even the designation “Fourth”, which implies a contrast with the other three states, is transcended, and the liberated person lives in natural spontaneity (sahaja), without effort to maintain any state of awareness. The theistic schools read the Fourth differently: Madhva, for example, took the four quarters of the Māṇḍūkya as four forms of Viṣṇu presiding over the states of the soul (Section 3.2).

docs.title: 10.7 Modern Resonances: Consciousness Studies
docs.text:
The Upaniṣadic analysis of consciousness has attracted attention from modern philosophers of mind and some researchers in consciousness studies. The comparisons below are analogies between different frameworks, not evidence that the Upaniṣads anticipated modern findings:

  1. The distinction between the content of consciousness (objects, thoughts, emotions) and consciousness itself (the “knowing” quality) parallels the modern distinction between “access consciousness” and “phenomenal consciousness.”

  2. The Vedāntic claim that consciousness is not reducible to brain activity is a metaphysical position, not an empirical finding; it is nonetheless relevant to the debate over what David Chalmers calls the “hard problem of consciousness”. Modern sleep science, for its part, shows that the sleeping brain is highly active, and debates whether any form of awareness persists in dreamless sleep — a question on which philosophers such as Evan Thompson have engaged Indian sources (Thompson 2015).

  3. Some researchers in contemplative science study reports by experienced meditators of “contentless” or “non-dual” awareness, and compare them with descriptions of Turīya. Such comparisons are suggestive, but the identification of any measured brain state with Turīya would go beyond the evidence.

In the Vedāntic reading the analysis of the four states is an argument as well as a description: it points to an invariant, self-luminous awareness underlying all states. For Advaita this awareness — Turīya — is not a state to be attained but a reality to be recognised.

docs.title: 10.8 The Phenomenology of the Three States
docs.text:
Later Vedānta compared the three ordinary states — waking (jāgrat), dream (svapna), and deep sleep (suṣupti) — feature by feature (Table 10.2). The designations Viśva, Taijasa and Prājña are Gauḍapāda’s; the Māṇḍūkya itself calls the waking self Vaiśvānara.

Table 10.2. Phenomenological Analysis of the Three States of Consciousness Feature Waking (Jāgrat) Dream (Svapna) Deep Sleep (Suṣupti) Object-type Gross external objects Subtle mental impressions No objects at all Sense-organs Active; engaged with objects Inactive; impressions are internal Inactive; completely withdrawn Mind Active; outward-directed Active; inward-directed Latent; merged in causal ignorance Ego-sense “I am this body”; strong identification with the physical “I am the dreamer”; identification with the subtle body “I know nothing”; ego is latent but not destroyed Time-experience Linear, sequential Non-linear, compressed Timeless; no experience of duration Space-experience Three-dimensional external space Private internal space No spatial experience Designation Viśva (the universal experiencer) Taijasa (the luminous one) Prājña (the knower)

docs.title: 10.8.1 The Witness in All Three States
docs.text:
Advaita argues that there must be a witness (sākṣin) that is present in all three states yet identical with none of them. The evidence it offers is threefold:

  1. Memory of transitions: Upon waking, one can say “I was dreaming” and “I slept deeply.” This memory presupposes a continuous awareness that was present during all three states and can now compare them.

  2. Unity of the experiencer: The same “I” that was awake is the same “I” that was dreaming and the same “I” that slept. If the experiencer were identical with any one state, it would cease to exist in the other states, and continuity of personal identity would be impossible.

  3. Awareness of absence: In deep sleep, one experiences “nothing,” yet this very experience of “nothing” is itself a form of awareness — the point of Yājñavalkya’s statement that the seeing of the seer never ceases (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.23).

docs.title: 10.9 Meditation on Oṃ and the Four States
docs.text:
The Māṇḍūkya (8–12) maps the four states onto the parts of the syllable Oṃ — A, U and M, and the measureless fourth (Section 3.2 and Table 3.2). In the tradition this correlation is also a practice, continuing the Praśna’s graded meditation on the measures of Oṃ (Section 2.4). With “A” awareness rests in the waking world, with “U” in the inner world of dream, with “M” in the undifferentiated ground of deep sleep, and in the silence that follows it recognises itself as Turīya. This union of doctrine and practice is one reason the Muktikā could call the Māṇḍūkya alone sufficient for liberation.

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: 11.1 Introduction: Why Commentaries?
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads invite interpretation. Their terse, often enigmatic style, their use of symbol, metaphor and paradox, and their apparent contradictions (Section 3.5) produced a commentarial literature that has continued for more than twelve centuries.

The commentarial tradition on the Upaniṣads is anchored in the Prasthānatraya — the “Triple Foundation” of Vedāntic philosophy (Figure 11.1).

Figure 11.1. The Prasthānatraya — Triple Foundation of Vedāntic Philosophy

A major ācārya (philosophical teacher) who founded a sampradāya (school of thought) was ideally expected to write commentaries (bhāṣyas) on all three of these foundations, though not all did: Śaṅkara and Madhva commented on the principal Upaniṣads, whereas Rāmānuja wrote on the Brahmasūtra and the Gītā and set out his reading of the Upaniṣads in the independent Vedārthasaṅgraha. It is through these commentaries that the diverse schools of Vedānta — Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, and others — emerged.

docs.title: 11.2 Before the Commentators: The Brahmasūtra and Early Vedānta
docs.text:
The commentaries examined in this chapter are not the first systematic readings of the Upaniṣads. Between the latest principal Upaniṣads and Śaṅkara lie several centuries of Vedāntic thought, known to us mainly through one surviving text, the Brahmasūtra, and through fragments and reports of teachers whose works are lost (Nakamura 1983; Potter 1981).

The Brahmasūtra (also called Vedāntasūtra or Śārīrakasūtra), ascribed by tradition to Bādarāyaṇa, consists of about 555 aphorisms (the count differs between commentators) in four chapters (adhyāyas) of four quarters each. Its date is uncertain. Its final form is usually placed somewhere in the first five centuries CE, and Hajime Nakamura argued for c. 400–450 CE, though the work incorporates older material (Nakamura 1983). The sūtras are too terse to be understood without a commentary: many consist of two or three words that point to an Upaniṣadic passage and a conclusion about it. The oldest commentary to survive complete is Śaṅkara’s.

The text has a clear programme:

  • The first chapter (samanvaya, “harmony”) argues that all the Upaniṣadic passages about the cause of the world refer, coherently, to Brahman. It opens with “Now, therefore, the enquiry into Brahman” (athāto brahmajijñāsā, 1.1.1), defines Brahman as “that from which the origin and so on of this world proceed” (janmādy asya yataḥ, 1.1.2), alluding to Taittirīya 3.1, and declares this established “because of harmony” (tat tu samanvayāt, 1.1.4). It then works through passages in which a word such as “space”, “breath”, “light” or “the self made of bliss” might seem to name something other than Brahman.

  • The second chapter (avirodha, “non-contradiction”) defends this conclusion against rival doctrines — above all the Sāṅkhya theory that unconscious matter is the cause of the world, but also the Vaiśeṣikas, Buddhists, Jains and Pāśupatas — and reconciles apparently conflicting Upaniṣadic statements about creation and the self.

  • The third chapter (sādhana, “means”) treats rebirth, the states of the self and the meditations (vidyās): which vidyās taught in different Upaniṣads are the same, and which may be combined (Section 4.3).

  • The fourth chapter (phala, “fruit”) describes the result: the journey of the knower by the path of the gods and the nature of liberation.

The work thus treats the Upaniṣads as a single body of doctrine, to be harmonised by rules of interpretation adapted from the Mīmāṃsā of the ritual texts.

Bādarāyaṇa was not alone. The sūtras name earlier teachers and their views. On the relation between the individual self and Brahman (1.4.20–22), Āśmarathya held that the self is neither wholly different from Brahman nor wholly identical with it; Auḍulomi, that it is different while embodied and becomes one with Brahman on liberation; and Kāśakṛtsna, that Brahman itself exists as the individual self. Others named include Jaimini, Bādari and Kārṣṇājini. Later sources add teachers whose works are lost. Bhartṛprapañca, whose views Śaṅkara attacks in his commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (later commentators supply the name), combined knowledge with ritual action and taught a doctrine of difference-in-identity (bhedābheda). Rāmānuja says that he follows an extensive commentary (vṛtti) by Bodhāyana, and he cites Ṭaṅka and Dramiḍa among his predecessors; Śaṅkara refers to Upavarṣa. Gauḍapāda’s Kārikā (Section 3.2.5) and the grammarian Bhartṛhari’s philosophy of the word (5th century) show that non-dualist positions were also in the field before Śaṅkara.

Two points follow for the reader of this volume. First, the classical commentators did not read the Upaniṣads directly but through the Brahmasūtra’s harmonising programme, which already treated the texts as one consistent revelation. Second, the earliest Vedānta of which we have reports was probably a form of difference-in-identity, and Śaṅkara’s strict non-dualism was one position among several, argued against predecessors (Nakamura 1983). The theistic schools that came after him could therefore claim older precedents than modern accounts dominated by Advaita often suggest.

docs.title: 11.3 The Three Great Ācāryas
docs.text:
Figure 11.2 introduces the three ācāryas whose readings of the Upaniṣads are examined in this chapter.

Figure 11.2. The Three Great Ācāryas of the Vedāntic Tradition

docs.title: 11.4.1 Life and Legacy
docs.text: Śaṅkara is the most influential of the Vedāntic commentators. The conventional dates 788–820 CE derive from late traditional sources; many scholars now place him earlier, around 700–750 CE (Nakamura 1983). According to the hagiographies (the Śaṅkaradigvijaya texts, composed many centuries after his death), he was born at Kālaṭi (Kalady) in Kerala, renounced the world as a boy, studied under Govindapāda (said to be a disciple of Gauḍapāda), and died young. His authentic works include commentaries on the ten principal Upaniṣads, the Brahmasūtra and the Bhagavad Gītā, and the independent Upadeśasāhasrī (Mayeda 1979); many other works traditionally ascribed to him, such as the Vivekacūḍāmaṇi, are of doubtful authenticity (Potter 1981).

docs.title: 11.4.2 Key Principles of Śaṅkara’s Upaniṣadic Interpretation
docs.text:
1. Brahman as the sole reality (brahma satyaṃ): Brahman, pure consciousness (later Advaita’s Sat-Cit-Ānanda), is the only ultimate reality. Everything else is a superimposition (adhyāsa) upon Brahman.

  2. The world as appearance (jagan mithyā): The phenomenal world is neither absolutely real (sat) nor absolutely unreal (asat); it is mithyā — an appearance that has empirical reality (vyāvahārika sattā) but no ultimate reality (pāramārthika sattā).

  3. The jīva is Brahman (jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ): The individual self is not a separate entity; it is Brahman itself, appearing as an individual due to the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of body, mind, and ego.

  4. Liberation through knowledge alone: Mokṣa is achieved not through action (karma), not through devotion alone (bhakti), but through jñāna — the direct, intuitive knowledge of one’s identity with Brahman.

  5. Adhyāsa (Superimposition): The fundamental error is adhyāsa — the mutual superimposition of the Self and the not-Self, of the subject and the object, of Ātman and anātman.

brahma satyaṃ jagan mithyā jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ Translation: “Brahman is real; the world is an appearance; the individual self is none other than Brahman.” — A popular Advaita summary attributed to Śaṅkara: Brahmajñānāvalīmālā 20; the first half also Vivekacūḍāmaṇi 20 (numbering varies); not in his major commentaries

docs.title: 11.4.3 Śaṅkara’s Method: Adhyāropa-Apavāda
docs.text:
Śaṅkara’s commentarial method is grounded in the hermeneutical technique of adhyāropa-apavāda (superimposition and subsequent negation), which he cites as a maxim of “those who know the tradition” (commentary on Gītā 13.13). This technique proceeds in two stages (Table 11.1):

  1. Adhyāropa (Superimposition): The teacher provisionally accepts the dualistic framework of common experience — the existence of the world, the reality of the individual soul, the distinction between God and soul — in order to communicate with the student at the student’s level of understanding.

  2. Apavāda (Negation): Having used this provisional framework to convey certain truths, the teacher then systematically negates the framework itself, revealing that the dualities it posited were appearances only. Brahman alone is real.

Table 11.1. Śaṅkara’s Key Hermeneutical Distinctions Distinction Sanskrit Application to Upaniṣadic Interpretation Empirical vs. Ultimate truth Vyāvahārika / Pāramārthika Creation passages describe empirical reality; identity passages describe ultimate truth Conditioned vs. Unconditioned Brahman Saguṇa / Nirguṇa Passages attributing qualities to Brahman refer to the conditioned; neti neti passages reveal the unconditioned Determination of purport Tātparya The intended teaching of every Upaniṣad is the non-dual Brahman; other topics are subsidiary. Later Advaita determines purport by six marks (ṣaḍ-liṅga): beginning and conclusion, repetition, novelty, result, eulogy, and reasoning

docs.title: 11.4.4 Three Levels of Reality
docs.text:
Śaṅkara distinguishes the empirical and the ultimate standpoints; his successors systematised this into three levels of reality (Figure 11.3).

Figure 11.3. The Three Levels of Reality in Advaita (post-Śaṅkara systematisation)

docs.title: 11.5.1 Life and Legacy
docs.text: Rāmānuja (traditionally 1017–1137 CE, a lifespan of 120 years; many scholars prefer c. 1077–1157) was born in Śrīperumbudūr, near modern Chennai, and became the most influential teacher of the Śrī Vaiṣṇava tradition, which joined Sanskrit Vedānta to the Tamil devotional poetry of the Āḻvārs (Carman 1974). His magnum opus, the Śrībhāṣya (commentary on the Brahma Sūtras), established Viśiṣṭādvaita (“qualified non-dualism”) as a major philosophical school.

docs.title: 11.5.2 Key Principles of Rāmānuja’s Interpretation
docs.text:
1. Brahman is Nārāyaṇa: The Supreme Brahman is not impersonal but is Lord Nārāyaṇa (Viṣṇu), possessed of infinite auspicious qualities (ananta-kalyāṇa-guṇas).

  2. The world is real: Unlike Śaṅkara’s mithyā, Rāmānuja affirms that the world is absolutely real — it is the body (śarīra) of Brahman.

  3. Śarīra-Śarīrī Bhāva: The relationship between Brahman and the world/souls is that of soul (śarīrī) to body (śarīra). Brahman is the inner controller (antaryāmin) of all souls and of the material world.

  4. Three real categories: God (Īśvara), individual souls (cit), and matter (acit) are all real, but the latter two are entirely dependent upon and controlled by God.

  5. Liberation through devotion: In the Śrībhāṣya the means to liberation is bhakti, understood as meditation (upāsana) in the form of loving and unbroken remembrance of the Lord, made possible by his grace; liberation consists in eternal, blissful service to Nārāyaṇa in Vaikuṇṭha. Surrender (prapatti) as an independent and sufficient means is emphasised by the later Śrīvaiṣṇava teachers (Section 11.12.4); it is taught most explicitly in the three Gadyas ascribed to Rāmānuja, whose authorship has been debated (Carman 1974).

docs.title: 11.5.3 Rāmānuja’s Reading of Tat Tvam Asi
docs.text: Rāmānuja reads Tat tvam asi not as asserting absolute identity between the individual self and Brahman, but as asserting that the individual self has Brahman as its inner Self. The asi (“art”) denotes not bare identity but the relationship of the ensouled body to its indwelling controller. The individual soul is a real “mode” (prakāra) and part (aṃśa) of Brahman, inseparable from it (apṛthaksiddhi) as an attribute is from its substance, yet never identical with it; the world of souls and matter is Brahman’s body and is wholly real (Table 11.2).

docs.title: 11.6.1 Life and Legacy
docs.text: Madhvācārya (traditionally 1238–1317 CE; some scholars prefer 1199–1278), also known as Ānanda-tīrtha or Pūrṇa-prajña, hailed from the region of Udupi in coastal Karnataka. He established Dvaita (“dualism”) as the third major school of Vedānta, in sharp opposition to Śaṅkara’s Advaita (Sharma 1962).

docs.title: 11.6.2 Key Principles of Madhva’s Interpretation
docs.text:
1. Five eternal distinctions (pañca-bheda):

    1. God and individual soul (jīva-Īśvara bheda)

    2. God and matter (jaḍa-Īśvara bheda)

    3. Individual souls and matter (jīva-jaḍa bheda)

    4. Between individual souls (jīva-jīva bheda)

    5. Between material things (jaḍa-jaḍa bheda)

  2. Viṣṇu is the Supreme Being: Lord Viṣṇu is the independent (svatantra) Supreme Being; all else is dependent (paratantra).

  3. The world is real: The material world is fully real, not an illusion.

  4. Liberation through grace and devotion: Liberation is granted by the grace of Viṣṇu to those who are devoted to Him. It consists in the eternal experience of bliss in His presence.

  5. Hierarchy of souls: Madhva posits an inherent gradation (tāratamya) among souls, with different souls having different innate capacities; uniquely in Vedānta, he holds that some souls are eternally bound in saṃsāra and some destined for eternal darkness.

Madhva reads the identity statements of the Upaniṣads in the light of these distinctions. “Tat tvam asi” is read either by dividing the preceding words so as to give “atat tvam asi” (“Thou art not That”), or with tat in the sense of “His” (“Thou art His”). Other traditions contest these readings, but they show how far a consistent doctrine of difference could take the interpretation of the same texts.

docs.title: 11.7 Comparative Analysis
docs.text:
Table 11.2 compares the three schools on key issues.

Table 11.2. Comparative Table: Three Schools of Vedānta on Key Issues Issue Advaita (Śaṅkara) Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja) Dvaita (Madhva) Nature of Brahman Nirguṇa (without attributes) Saguṇa (with infinite auspicious attributes) Saguṇa (supremely independent) Brahman-World World is mithyā (appearance) World is Brahman’s body World is real and distinct from God Brahman-Jīva Absolute identity Part-Whole (body-soul) Eternal difference Cause of bondage Avidyā (ignorance) Turning away from God Ignorance of God’s supremacy Path to Mokṣa Jñāna (knowledge) Bhakti as meditation, with grace (prapatti stressed by the later school) Bhakti & God’s grace Nature of Mokṣa Realisation of identity with Brahman Eternal service to Nārāyaṇa Eternal blissful proximity to Viṣṇu Tat tvam asi “Thou art That” (identity) “Thou hast That as thy Self” “Thou art not That” / “Thou art His”

docs.title: 11.8 Other Important Commentators
docs.text:
Beyond the three great Ācāryas, several other commentators have made significant contributions (Figure 11.4):

  • Gauḍapāda (pre-Śaṅkara): Author of the Māṇḍūkya Kārikā; teacher of Śaṅkara’s teacher Govindapāda. Proponent of ajāti-vāda.

  • Sureśvarācārya: Direct disciple of Śaṅkara; wrote the Vārttikas (sub-commentaries) on the Taittirīya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Bhāṣyas.

  • Padmapādācārya: Another direct disciple; wrote the Pañcapādikā on Śaṅkara’s Brahma Sūtra Bhāṣya.

  • Nimbārkācārya: Proponent of Dvaitādvaita (dualistic non-dualism); wrote on the Brahma Sūtras.

  • Vallabhācārya: Proponent of Śuddhādvaita (pure non-dualism); emphasised Kṛṣṇa-bhakti.

  • Bhāskara (c. 8th–9th century): Proponent of bhedābheda (difference-in-identity) and an early critic of Śaṅkara’s doctrine of māyā.

  • Raṅgarāmānuja (16th century): Wrote Viśiṣṭādvaita commentaries on the principal Upaniṣads, filling the gap left by Rāmānuja.

  • Upaniṣadbrahmayogin (18th century): Wrote Advaita commentaries on all 108 Upaniṣads of the Muktikā canon, including the Yoga and Sannyāsa Upaniṣads.

  • Vivaraṇa and Bhāmatī sub-schools: Within Advaita itself, two major sub-schools developed, offering differing interpretations of key doctrinal points.

Figure 11.4. Śaṅkara with his disciples: a popular devotional image after the painting by Raja Ravi Varma (1904) Painting: Raja Ravi Varma (died 1906), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

The commentarial tradition shows that the Upaniṣads do not carry a single message. They are varied enough to support several internally consistent interpretations, and the argument between the schools has continued for more than a thousand years.

docs.title: 11.9 The Vivaraṇa and Bhāmatī Sub-Schools of Advaita
docs.text:
Within Śaṅkara’s own Advaita tradition, two major sub-schools emerged, differing primarily on the nature and locus of avidyā (ignorance) (Table 11.3).

Table 11.3. The Vivaraṇa and Bhāmatī Sub-Schools Compared Issue Vivaraṇa (Prakāśātman) Bhāmatī (Vācaspati Miśra) Locus of avidyā Brahman is the locus of ignorance (avidyā) The individual soul (jīva) is the locus of ignorance Object of avidyā Brahman itself is concealed by avidyā Brahman is the object; the soul misperceives it Jīva’s relation to Brahman Reflection theory (pratibimba-vāda): the jīva is Brahman reflected in ignorance Delimitation theory (avaccheda-vāda): the jīva is Brahman delimited by ignorance, like space in a jar

docs.title: 11.10 Modern Western Engagement with Upaniṣadic Commentary
docs.text:
The Western engagement with the Upaniṣadic commentarial tradition has been transformative for comparative philosophy. Paul Deussen’s Die Philosophie der Upaniṣad’s (1899; English translation 1906) (Deussen 1906), Rudolf Otto’s comparison of Śaṅkara and Meister Eckhart in Mysticism East and West (German 1926, English 1932) (Otto 1932), and more recently the translations of Patrick Olivelle and Valerie Roebuck (Olivelle 1998; Roebuck 2003) have made the Upaniṣads and their interpretive traditions accessible to readers without Sanskrit.

Scholarly Note: Max Müller and the Sacred Books of the East

F. Max Müller’s translation of twelve Upaniṣads in volumes 1 (1879) and 15 (1884) of the Sacred Books of the East was a watershed in the Western reception of the Upaniṣads (Müller 1879). Translations of this generation reached many Western writers. T. S. Eliot, who had studied Sanskrit at Harvard, built the closing section of The Waste Land (1922) on the thunder’s “Da” of Bṛhadāraṇyaka 5.2 and ended it with śāntiḥ; Aldous Huxley drew on Vedānta in The Perennial Philosophy (1945); and Erwin Schrödinger, in Mind and Matter (1958), wrote that “consciousness is a singular of which the plural is unknown”, an idea he explicitly associated with the Upaniṣads. Which translations Schrödinger read is not documented, and his views were personal philosophical convictions, not conclusions of physics.

docs.title: 11.11 Other Schools of Vedānta: Nimbārka, Vallabha, and Caitanya
11.11.1 The Later Vedāntic Ācāryas
docs.text:
Beyond the three great ācāryas — Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, and Madhva — several other teachers established distinctive schools of Vedānta, each with its own reading of the Upaniṣads and its own devotional emphasis.

Nimbārkācārya (dated variously between the 7th and the 13th century; most scholars favour the 12th–13th) established the school of Dvaitādvaita (dualistic non-dualism), which holds that Brahman is simultaneously identical with and different from the world and the individual souls — just as the sun is both identical with and different from its rays. Vallabhācārya (1479–1531) established Śuddhādvaita (pure non-dualism), which rejects Śaṅkara’s concept of māyā and holds that the world is entirely real, being a direct manifestation of Brahman (specifically, Kṛṣṇa). Caitanya (1486–1534) inspired the school of Acintya-bhedābheda (inconceivable simultaneous oneness and difference), systematised by his follower Jīva Gosvāmī, which holds that the relationship between God, souls, and matter is characterised by an inconceivable combination of identity and difference (Table 11.4).

Table 11.4. The Six Major Schools of Vedānta School Founder Date (approx.) Central Thesis Advaita Śaṅkara 8th century Brahman alone is real; the world is appearance; the jīva is Brahman Viśiṣṭādvaita Rāmānuja 11th–12th century Brahman is qualified by real souls and matter, which are its body Dvaita Madhva 13th century God, souls, and matter are eternally distinct; five real differences Dvaitādvaita Nimbārka 12th–13th century Brahman is simultaneously identical with and different from souls and matter Śuddhādvaita Vallabha 15th–16th century The world is a real transformation of Brahman (Kṛṣṇa); no māyā Acintya-bhedābheda Caitanya tradition 16th century Inconceivable simultaneous oneness and difference characterises all relations

docs.title: 11.11.2 The Hermeneutical Methods of the Ācāryas
docs.text:
Each school of Vedānta developed its own methods for interpreting the Upaniṣads, drawing on the principles of textual interpretation (mīmāṃsā nyāyas) worked out for the ritual texts. All accept the Brahmasūtra’s principle of samanvaya (harmonisation): the Upaniṣadic texts must be interpreted as a coherent whole, and apparent contradictions resolved by systematic rules (Section 11.2).

Śaṅkara employs the principle that passages teaching non-duality represent the tātparya (intended meaning) of the Upaniṣads, while passages suggesting duality are contextual, preparatory, or figurative. Rāmānuja employs sāmānādhikaraṇya (co-reference): in “Tat tvam asi” two words with different connotations refer to one and the same reality, Brahman, qualified in one case as the cause of the world and in the other as the inner Self of the individual soul, which is its body. Madhva gives primacy to the many passages that state difference, reading identity-statements as expressions of similarity, dependence or the Lord’s indwelling; his concept of viṣeṣa (“distinguishing particularity”) explains how God and his attributes, though not different in substance, can still be spoken of as distinct.

docs.title: 11.12 The Upaniṣads in Tamil: Ubhaya-Vedānta
docs.text:
The commentaries discussed so far were written in Sanskrit for readers of Sanskrit. In the Tamil country two theistic traditions, the Śrīvaiṣṇava and the Śaiva Siddhānta, also possessed a scripture in Tamil, and each had to say how that scripture stood to the Upaniṣads. Their answers are easily missed when Vedānta is told only through its Sanskrit texts. The Āḻvārs and Nāyaṉmārs as poets, their temples, and the doctrines of the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta are treated in Volume 6 (Tantra–Āgama) and Volume 8 (Kāvya Kalpalatā); this section and the next ask only how these traditions read the Upaniṣads and claimed their authority (Table 11.5).

Table 11.5. Milestones in the Tamil Reception of the Upaniṣads Figure or work Date (approx.) Significance for the Upaniṣads Tēvāram of Campantar, Appar and Cuntarar 7th–8th c. Tamil Śaiva hymns that praise Śiva as the Lord of the four Vedas Nammāḻvār, Tiruvāymoḻi probably 9th c. The “Tamil Veda”, called in Sanskrit the Drāmiḍopaniṣad Nāthamuni c. 10th c. Compiles the Āḻvārs’ hymns (tradition); temple recitation Yāmuna (Āḷavantār) c. 10th–11th c. First Śrīvaiṣṇava works of Sanskrit philosophy Rāmānuja c. 1077–1157 Sanskrit exegesis of the Upaniṣads; no citation of the Tamil hymns Piḷḷāṉ, Ārāyirappaṭi 12th c. First commentary on the Tiruvāymoḻi, in Maṇipravāḷa Meykaṇṭār, Civañāṉapōtam 13th c. Founding treatise of Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta The Īṭu (Nampiḷḷai’s lectures) 13th c. The longest classical commentary on the Tiruvāymoḻi Vedānta Deśika 1268–1369 (trad.) Sanskrit summaries of the “Tamil Upaniṣad”; teacher of the Vaṭakalai Maṇavāḷa Māmuṉi 1370–1443 (trad.) Teacher of the Teṉkalai; Tamil summary of the Tiruvāymoḻi Civañāṉa Muṉivar 18th c. Tamil “great commentary” on Meykaṇṭār’s treatise

docs.title: 11.12.1 A Veda in Tamil
docs.text:
Śrīvaiṣṇavas describe their theology as ubhaya-vedānta, “the Vedānta of both”: of the Sanskrit Upaniṣads and of the Tamil hymns of the twelve Āḻvārs, gathered as the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham (“Four Thousand Sacred Compositions”). Tradition credits the collection to Nāthamuni (c. tenth century), who is said to have recovered the hymns of Nammāḻvār after they had been lost and to have set them to music for recitation in the temple. The story of the recovery belongs to hagiography, but the compilation of the canon and the institution of its temple recitation are generally placed in his time (Narayanan 1994).

At the centre of the canon stands Nammāḻvār (probably ninth century), a poet of a non-Brahmin cultivating community from Kurukūr on the Tāmira­pa­raṇi river. Tradition matches his four works to the four Vedas: the Tiruviruttam to the Ṛgveda, the Tiruvāciriyam to the Yajurveda, the Periya Tiruvantāti to the Atharvaveda, and the longest, the Tiruvāymoḻi of 1,102 verses, to the Sāmaveda, because like the Sāman it is sung. The Tiruvāymoḻi is called the “Tamil Veda” (Tamiḻ maṟai) and, in Sanskrit, the Drāmiḍopaniṣad, “the Tamil Upaniṣad”. The claim is meant in earnest. For the tradition the Tamil hymns reveal the same Lord as the Upaniṣads, and the commentators give them the reverence, the rules of recitation and the methods of interpretation that the Sanskrit Veda receives (Carman and Narayanan 1989).

Two features made the claim unusual. The poet was not a Brahmin. And the Tamil Veda, unlike the Sanskrit, could be learned and recited by Śrīvaiṣṇavas of every caste and by women. The tradition is proud of both facts. It did not, however, abolish caste: temple ritual and Vedic recitation remained in Brahmin hands, the recitation of the Prabandham was itself organised by community and office, and the commentators debated how far birth mattered among devotees (Narayanan 1994). The Tamil Veda widened access to revelation without dissolving the social order that restricted Sanskrit learning (Section 1.15).

Nāthamuni’s grandson Yāmuna, called Āḷavantār (c. tenth–eleventh century), gave the tradition its first works of Sanskrit philosophy. His Siddhitraya argues for the reality of the self and of God against Advaita, and his Āgamaprāmāṇya defends the Pāñcarātra scriptures as authoritative alongside the Veda. The Sanskrit and Tamil sides of the tradition were thus already joined before Rāmānuja.

docs.title: 11.12.2 Rāmānuja’s Upaniṣads
docs.text:
Rāmānuja himself wrote only in Sanskrit (Section 11.5). His Śrībhāṣya, his Vedārthasaṅgraha and his Gītā commentary never quote the Āḻvārs. Scholars have long remarked on this silence (Carman 1974). The likeliest explanation is that he was arguing in the wider world of Sanskrit learning, where only the Sanskrit Veda counted as evidence. The hagiographies, for their part, show him expounding the Tiruvāymoḻi to his disciples and commissioning the first commentary on it.

What his Sanskrit works do show is an Upaniṣadic canon with a different centre from Śaṅkara’s. Advaita builds on the identity statements (Chapter 5). Rāmānuja builds on the passages that describe Brahman as the inner controller of all things. Chief among them is the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.7). There Yājñavalkya tells Uddālaka Āruṇi that the one who dwells in earth, water, fire and every other thing, whom they do not know, whose body they are and who controls them from within, is “your self, the inner controller, the immortal”. Rāmānuja often cites this passage in the Mādhyandina recension. That version includes the self itself among the things whose inner controller Brahman is (yasyātmā śarīram, “whose body is the self”), where the Kāṇva text that Śaṅkara used has “consciousness” (vijñāna) at that point. Alongside the Bṛhadāraṇyaka he relies on texts that Śaṅkara did not comment on. These are the Subāla Upaniṣad, which names the inner self of all beings as “the one divine God, Nārāyaṇa”, and the Mahānārāyaṇa (Chapter 9).

On this basis the Vedārthasaṅgraha sorts the Upaniṣadic texts into three groups:

  • texts that teach difference between Brahman, souls and matter (bheda-śruti);

  • texts that teach non-difference (abheda-śruti);

  • “connecting” texts (ghaṭaka-śruti), above all the inner-controller passages, which show how the first two kinds can both be true. A body is distinct from its soul, yet it exists only as the soul’s mode.

The method reverses Advaita’s. For Śaṅkara the texts of difference are provisional (Section 11.4.3). For Rāmānuja no group of texts is set aside, because the relation of body and soul reconciles them all.

docs.title: 11.12.3 Piḷḷāṉ and the Maṇipravāḷa Commentaries
docs.text:
The first commentary on the Tiruvāymoḻi was written in the twelfth century by Rāmānuja’s cousin and disciple Tirukkurukaippirāṉ Piḷḷāṉ, by tradition at Rāmānuja’s request. It is known as the Ārāyirappaṭi, “the Six Thousand”, after its length in paṭi, units of thirty-two syllables. Four more classical commentaries followed: the Nine Thousand of Nañjīyar, the Twenty-four Thousand of Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai, the Twelve Thousand of Vādikesari Aḻakiya Maṇavāḷa Jīyar, and the Thirty-six Thousand, called the Īṭu, in which Vaṭakku Tiruvīti Piḷḷai recorded the lectures of his teacher Nampiḷḷai (Clooney 1996). All are written in Maṇipravāḷa (“pearls and coral”), a learned prose that mixes Tamil and Sanskrit freely. In it the Tamil verses are explained in Sanskrit categories and supported by quotations from the Upaniṣads, the Gītā and the Purāṇas.

Carman and Narayanan’s study of the Six Thousand shows how this worked (Carman and Narayanan 1989). Piḷḷāṉ reads the poet’s ecstasies and laments through the categories of Viśiṣṭādvaita: the Lord’s own nature (svarūpa) and his auspicious qualities; the soul as his body and as wholly his (śeṣa); and devotion and surrender as the means. The opening decad of the poem praises the Lord who pervades all things, hidden in them as life is in a body. In the commentary it becomes a Tamil statement of the body–soul doctrine of the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa.

The hardest test came with verses that sound like statements of identity. In one decad (5.6) a mother reports that her daughter, possessed by love of the Lord, speaks as though she herself had made the world and were the Lord. The commentators do not read such verses as Advaitic identity. They give two explanations. The first is that the beloved, in separation, imitates the Lord, like the cowherd women of the Purāṇas who acted out Kṛṣṇa’s deeds. The second is that whatever is the Lord’s body may be called by the Lord’s name. This is the principle by which Vedānta explains Vāmadeva’s declaration “I was Manu, I was the sun” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.10; Brahmasūtra 1.1.30). Through such readings the Tamil hymns and the Sanskrit Upaniṣads came to interpret one another. Francis Clooney has used these commentaries as a model of how a tradition reads two scriptures together (Clooney 1996).

docs.title: 11.12.4 Vedānta Deśika and the Two Schools
docs.text:
Vedānta Deśika (Veṅkaṭanātha; by traditional reckoning 1268–1369) was the most prolific of the Śrīvaiṣṇava ācāryas after Rāmānuja. He wrote in Sanskrit, Tamil, Maṇipravāḷa and Prakrit, and was poet and philosopher alike (Hopkins 2002). Two of his Sanskrit works sum up the Tiruvāymoḻi decad by decad: the Drāmiḍopaniṣat-tātparya-ratnāvalī (“Jewel-string of the Purport of the Tamil Upaniṣad”) and the shorter Drāmiḍopaniṣat-sāra. The Ratnāvalī names, for each decad, the qualities of the Lord that it celebrates. Their titles declare that the Tamil hymn is an Upaniṣad, and by setting out its purport (tātparya) in Sanskrit verse Deśika carried the claim of the Tamil Veda into the Sanskrit world. His other works include the Tattvamuktākalāpa, the polemical Śatadūṣaṇī against Advaita, and the Maṇipravāḷa Rahasyatrayasāra on the theology of surrender (prapatti). A short commentary on the Īśā Upaniṣad is also ascribed to him. For prapatti the tradition finds Upaniṣadic warrant in the Śvetāśvatara’s “desiring release, I go for refuge” (mumukṣur vai śaraṇam ahaṃ prapadye, 6.18) and in the Kaṭha’s teaching that the Self is won by the one whom it chooses (1.2.23).

After Deśika the community divided into two schools. The Vaṭakalai (“northern”) looks to Deśika. The Teṉkalai (“southern”) looks to Piḷḷai Lokācārya (traditionally 1205–1311) and Maṇavāḷa Māmuṉi (traditionally 1370–1443). Their best-known difference is summed up in two images. For the Vaṭakalai the soul is like the young monkey, which clings to its mother (markaṭa-nyāya); for the Teṉkalai it is like the kitten, which is carried by the scruff of its neck (mārjāra-nyāya). The question is whether surrender is an act the soul must perform or simply the acceptance of a grace that does everything. It is often said that the Teṉkalai gives more weight to the Tamil Prabandham and the Vaṭakalai to the Sanskrit, but both remain ubhaya-vedāntins. Māmuṉi’s Tamil Tiruvāymoḻi Nūṟṟantāti, one verse for each of the hundred decads, is the Tamil counterpart of Deśika’s Sanskrit summary.

The Śrīvaiṣṇava case matters for the history of the Upaniṣads in three ways. It shows the category “Upaniṣad” being extended to a text in another language, a counterpart to the composition of new sectarian Upaniṣads in Sanskrit (Chapter 9). It shows the Upaniṣads being read inside a liturgical life of temple recitation, not only in the study. And it shows how a theistic Vedānta could treat devotional poetry as evidence for the meaning of the Upaniṣads.

docs.title: 11.13 Śaiva Siddhānta and the Upaniṣads
docs.text:
The Tamil Śaivas faced the same question and answered it differently. Their canon, the twelve books of the Tirumuṟai, opens with the Tēvāram hymns of Campantar, Appar and Cuntarar (seventh–eighth century). These poets repeatedly praise Śiva as the Lord of the four Vedas and their six auxiliary sciences, and present themselves as champions of Vedic religion against the Jains and Buddhists. The primary scriptures of the Siddhānta’s theology, however, are the Śaiva Āgamas (Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama). The relation between Veda and Āgama is stated in a well-known verse of Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram, the tenth book of the canon. Veda and Āgama, it says, are both the true word of the Lord: the Veda is the general teaching and the Āgama the special one, and to the wise there is no difference between them. The Upaniṣads are thus accepted as revelation but read in the light of the Āgamas. This is the reverse of the Advaitin’s procedure, which measures the Āgamas by the Upaniṣads.

Meykaṇṭār’s Civañāṉapōtam (thirteenth century) and the works of his successors organise the Siddhānta around three realities: the Lord (pati), the bound soul (paśu) and the bonds (pāśa) (Dhavamony 1971). The Siddhāntins found an Upaniṣadic anchor for this scheme in the Śvetāśvatara. That Upaniṣad calls God “the lord of lords” (patiṃ patīnām, 6.7), names him Rudra, Hara and Śiva, and repeats the refrain “knowing God, one is freed from all fetters” (jñātvā devaṃ mucyate sarvapāśaiḥ; for example 1.8 and 2.15). As Section 4.6.6 noted, the Śaiva theologians read it as their own Upaniṣad.

The Siddhānta also took over the Upaniṣadic word advaita but gave it its own sense. “Not two” denies separation, not distinctness. In the school’s formula, Śiva is one with souls, other than them and together with them (oṉṟāy, vēṟāy, uṭaṉāy), as a vowel pervades the consonants it sounds with. In liberation the soul does not become Śiva. Freed from its bonds, it rests in Śiva’s bliss, inseparable from him and still a soul (Dhavamony 1971). Upaniṣadic statements of identity are read in this sense, much as Rāmānuja read them through the relation of body and soul.

In the eighteenth century Civañāṉa Muṉivar of the Tiruvāvaṭutuṟai monastery wrote a large Tamil commentary on Meykaṇṭār’s treatise. Its title, Drāviḍa Mahābhāṣya (“the Great Tamil Commentary”), deliberately matches the Sanskrit commentaries on the Brahmasūtra, and it presents the Siddhānta, in the manner of a Vedāntic bhāṣya, as the correct reading of scripture as a whole. The poet Tāyumāṉavar of the same century sang of a “harmony of Vedānta and Siddhānta” (vētānta-cittānta camaracam), an ideal that Śaiva tradition traces back to Tirumūlar. In Sanskrit, Śrīkaṇṭha’s Śaiva commentary on the Brahmasūtra, defended by Appayya Dīkṣita in the sixteenth century, offered a Śaiva Vedānta close to Rāmānuja’s (see Volume 3, Darśana Darpaṇa).

docs.title: 11.14 Regional-Language Renderings
docs.text:
Before the age of print, few people met Upaniṣadic teaching through translations of the Upaniṣads themselves. Most met it through works in their own language that taught Vedānta in new words, usually in verse and usually from the standpoint of a particular school. A few examples show the range.

  • Marathi. Jñāneśvar (thirteenth century), whose Jñāneśvarī on the Gītā is discussed in Volume 8, also wrote the Amṛtānubhava. This independent Marathi poem on non-dual experience draws, in the view of many scholars, on Śaiva thought as well as on Advaita.

  • Hindi. The Sant poets such as Kabīr spoke of a formless Lord within but rejected the authority of the Veda and of Brahmin learning, so they are a parallel to Vedānta rather than a reception of it (Volume 8). Within the Sant tradition, the Dādūpanthī poet Sundardās, who had studied Sanskrit at Banaras, set out Vedāntic doctrine systematically in Hindi verse.

  • Tamil Advaita. The Kaivalya Navanītam (“Cream of Liberation”), ascribed to Tāṇṭavarāya Cuvāmikaḷ and probably of the seventeenth century, is a Tamil verse manual of Advaita in the form of a dialogue between teacher and pupil. It became a standard text in Tamil monasteries and was among the books recommended by Ramaṇa Maharṣi (1879–1950), whose own Tamil Uḷḷatu Nāṟpatu (“Forty Verses on Reality”) is an independent composition.

  • Malayalam. Nārāyaṇa Guru (1856–1928), whose challenge to caste exclusion is discussed in Volume 24 (Samanvaya), wrote the Ātmopadeśaśatakam (“Hundred Verses of Self-Instruction”) in Malayalam and a Malayalam verse rendering of the Īśā Upaniṣad. Through him the Advaitic reading of the Upaniṣads became an argument against the caste restrictions that classical Vedānta had upheld.

  • Bengali. Rām Mohan Roy’s Bengali and English versions of several Upaniṣads (1816–19), among the earliest printed translations of the Upaniṣads into a modern Indian language and meant for a general readership, are discussed in Section 12.2 and, more fully, in Volume 24.

In the twentieth century, publishers such as the Gita Press of Gorakhpur (founded 1923) and the presses of the Ramakrishna Order issued inexpensive editions of the principal Upaniṣads. These carried Śaṅkara’s commentary and translations into Hindi, Bengali, Tamil and other languages, and they made the texts widely available for the first time. Most of these readers met the Upaniṣads through a school, most often Advaita, sometimes Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita. Here too, as throughout this volume, the reader should distinguish the texts from the readings that carried them.

Oṃ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ Śāntiḥ

docs.title: Chapter 12: Contemporary Relevance of the Upaniṣads
docs.text:
“In the whole world there is no study, except that of the originals, so beneficial and so elevating as that of the Oupnekhat. It has been the solace of my life, it will be the solace of my death!”

— Arthur Schopenhauer, Parerga und Paralipomena (1851), vol. 2, §185, as translated by F. Max Müller (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 1)

docs.title: 12.1 Introduction: A Living Tradition
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads are not only objects of historical study. They are read, chanted, studied, debated and used as guides to practice today — by traditional paṇḍits in Sanskrit pāṭhaśālās, by monastic orders and lay study groups, and by philosophers, psychologists and general readers across the world.

This chapter traces the Neo-Vedānta movement that carried Upaniṣadic ideas into the modern world; the Western reception of the Upaniṣads, from their passage to Europe through Persian and Latin to the present; the claims made about the Upaniṣads and modern physics, and why most of them should be rejected; engagements with psychology and consciousness studies; the history of academic Upaniṣadic scholarship; practices of meditation and self-enquiry; and the place of the Upaniṣads in contemporary Indian education. Throughout, the aim is to distinguish genuine historical influence and fruitful comparison from exaggerated claims of priority.

docs.title: 12.2 Neo-Vedānta: Upaniṣadic Thought in the Modern World
docs.text: The term Neo-Vedānta refers broadly to the reformulation of Upaniṣadic and Vedāntic philosophy for the modern educated reader, Indian and global. The movement emerged in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, in the context of colonial rule, Christian missionary criticism and India’s encounter with Western science and philosophy. Earlier figures such as Rām Mohan Roy (1772–1833), who translated several Upaniṣads into Bengali and English between 1816 and 1819 and founded the Brāhmo Samāj, had already presented the Upaniṣads as the basis of a rational, monotheistic Hinduism (Figure 12.1).

docs.title: 12.2.1 Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṃsa
docs.text:
Śrī Rāmakṛṣṇa Paramahaṃsa (1836–1886) was a priest at the Kālī temple at Dakṣiṇeśvar near Calcutta. According to his biographers he practised a succession of spiritual disciplines — Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, Advaita (under the monk Totāpurī) and, briefly, Islamic and Christian devotion — and concluded yata mat, tata path (“as many views, so many paths”). His followers connected this conclusion with the Ṛg-Vedic verse:

ekaṃ sad viprā bahudhā vadanti Translation: That which exists is One; the wise speak of it in many ways. — Ṛgveda 1.164.46

docs.title: 12.2.2 Svāmī Vivekānanda
docs.text:
Rāmakṛṣṇa’s foremost disciple, Svāmī Vivekānanda (1863–1902), born Narendranath Datta in Calcutta and educated in Western philosophy, carried Vedāntic ideas to an international audience. His addresses at the World’s Parliament of Religions in Chicago in September 1893 presented Advaita Vedānta as a universal philosophy grounded in the Upaniṣadic teaching that the Ātman in every being is identical with the infinite Brahman. His main emphases were:

  1. Practical Vedānta: The knowledge of the divine Ātman in all beings must express itself as service (sevā); to serve a human being is to serve God.

  2. Synthesis of the four yogas: Jñāna, bhakti, karma and rāja yoga, each suited to a different temperament.

  3. Vedānta and science: He presented Advaita as consonant with modern science and reason.

  4. Universal religion: Religion understood not as a sect but as the realisation of the divine within.

docs.title: 12.2.3 Sri Aurobindo
docs.text:
Sri Aurobindo Ghose (1872–1950) — Cambridge-educated, a revolutionary nationalist and later a yogin at Pondicherry — offered one of the most philosophically ambitious modern readings of the Upaniṣads. He held that their teaching does not negate the world but affirms it as the self-expression of Brahman, and in The Life Divine (serialised 1914–19) he combined the Īśā, Taittirīya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka with an evolutionary vision of consciousness ascending through life and mind to what he called the “supermind”, which he linked with the Taittirīya’s vijñāna.

Scholarly Note: Neo-Vedānta and its critics

Historians of Indian philosophy such as Paul Hacker and Wilhelm Halbfass have shown that Neo-Vedānta was not simply a restatement of Śaṅkara: it reworked Advaita in response to European thought, giving new prominence to experience, social service, tolerance and the harmony of religions, themes that are marginal or absent in classical Advaita (Halbfass 1995; Halbfass 1988). Recognising this does not diminish the movement; it helps readers distinguish the classical texts from their modern interpretations.

Figure 12.1. Three influential figures of Neo-Vedānta

docs.title: 12.3 Western Reception of the Upaniṣads
docs.text: The encounter between Western intellectual life and the Upaniṣads began in earnest with the Latin Oupnek’hat of 1801–02, and it shaped European philosophy, Indology and, in turn, the Indian reception of the texts (Halbfass 1988).

docs.title: 12.3.1 The Persian Route: Sirr-i Akbar and Oupnek’hat
docs.text:
Europe’s first reading of the Upaniṣads as a body of texts passed through two translations. The first was the Persian Sirr-i Akbar (“The Great Secret”), made in 1657 for the Mughal prince Dārā Shikōh (1615–1659). His life, his Sufi affiliation and his Majma’-ul-Baḥrain, which sets Sufi and Vedāntic vocabularies side by side, are treated in Volume 24 (Samanvaya) (Gandhi 2020). Here the translation is considered as a text. In his preface Dārā explains that he had looked for the meaning of God’s unity in the scriptures of the Jews and Christians and found it most fully in the Upaniṣads. He identified these with the “hidden book” of which the Qur’ān speaks (56:77–80), and so had them rendered into Persian with the help of paṇḍits and renunciants.

The collection contains about fifty texts. The principal Upaniṣads stand beside many of the shorter Atharvan Upaniṣads on yoga, renunciation and the sectarian deities, together with a few pieces that are not Upaniṣads in the usual sense. It is, in other words, a seventeenth-century North Indian Vedāntin’s corpus, not the ten or thirteen texts that modern scholarship treats as the early Upaniṣads (Section 1.6). The translation is also an interpretation. Sanskrit terms are kept and explained, explanatory glosses — many of them drawn, it appears, from commentaries in the tradition of Śaṅkara — are worked into the running text, and key ideas are rendered in the technical vocabulary of Sufism. What the Persian reader received was the Upaniṣads as Advaita read them, seen through the Sufi doctrine of the “unity of being” associated with the school of Ibn ‘Arabī.

The second translation was made from the Persian. Abraham-Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron (1731–1805) had travelled in India in the 1750s and had published the first European translation of the Zoroastrian Avesta (1771). In 1775 he received a copy of the Persian Upaniṣads through Jean-Baptiste Gentil, a French officer at the court of Awadh.
