He made a French version, which remained unpublished, and then a Latin one, printed at Strasbourg in two volumes in 1801–02 as Oupnek’hat (id est, Secretum tegendum), “the secret to be kept” (Schwab 1984). The Latin follows the Persian almost word for word. It keeps Persian syntax and many Persian and Sanskrit words in transliteration, and adds long notes in which Anquetil compares the doctrine with that of Western philosophers and theologians. The result is a Latin version of a Persian version of a Sanskrit text, doubly interpreted and often obscure.

It was nevertheless this book that made the Upaniṣads a force in European philosophy. Schopenhauer was introduced to Indian literature in Weimar by the orientalist Friedrich Majer and began reading the Oupnek’hat in 1814; it remained his preferred Upaniṣad text (Halbfass 1988). Work made directly from the Sanskrit came only gradually: William Jones’s English version of the Īśā, printed in his collected works (1799); H. T. Colebrooke’s essay “On the Vedas” in Asiatic Researches (1805), which described the Upaniṣads and translated extracts; Rām Mohan Roy’s Bengali and English versions (1816–19; Section 12.2); and the editions and translations of the mid-nineteenth century that led to Max Müller’s (Section 11.10). The early European picture of the Upaniṣads as a single mystical doctrine of unity owes something to this history: the first text Europe read had already been unified by a Vedāntic and a Sufi reading before it reached Latin.

docs.title: 12.3.2 Arthur Schopenhauer
docs.text: Of all Western philosophers, Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was the most openly indebted to the Upaniṣads. In the preface to The World as Will and Representation (1818) he named Kant, Plato and the Upaniṣads as the sources that best prepared a reader for his work, and in later writings he praised the Oupnek’hat in the terms quoted at the head of this chapter. His view of the world of experience as mere “representation” invited comparison with māyā, and he presented his ethics of compassion as agreeing with the teaching tat tvam asi. Many of his central ideas, however, were formed from Kant and Plato before he studied Indian texts closely, so the relation is one of confirmation and affinity as much as of influence.

docs.title: 12.3.3 The American Transcendentalists
docs.text:
In America, Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) and Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862) read Indian texts in translation. Emerson’s essay “The Over-Soul” (1841) shows affinities with the idea of a universal Self, and his poem “Brahma” (1857) paraphrases a verse found in both the Kaṭha Upaniṣad (1.2.19) and the Gītā (2.19): “If the red slayer think he slays…”. The Kaṭha verses behind the poem, including the preceding verse on the unborn Self that the Gītā also adapts, are quoted in Section 2.3.

Thoreau wrote in Walden (1854) that in the morning he bathed his intellect in “the stupendous and cosmogonal philosophy of the Bhagvat Geeta”; he also read the Laws of Manu and other Indian texts.

docs.title: 12.3.4 German Romanticism and Early Indology
docs.text: The German Romantics were deeply attracted to Indian thought. Friedrich Schlegel’s Über die Sprache und Weisheit der Indier (1808) celebrated Sanskrit and Indian philosophy, and Wilhelm von Humboldt devoted a celebrated academic study (1825–26) to the Gītā. Through Schopenhauer the Upaniṣads in turn influenced Paul Deussen, Friedrich Nietzsche’s friend, who became their leading nineteenth-century interpreter.

docs.title: 12.4 Physics and the Upaniṣads: Claims and Cautions
docs.text:
Popular literature since the 1970s has often claimed that modern physics, especially quantum mechanics, confirms or was anticipated by the Upaniṣads, and that the founders of quantum theory were inspired by them. Most of these claims do not survive examination.

  • Erwin Schrödinger is the one major physicist who wrote about Vedānta at length and sympathetically, in the epilogue to What Is Life? (1944), in Mind and Matter (1958) and in the essay My View of the World (written in 1925, published 1961). There he expressed the conviction that consciousness is one, an idea he associated with the Upaniṣads. These were personal metaphysical views, which he did not derive from, or present as part of, quantum theory (Moore 1989). No essay by him entitled “The Vedantic Vision” exists.

  • Werner Heisenberg’s visit to Rabindranath Tagore in 1929 is known chiefly from Fritjof Capra’s much later recollection of conversations with Heisenberg; Heisenberg’s own writings do not credit Indian philosophy with shaping his physics.

  • Niels Bohr’s interest in Eastern thought (his coat of arms bore the Chinese taiji symbol) concerned Chinese, not Upaniṣadic, ideas.

Tables that equate quantum entanglement with “all this is Brahman”, the uncertainty principle with māyā, or the quantum vacuum with pūrṇam rest on verbal resemblances between very different concepts. Physics describes measurable regularities through mathematics verified by experiment; the Upaniṣads seek knowledge of the Self through reflection, discipline and teaching. The Upaniṣads may legitimately be brought into philosophical dialogue with science — for example, on the place of consciousness in nature — but they neither anticipated nor confirm the results of modern physics.

docs.title: 12.5 Psychological Applications
docs.text: Western depth psychology, humanistic psychology and transpersonal psychology have all engaged with Upaniṣadic and other Indian concepts.

docs.title: 12.5.1 Carl Gustav Jung
docs.text: Carl Gustav Jung (1875–1961) was strongly interested in Indian thought. He wrote forewords to D. T. Suzuki’s Introduction to Zen Buddhism and to Richard Wilhelm’s I Ching, lectured on Kuṇḍalinī yoga, and engaged with the Upaniṣads partly through his friend the Indologist Heinrich Zimmer. His concept of the Self as the centre and totality of the psyche, embracing both conscious and unconscious, invites comparison with the Upaniṣadic Ātman, although Jung himself insisted that his Self was a psychological concept, not a metaphysical absolute. Likewise, the Indian notion of latent impressions (saṃskāras) can be compared with Jung’s complexes.

docs.title: 12.5.2 Abraham Maslow
docs.text: Abraham Maslow (1908–1970), a founder of humanistic psychology, described “peak experiences” — moments of unity, joy and loosening of ego-boundaries — and in his late work added self-transcendence above self-actualisation. These descriptions have often been compared with Upaniṣadic accounts of ānanda and absorption, although Maslow’s categories were drawn from empirical interviews within a Western psychological framework.

docs.title: 12.5.3 Upaniṣadic Concepts and Contemporary Practice
docs.text:
Table 12.1 lists Upaniṣadic concepts alongside the modern psychological ideas with which they are often compared.

Table 12.1. Upaniṣadic Concepts and Modern Psychological Parallels Upaniṣadic Concept Psychological Analogue Modern Framework Sākṣin (witness) Non-judgemental awareness of thoughts and emotions Metacognition; mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) Pañca-kośa (five sheaths) Multi-dimensional view of wellbeing: physical, vital, mental, intellectual, spiritual Biopsychosocial-spiritual models; integrative health Neti neti (not this, not this) Dis-identification from limiting self-concepts Cognitive defusion (ACT); psychosynthesis Avidyā (ignorance) Habitual patterns that distort perception of self and world Cognitive distortions (CBT) Viveka (discrimination) Distinguishing helpful from unhelpful mental patterns Metacognitive awareness

Modern Relevance: The Observing Self

Several psychotherapists have described a therapeutic shift of attention from transient mental states to the “observing self” that is aware of them — for example Arthur Deikman in The Observing Self (1982) and Roberto Assagioli in the “dis-identification” exercises of psychosynthesis. These approaches draw on several sources, including Indian ones, and parallel the Upaniṣadic teaching of the witness (sākṣin). The parallel is real, but the therapeutic aim (relief of suffering within ordinary life) differs from the Upaniṣadic aim of liberation, and Upaniṣadic practice should not be presented as a substitute for professional treatment.

Key Insight

Contemporary philosophy of mind continues to debate what David Chalmers calls the hard problem of consciousness: why there is subjective experience at all. The Vedāntic tradition offers an alternative starting point, treating consciousness (cit) not as a product of matter but as the ground of being — a philosophical position to be argued for, not a scientific result.

docs.title: 12.6 The Perennial Philosophy
docs.text:
The term philosophia perennis, used in the Renaissance and by Leibniz, was popularised by Aldous Huxley’s anthology The Perennial Philosophy (1945). It holds that beneath the diversity of religious traditions lies a common metaphysical core: a transcendent Reality that is also the ground of the soul, and a knowledge of it that is the highest human fulfilment. Huxley drew extensively on the Upaniṣads, the Gītā and Śaṅkara.

sarvaṃ khalv idaṃ brahma tajjalān iti śānta upāsīta Translation: “All this is Brahman. One should venerate it in tranquillity as that from which all things are born, into which they dissolve, and in which they breathe.” — Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1

Other figures associated with perennialism include René Guénon, Frithjof Schuon, Ananda Coomaraswamy (1877–1947), who wrote influential essays comparing Platonic and Vedāntic thought, and Huston Smith, whose The Religions of Man (1958; later The World’s Religions) introduced many Western readers to the Upaniṣads. Scholars of religion have criticised perennialism for underplaying real differences between traditions; the Upaniṣads themselves, as the preceding chapters show, support several quite different metaphysical systems.

docs.title: 12.7 Academic Upaniṣadic Studies
docs.text: The scholarly study of the Upaniṣads in the modern era has produced a substantial body of editions, translations and philosophical analyses.

docs.title: 12.7.1 Paul Deussen
docs.text: Paul Deussen (1845–1919), a German philosopher and friend of Friedrich Nietzsche, translated sixty Upaniṣads (Sechzig Upaniṣad’s des Veda, 1897) and wrote the first systematic philosophical study of them, Die Philosophie der Upaniṣad’s (1899; English translation 1906) (Deussen 1906). He read the Upaniṣadic doctrine of the Ātman as anticipating Kant’s transcendental idealism and Schopenhauer’s philosophy, held Advaita in very high esteem, and founded the Schopenhauer Society in 1911.

docs.title: 12.7.2 Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
docs.text: Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan (1888–1975), philosopher and later Vice-President (1952–62) and President (1962–67) of India, wrote the two-volume Indian Philosophy (1923, 1927) and The Principal Upaniṣads (1953), with Sanskrit text, translation and notes (Radhakrishnan 1923, 1953). He presented the Upaniṣads as a universal philosophy of spirit grounded in intuitive experience.

docs.title: 12.7.3 A Survey of Key Scholars and Translators
docs.text:
Table 12.2 lists some of the scholars and translators through whom the Upaniṣads reached modern readers.

docs.title: 12.8 Modern Commentators and Teachers
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads have continued to attract commentators who maintain the tradition of exposition while addressing contemporary questions.

  • Svāmī Ranganathananda (1908–2005), thirteenth President of the Ramakrishna Math and Mission, wrote The Message of the Upaniṣads (1968) and the three-volume Universal Message of the Bhagavad Gita, bringing the texts into dialogue with modern science and democratic values.

  • Svāmī Chinmayānanda (1916–1993) founded the Chinmaya Mission and gave public lecture series (jñāna-yajñas) on the Upaniṣads in India and abroad; his English commentaries made demanding texts accessible to lay readers.

  • Svāmī Dayānanda Sarasvatī (1930–2015) of the Ārṣa Vidyā tradition trained many teachers in residential courses of traditional Vedānta, insisting on careful grammatical and contextual analysis; he founded the Ārṣa Vidyā Gurukulam in Pennsylvania and in Coimbatore.

  • Sri Ramana Maharshi (1879–1950) of Tiruvannamalai taught self-enquiry (ātma-vicāra) in a direct, non-scholastic form that has reached readers worldwide.

docs.title: 12.9 The Upaniṣads and Interfaith Dialogue
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads have played a significant role in modern interfaith dialogue. At the World’s Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893, an event organised largely by liberal Christians, Vivekānanda’s Vedāntic addresses on the harmony of religions attracted great attention. Several comparisons have since been explored:

  • the Upaniṣadic Brahman and the “Godhead” (Gottheit) of the Christian mystic Meister Eckhart, compared by Rudolf Otto;

  • the Sufi concept of fanā’ (passing away in God) and the Upaniṣadic merging of the individual in Brahman — a comparison already made in the seventeenth century by Dārā Shikōh in his Majma’-ul-Baḥrain (“The Mingling of the Two Oceans”);

  • the Buddhist concept of śūnyatā and the Upaniṣadic Brahman as beyond predication — though Buddhist thinkers have generally insisted on the difference;

  • the Kabbalistic Ein Sof (the Infinite) and Brahman as beyond all attributes.

docs.title: 12.10 Practice: Meditation and Self-Enquiry
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads contain numerous vidyās — contemplative disciplines focused on aspects of Brahman, such as the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā (Chāndogya 3.14), the meditation on breath as the inner fire-offering (prāṇāgnihotra, Chāndogya 5.19–24) and the progressive enquiry through the five “selves” of the Taittirīya (see Sections 3.3 and 4.3). Teachers in several modern lineages adapt such meditations for contemporary students.

Ātma-vicāra (self-enquiry) is the meditative investigation into the nature of the self. Its Upaniṣadic antecedents include Janaka’s question “Which is the self?” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.7) and the progressive questioning of Indra by Prajāpati (Chāndogya 8.7–12). Ramana Maharshi made the question “Who am I?” the centre of his teaching: tracing the “I”-thought to its source, he taught, reveals the Ātman as pure awareness.

The modern mindfulness movement, including Jon Kabat-Zinn’s mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR), derives chiefly from Buddhist meditation rather than from the Upaniṣads. The Upaniṣadic idea of the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) nevertheless offers a close philosophical parallel to the “metacognitive awareness” that such programmes cultivate.

docs.title: 12.11 Contemporary Vedānta Centres
docs.text: The teachings of the Upaniṣads are transmitted today through a network of monasteries, study centres and educational organisations. They include the monasteries of the Śāṅkara tradition, such as the Śṛṅgerī Śāradā Pīṭham in Karnataka; the Mādhva and Śrīvaiṣṇava maṭhas of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, which teach the Upaniṣads in the Dvaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita traditions; and the modern organisations whose teachers are described above — the Ramakrishna Math and Mission with its Vedanta Societies abroad, the Chinmaya Mission, the Ārṣa Vidyā Gurukulam and the Divine Life Society of Rishikesh — which offer courses in English and Indian languages to lay students.

docs.title: 12.12 Sanskrit Learning and Digital Humanities
docs.text: Digital resources are transforming Upaniṣadic scholarship. GRETIL (Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages), the Digital Corpus of Sanskrit, the Sanskrit Library, TITUS and SARIT make Sanskrit texts, including the principal Upaniṣads and some of their commentaries, searchable online, and standard dictionaries such as Monier-Williams are freely available. Organisations such as Samskrita Bharati promote spoken Sanskrit through short residential camps, and the Central Sanskrit University and other universities provide higher education in Sanskrit.

docs.title: 12.13 NEP 2020 and Indian Knowledge Systems
docs.text:
India’s National Education Policy 2020 calls for the integration of Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS) into the curriculum from school to higher education, and an IKS Division was set up under the Ministry of Education in 2020. The Upaniṣads, as a foundation of Indian philosophy, are an obvious part of this initiative: in philosophy, education and humanities programmes, in the study of Sanskrit alongside other Indian languages, and in multidisciplinary courses that set the Upaniṣads beside psychology, ethics and the history of ideas.

Teaching the Upaniṣads well within this framework requires the same standards as any other subject: accurate texts and translations, honest dating, attention to the diversity of interpretations (Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita and others), and a frank treatment of the social context in which the texts were transmitted, including the restriction of Vedic learning by caste and gender. Claims that the Upaniṣads anticipated modern science, which are common in popular material, should be avoided.

docs.title: 12.14 The Living Guru-Śiṣya Tradition
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads are records of dialogue between teacher and student, and the guru-śiṣya paramparā remains a living vehicle of their transmission — in monastic courses, in public lecture series and, increasingly, online.

parīkṣya lokān karmacitān brāhmaṇo nirvedam āyān nāsty akṛtaḥ kṛtena tadvijñānārthaṃ sa gurum evābhigacchet samitpāṇiḥ śrotriyaṃ brahmaniṣṭham Translation: “Having examined the worlds won by action, a Brāhmaṇa should arrive at dispassion: what is not made is not won by what is made. To understand That, he should go, fuel in hand, to a teacher learned in the Veda and established in Brahman.” — Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12

The verse encapsulates the ethos of the tradition: one must see the limits of ritual action, cultivate dispassion (vairāgya) and approach a qualified teacher with humility. It also reminds us that the classical tradition addressed this instruction to a Brāhmaṇa; the opening of Upaniṣadic study to all, regardless of caste or gender, is a modern development that reformers from Rām Mohan Roy and Vivekānanda onward fought for.

docs.title: 12.15 The Upaniṣads and Ecology
docs.text:
Modern environmental thinkers have drawn on the Upaniṣadic teaching that “all this is Brahman” (Chāndogya 3.14.1). These are modern readings rather than the texts’ own concerns, but they show how the Upaniṣads continue to be put to new uses (Table 12.3).

Table 12.3. Upaniṣadic Principles and Modern Ecological Readings Upaniṣadic Principle Source Ecological Reading Seeing all beings in the Self Īśā 6–7 Intrinsic worth of every living being; biocentric rather than anthropocentric ethics The elements emerging from Brahman Taittirīya 2.1 Earth, water, fire, air and space as sacred One Being in all things Chāndogya 6.8–16 Interdependence of living beings Restraint and non-covetousness Īśā 1 “Enjoy through renunciation”; sustainable living rather than unlimited consumption

The Īśā Upaniṣad and Environmental Ethics

The opening verse of the Īśā Upaniṣad — “The Lord pervades all this, whatever moves in this moving world. By renunciation, enjoy. Do not covet the wealth of any” — has become a favourite text for Indian environmental thinkers. It can be read as combining three principles: the divine presence in all things, enjoyment through restraint rather than exploitation, and the rejection of greed. Applied to the ecological crisis, these principles are a modern extension of an ancient spiritual teaching.

docs.title: 12.16 The Future of Upaniṣadic Studies
docs.text:
Several developments promise to deepen our understanding of these texts:

  1. Philology and digital humanities: critical editions of the less-studied Upaniṣads, digitisation of manuscripts and commentaries, and computational tools for textual analysis.

  2. History: better dating of the minor and sectarian Upaniṣads and clearer understanding of their relation to Haṭha Yoga, Tantra and the bhakti movements.

  3. Comparative philosophy: sustained dialogue between Upaniṣadic thought and Western, East Asian, Islamic and African philosophical traditions.

  4. Philosophy of mind: careful engagement, free of claims of scientific anticipation, with contemporary debates about consciousness and the self.

  5. Traditional learning: the continued vitality of traditional Vedāntic teaching alongside academic study.

docs.title: 12.17 Conclusion: The Upaniṣads as Living Philosophy
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads have travelled from the ritual schools of the late Vedic period to the monasteries of the commentators, the Persian translation of a Mughal prince, the libraries of European philosophers and the lecture halls and meditation groups of the present. What sustains their relevance is that they address the deepest questions of human existence — the nature of the self, of reality and of freedom — with rigour and subtlety, and that they have repeatedly provoked new thinking in those who read them. A student who opens the Upaniṣads today joins a conversation that has continued for well over two and a half thousand years.

Key Insight

In the Vedāntic reading, the Upaniṣads teach that a single Reality underlies the world of multiplicity and is one’s own deepest Self. Whether that insight is interpreted with Advaita as identity, or with the theistic schools as an inseparable relation to God, it has been understood to dissolve the fear of death, the compulsion of ego and the violence born of ignorance. That is the main reason these ancient texts continue to be read.

docs.title: Glossary of Sanskrit Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Adhikāra Qualification or fitness of a student to receive a teaching Adhyāropa-apavāda Provisional attribution followed by negation; Śaṅkara’s method of teaching Adhyāsa Superimposition; in Advaita, the mistaking of the not-Self for the Self and vice versa Advaita “Non-duality”; the Vedānta school of Gauḍapāda and Śaṅkara Ajāti-vāda Gauḍapāda’s doctrine that nothing has ever truly originated Akṣara The imperishable; also “syllable”, especially Oṃ Āḻvār (Tamil) One of the twelve Śrīvaiṣṇava poet-saints whose hymns form the Divya Prabandham Ānanda Bliss; identified with Brahman in the Taittirīya Anātman “Not-self” (Pali anattā); the Buddhist denial of a permanent self, directed against the Upaniṣadic ātman Anekāntavāda “Many-sidedness”; the Jain doctrine that reality has many aspects, used against one-sided (ekānta) views such as strict non-duality Anirvacanīya “Indeterminable” as either real or unreal; in Advaita, the status of māyā and of the world Antaryāmin The “inner controller” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.7) Aparā vidyā Lower knowledge, including the Vedas and their auxiliaries (Muṇḍaka 1.1.5) Aparokṣa-jñāna Direct, immediate knowledge Apṛthaksiddhi “Inseparability”; in Viśiṣṭādvaita, the relation of souls and matter to Brahman, as of an attribute to its substance or a body to its soul Āraṇyaka “Forest text”; Vedic genre between the Brāhmaṇas and the Upaniṣads Āśrama Stage or way of life (student, householder, forest-dweller, renouncer) Ātman The self; the innermost Self Avidyā Ignorance; in Advaita, the root cause of bondage Bandhu A hidden “connection” or equivalence between ritual, cosmos and person, the object of Brāhmaṇa and early Upaniṣadic speculation Bhakti Devotion to a personal God Bhāṣya Commentary Bhedābheda “Difference-in-identity”; the view that the self and the world are both different from and identical with Brahman, held by Bhartṛprapañca and Bhāskara Brahman The ultimate reality, ground of the world Brahmodya A formal contest of riddles or questions on Brahman, held at a sacrifice or a royal court (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3) Brahmasūtra Bādarāyaṇa’s aphorisms systematising the Upaniṣads; one of the three foundations of Vedānta Brahmavādinī A woman who discourses on Brahman (e.g. Maitreyī) Cakra “Wheel”; a centre of the subtle body in later yoga Dakṣiṇā The fee or gift given to priests at a sacrifice, and to a teacher Devāyana The “path of the gods” after death, leading to no return Dvaita “Duality”; the Vedānta school of Madhva Ghaṭaka-śruti “Connecting text”; in Rāmānuja’s classification, a passage (such as the inner-controller texts) that reconciles the texts of difference (bheda-śruti) and of non-difference (abheda-śruti) Īśvara The Lord; a personal God Jāgrat Waking Jñāna Knowledge, especially liberating knowledge of the Self Jīva The individual, embodied self Jīvanmukti Liberation while still living Karma Action, especially ritual action; its consequences Kośa “Sheath”; one of the five layers of the self in later readings of the Taittirīya Kuṇḍalinī The coiled power at the base of the spine in Tantra and Haṭha Yoga Lakṣaṇā Secondary or indicative meaning of a word Mahāvākya “Great saying”; one of four Upaniṣadic sentences on the Self and Brahman Manana Reflection; the second stage of Vedāntic study Maṇipravāḷa “Pearls and coral”; the mixed Tamil–Sanskrit prose of the Śrīvaiṣṇava commentaries Māyā The power by which the one appears as many; in Advaita, cosmic illusion Mithyā “False”; in Advaita, the status of the world as neither real nor unreal, an appearance sublated by the knowledge of Brahman Mokṣa Liberation from the cycle of rebirth Mukhya Upaniṣad One of the principal (classical) Upaniṣads Nāḍī A channel of the subtle body Neti neti “Not this, not this”; Yājñavalkya’s negative description of the Self Nididhyāsana Sustained contemplation; the third stage of Vedāntic study Nirguṇa Without attributes (of Brahman) Oṃ The sacred syllable, analysed in the Māṇḍūkya Parā vidyā Higher knowledge, by which the imperishable is grasped Paramparā Tradition; lineage of transmission Pariṇāma Real transformation of a cause into its effect, as milk into curd; in Viśiṣṭādvaita, the world as a real transformation of Brahman’s body Pati, paśu, pāśa The Lord, the bound soul and the bonds; the three realities of Śaiva Siddhānta Pitṛyāna The “path of the fathers” after death, leading to rebirth Prājña “The knowing one”; the self in dreamless sleep, the third quarter of the Māṇḍūkya Prajñāna Consciousness, intelligence (Aitareya 3.1.3) Prāṇa Breath; vital force Prāṇāyāma Breath control Prapatti Surrender to God as the means of liberation, in Śrīvaiṣṇava theology Prasthāna-traya The “triple foundation” of Vedānta: Upaniṣads, Gītā, Brahmasūtra Saguṇa With attributes (of Brahman) Śākhā A Vedic school or recension Sākṣin The witness; consciousness that observes all states Samanvaya “Harmony”; the principle of the Brahmasūtra that all Upaniṣadic passages teach one coherent doctrine of Brahman Saṃhitā The collection of mantras forming the core of each Veda Samitpāṇi “With fuel in hand”; the posture of a pupil approaching a teacher Saṃsāra The cycle of birth, death and rebirth Saṃskāra Latent impression left by experience or action Sannyāsa Formal renunciation Śānti mantra Invocation for peace recited before Upaniṣadic study Sat Being, the existent (Chāndogya 6.2) Sat-cit-ānanda Being–consciousness–bliss; a later formula for Brahman Satkāryavāda The doctrine that the effect pre-exists in its cause (cf. Chāndogya 6.1.4) Śravaṇa Hearing the teaching; the first stage of Vedāntic study Śreyas / preyas The good and the pleasant (Kaṭha 1.2.1–2) Śruti “What is heard”; revealed scripture, the Veda Suṣupti Dreamless deep sleep Svapna Dream Taijasa “The luminous one”; the self in dream, the second quarter of the Māṇḍūkya Tāratamya “Gradation”; Madhva’s doctrine of an inherent hierarchy among souls Tat tvam asi “That thou art” (Chāndogya 6.8–16) Turīya “The fourth”; the Self beyond waking, dream and deep sleep Ubhaya-vedānta “The Vedānta of both”; the Śrīvaiṣṇava joining of the Sanskrit Upaniṣads and the Tamil hymns of the Āḻvārs Upādhi A limiting adjunct; in Advaita, a condition such as the body or mind through which the one self appears limited and many Upāsanā Meditation or worship, often on a symbol of Brahman Vaiśvānara “Common to all men”; the self in the waking state, the first quarter of the Māṇḍūkya (Gauḍapāda’s Viśva) Vaṃśa A list of teachers in a line of transmission, closing sections of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Vidyā Knowledge; also a specific Upaniṣadic meditation Viśiṣṭādvaita “Non-duality of the qualified”; the Vedānta school of Rāmānuja Vivarta Apparent transformation; in Advaita, the world as an appearance of Brahman that leaves Brahman unchanged, as a rope appears as a snake Viveka Discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal
